87647.q: How do you often write a multi-line explanation in Python, for example at the start of a function?
a: With three quotation marks at the start and end
With a # at the end of each line
87647.e: Text like this is called a docstring. It goes between three quotation marks and may run over several lines.
87647.m: Docstrings go between three quotation marks.

87648.e: Here the # is inside a string. There it is a completely normal character and does not start a comment.
87648.m: Inside quotation marks the hash sign is not a comment.

87838.q: What is kept in a blood bank?
87838.e: Donated blood is stored in a blood bank. From there it goes to hospitals when patients need blood.
87838.m: A blood bank stores donated blood.

87839.q: What is donated blood kept in?
87839.e: Donated blood goes into special, clean plastic bags. They are called blood bags.
87839.m: Donated blood is stored in plastic bags.

87840.q: What is a bag of donated blood called?
87840.e: A bag of donated blood is called a blood bag. It is labelled very carefully.
87840.m: A bag of donor blood is called a blood bag.

87841.q: Where are bags of donated blood stored?
a: In a wooden cupboard in the corridor
87841.e: Donated blood is stored cold. That way it keeps for a few weeks.

87842.q: What must match between the blood of the donor and the person receiving it?
87842.e: Donor blood must match the blood group of the person receiving it. Otherwise it can be dangerous.
87842.m: For a blood transfusion the blood group must match.

87843.q: Which four blood groups are there in the best-known blood group system?
87843.e: In the ABO system there are the blood groups A, B, AB and O. The blood group is written on every blood bag.
87843.m: The four blood groups are A, B, AB and O.

87844.q: Why are new blood donations needed again and again?
a: Blood does not keep for ever
Blood can be made in factories
87844.e: Blood bags only keep for a limited time. That is why the blood bank constantly needs fresh donor blood.
87844.m: Blood banks constantly need new donations.

87845.q: What is it called when a patient in hospital is given blood from a bag?
87845.e: In a blood transfusion, donor blood flows through a tube into a vein. This helps, for example, after a lot of blood has been lost.
87845.m: In a blood transfusion you are given donor blood.

87846.q: Where is blood usually taken for a blood test?
a: From the inside of the elbow
From the top of the ear
87846.e: On the inside of the elbow there are easy-to-see veins just under the skin. Blood can be taken there easily.
87846.m: Blood is usually taken from the inside of the elbow.

87847.q: What is used to take blood from a vein for a blood test?
87847.e: A fine needle is put into the vein. The blood then flows into a small tube.
87847.m: A blood test needs a fine needle.

87848.q: What is often tied around the upper arm before blood is taken?
87848.e: The tourniquet briefly holds back the blood in the veins. Then they stand out more and are easier to find.
87848.m: A tourniquet makes the veins easier to see.

87849.q: Where is a blood sample examined closely?
87849.e: In the laboratory, experts test the blood with machines. That way you find out, for example, whether there is enough iron.
87849.m: Blood samples are examined in the laboratory.

87850.q: Where do you often prick for a single drop of blood?
87850.e: For a little blood, a small prick in the fingertip is enough. This is how blood sugar is measured, for example.
87850.m: For a drop of blood you prick the fingertip.

87851.q: What do you do at the spot where the needle went in after blood has been taken?
a: Press on it and put on a plaster
Have a hot bath straight away
87851.e: If you press on the spot for a moment, it soon stops bleeding. A plaster then protects the tiny wound.
87851.m: After blood has been taken, press on the spot and put on a plaster.

87852.q: What does it mean if you have to come to a blood test “fasting”?
a: Sleep for a long time beforehand
87852.e: Fasting means that you have not eaten anything for a while beforehand. Otherwise some blood values can come out wrong.
87852.m: Fasting means you have eaten nothing beforehand.

87853.q: Which kind of blood vessel is the needle put into when blood is taken from the arm?
87853.e: For blood samples, blood is almost always taken from a vein. In the arm, veins lie under the skin where they are easy to reach.
87853.m: When blood is taken, the needle goes into a vein.

87854.q: From what age can you give blood in Switzerland?
87854.e: In Switzerland you can give blood from the age of 18. Children cannot give blood yet.
87854.m: In Switzerland you can give blood from the age of 18.

87855.q: Roughly how much blood do you give in a blood donation in Switzerland?
87855.e: About 450 millilitres of blood are taken in a donation. That is a little less than half a litre.
87855.m: In a blood donation you give just under half a litre of blood.

87856.q: How much must you weigh at least to be allowed to give blood in Switzerland?
87856.e: Anyone who wants to give blood must weigh at least 50 kilograms. Lighter people have less blood in their bodies.
87856.m: Blood donors weigh at least 50 kilograms.

87857.q: Who does a blood donation help?
a: People who are ill or injured
87857.e: Donated blood is given, for example, to people after an accident or during an operation. It can save lives.
87857.m: A blood donation can save lives.

87858.q: Roughly how long does taking the blood itself last during a donation?
87858.e: The blood flows into the bag in about 10 to 15 minutes. With the questionnaire and resting afterwards, the visit takes a bit longer.
87858.m: Taking the blood during a donation only lasts a few minutes.

87859.q: Can you give blood every week?
a: No, only a few times a year
Yes, as often as you like
87859.e: After a donation the body has to make new blood. That is why you can only give blood a few times a year.
87859.m: You only give blood a few times a year.

87860.q: Why do you have to wait a long time between two blood donations?
a: The body has to make new blood
The blood has to get cold first
The needle has to grow back
87860.e: After a donation the body is missing some blood. It needs a few weeks to replace it.
87860.m: The body needs time between two blood donations.

87861.q: What should you make sure to do after giving blood?
87861.e: After a donation, drinking plenty helps the body replace the lost fluid. You should also rest for a short while.
87861.m: After giving blood you should drink plenty.

87862.q: Do you get money for giving blood in Switzerland?
87862.e: In Switzerland people give blood voluntarily and without pay. Often there is a small snack afterwards, though.
87862.m: Blood is given voluntarily and without pay.

87863.q: What do you fill in before giving blood?
87863.e: The questionnaire checks whether the donation is safe for the donor and the person receiving it. A short talk follows.
87863.m: Before giving blood you fill in a health questionnaire.

87864.q: Who has more blood in their body?
87864.e: How much blood a person has depends on their body weight. An adult is heavier and so has more blood.

87865.q: What mainly decides how much blood a person has?
87865.e: Blood makes up about 7 to 8 per cent of body weight. That is why heavier people have more blood.
87865.m: The amount of blood depends on body weight.

87866.q: Roughly how much blood does a newborn baby have?
87866.e: A newborn baby weighs about 3.5 kilograms and has about 300 millilitres of blood. That is about a large glassful.
87866.m: A newborn baby has about a glassful of blood.

87867.q: Which part of the blood is liquid and yellowish?
87867.e: If you remove the blood cells, a yellowish liquid is left. That is blood plasma.
87867.m: Blood plasma is the liquid, yellowish part of the blood.

87868.q: What is blood plasma mostly made of?
87868.e: Blood plasma is about 90 per cent water. Nutrients and other substances are dissolved in it.

87869.q: Why is it dangerous to lose a lot of blood?
a: The organs get too little oxygen
Your hair falls out at once
87869.e: Blood carries oxygen to all the organs. If a lot of blood is missing, they get too little of it.
87869.m: Losing a lot of blood is life-threatening.

87870.q: Does the body keep making new blood?
87870.e: The body constantly replaces old blood cells with new ones. This happens every day in the bone marrow.
87870.m: The body makes new blood every day.

87871.q: How much blood do you lose from a small prick in your finger?
87871.e: A small prick only lets out a few drops. That is no problem for the body.
87871.m: A small prick only costs a few drops of blood.

87872.e: Disinfectants kill bacteria and other germs. That way a wound is less likely to become infected.

87873.q: What do you often feel when disinfectant gets on an open wound?
a: It tickles for a long time
87873.e: Many disinfectants sting for a moment on open skin. But the stinging soon passes.
87873.m: Disinfectant can sting on a wound for a moment.

87874.q: Where do people disinfect their hands especially often?
87874.e: In hospital there are sick people who must be protected from germs. That is why hands are disinfected often there.
87874.m: In hospital, hands are disinfected especially often.

87875.q: Which substance is often in hand sanitiser?
87875.e: Many hand sanitisers contain a lot of alcohol. The alcohol kills germs on the skin.

87876.e: Disinfectant is only meant for skin or objects. If you drink it, it is poisonous and very dangerous.

87877.q: What should you keep disinfectant away from?
87877.e: Disinfectant can badly irritate the eyes. That is why you take care when using it.
87877.m: Disinfectant must not get into your eyes.

87878.q: Why does freshly applied hand sanitiser soon smell less strong?
87878.e: Alcohol evaporates very quickly in the air. That is why your hands are soon dry again.
87878.m: The alcohol in disinfectant evaporates quickly.

87879.q: What is better for small wounds than hand sanitiser?
87879.e: There are special disinfectants for wounds that are gentle on the skin. Cleaning products never belong on a wound.
87879.m: Wounds need a special wound disinfectant.

87880.q: What gives blood its red colour?
87880.e: Red blood cells contain a red pigment. Because there are so many of them, blood looks red.
87880.m: Red blood cells make blood red.

87881.q: Which blood cells are there most of in the blood?
87881.e: Red blood cells are by far the most numerous. There are many more of them than white blood cells.
87881.m: Red blood cells are the most common blood cells.

87882.q: What shape is a red blood cell?
87882.e: Red blood cells are round, flat discs that are dented in the middle. This helps them slide through narrow blood vessels.
87882.m: Red blood cells are small, round discs.

87883.q: How does someone who has too few red blood cells often feel?
87883.e: With too few red blood cells, less oxygen gets around the body. You are then often tired, weak and pale.
87883.m: Too few red blood cells make you tired.

87884.q: Roughly how long does a red blood cell live?
87884.e: A red blood cell lives about 120 days, which is about four months. Then it is broken down and replaced by a new one.
87884.m: A red blood cell lives about four months.

87885.q: Which substance from food does the body especially need to make red blood cells?
87885.e: The red blood pigment needs iron. Iron is found, for example, in meat, pulses and wholegrain foods.
87885.m: The body needs iron for red blood cells.

87886.q: Can you see a single red blood cell with the naked eye?
a: Yes, it is as big as a grain of rice
Yes, it is as big as a pea
Yes, but only in the dark
87886.e: Red blood cells are tiny. You can only see them under a microscope.
87886.m: You can only see red blood cells with a microscope.

87887.q: What does the blood carry from the body's cells back to the lungs?
87887.e: On the way back, the blood takes carbon dioxide with it. We breathe it out through the lungs.
87887.m: Blood carries carbon dioxide back to the lungs.

87888.q: What often happens to the number of white blood cells when you have an inflammation?
87888.e: During an inflammation the body makes more white blood cells. That way it can fight the germs better.
87888.m: With an inflammation you often have more white blood cells.

87889.q: What do some white blood cells, called scavenger cells, do with bacteria?
a: They take them to the lungs
87889.e: Scavenger cells surround bacteria and digest them. That way they make the invaders harmless.

87890.q: What is pus in an infected wound largely made of?
87890.e: Pus contains lots of white blood cells that have fought germs. There are also remains of germs and tissue.
87890.m: Pus contains lots of white blood cells.

87891.q: What are white blood cells sometimes called because they defend the body?
87891.e: White blood cells look for invaders and make them harmless. That is why they are compared to a police force.
87891.m: White blood cells are like the body's police.

87892.q: Can white blood cells leave the blood vessels?
a: Yes, they move into the tissue
87892.e: White blood cells can squeeze through the walls of tiny blood vessels. That way they reach the site of an inflammation.
87892.m: White blood cells can move into the tissue.

87893.q: Which system of the body do white blood cells belong to?
87893.e: White blood cells belong to the immune system. It protects us from germs that cause disease.
87893.m: White blood cells belong to the immune system.

87894.q: Are white blood cells really snow-white?
87894.e: White blood cells have no red pigment and are almost colourless. The name comes from the fact that they look pale compared with the red ones.
87894.m: White blood cells are actually almost colourless.

87895.q: Which invaders do white blood cells fight, for example?
87895.e: White blood cells attack bacteria, viruses and other germs. That is how we get well again.
87895.m: White blood cells fight bacteria and viruses.

87896.q: How should you best hold your head when you have a nosebleed?
87896.e: If you tilt your head slightly forward, the blood runs out of your nose and not down your throat. That way you don't swallow any blood.
87896.m: With a nosebleed, tilt your head slightly forward.

87897.q: Why shouldn't you tip your head back when you have a nosebleed?
a: The blood runs down your throat
87897.e: If your head is tipped back, the blood flows into your throat and is swallowed. That can make you feel sick.
87897.m: Blood in the throat can make you feel sick.

87898.q: What do you gently squeeze together when you have a nosebleed?
a: The soft sides of the nose
87898.e: Squeezing the soft sides of the nose presses the small blood vessels shut. That way the bleeding stops sooner.
87898.m: With a nosebleed, squeeze the soft part of your nose.

87899.q: What can you also put on the back of your neck when you have a nosebleed?
87899.e: Cold on the back of the neck can help the blood vessels narrow. Then it often bleeds less.
87899.m: A cool cloth on the neck can help with a nosebleed.

87900.e: Picking your nose can damage tiny blood vessels at the front of the nose. Then it starts to bleed.
87900.m: Picking your nose can make it bleed.

87901.q: Which kind of air in a room can dry out the nose and make nosebleeds more likely?
a: Very dry air from the heating
87901.e: In winter the air from the heating is often very dry. The skin inside the nose then becomes brittle and bleeds more easily.
87901.m: Dry air makes the nose sensitive.

87902.q: When should you see a doctor about a nosebleed?
a: When it doesn't stop for a long time
87902.e: Most nosebleeds stop by themselves after a few minutes. But if it bleeds for a very long time or very heavily, a doctor is needed.
87902.m: A heavy or long nosebleed needs a doctor.

87903.q: Are nosebleeds in children usually dangerous?
87903.e: Nosebleeds are common in children and usually harmless. The tiny vessels at the front of the nose are easily damaged.
87903.m: Nosebleeds in children are usually harmless.

87904.q: Roughly how long do you squeeze your nose during a nosebleed?
87904.e: You squeeze the soft part of the nose for about 10 minutes without a break. That gives the wound time to close.
87904.m: With a nosebleed you squeeze your nose for about 10 minutes.

87905.q: Which Swiss man founded the Red Cross movement?
87905.e: Henry Dunant had the idea of helping soldiers wounded in war. This led to the Red Cross.
87905.m: Henry Dunant founded the Red Cross.

87906.q: Which Swiss city did Henry Dunant come from?
87906.e: Henry Dunant was born in Geneva in 1828. The Red Cross was also founded in Geneva.

87907.q: Which symbol do many countries use instead of the Red Cross?
87907.e: In many countries the aid organisation is called the Red Crescent. It has the same tasks as the Red Cross.
87907.m: Many countries have the Red Crescent.

87908.q: Which famous prize did Henry Dunant receive in 1901?
87908.e: In 1901 Henry Dunant received the very first Nobel Peace Prize. He shared it with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy.
87908.m: Henry Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize.

87909.q: Who did the Red Cross mainly help at the beginning?
87909.e: After a battle, Henry Dunant saw many wounded soldiers with no help. So he wanted to found an aid organisation.
87909.m: The Red Cross first helped wounded soldiers.

87910.q: What is the short name of Switzerland's Red Cross organisation?
87910.e: SRK stands for Schweizerisches Rotes Kreuz, the Swiss Red Cross. Among other things, it runs courses and helps people in need.
87910.m: The Swiss Red Cross is called SRK for short.

87911.q: On which day is World Red Cross Day?
87911.e: World Red Cross Day is on 8 May. Henry Dunant was born on this day in 1828.
87911.m: World Red Cross Day is on 8 May.

87912.q: What do you first rinse a small, dirty cut with?
87912.e: Clean water rinses dirt out of the wound. Then you can disinfect it and put a dressing on it.
87912.m: Rinse a dirty wound with clean water.

87913.q: What do you do if a cut is bleeding heavily?
a: Press on it with a clean cloth
87913.e: Pressing on the wound slows the bleeding. If it is bleeding heavily, you also get help straight away.
87913.m: Press on a bleeding wound with a clean cloth.

87914.q: What is the safest way to clear up broken glass?
a: With a wet cloth and no gloves
87914.e: Broken glass is very sharp and easily cuts the skin. That is why you sweep it up with a brush and dustpan.
87914.m: Clear up broken glass with a brush and dustpan.

87915.q: What does a doctor often do with a deep, gaping cut?
87915.e: Deep wounds with wide-open edges are often stitched or glued. That way the edges grow back together well.

87916.q: What is the safest way to cut with a knife?
87916.e: If you cut away from your body, the knife won't hit you if it slips. This protects you from cuts.
87916.m: Always cut away from your body with a knife.

87917.q: Which dangerous disease does a vaccination protect against that matters with dirty wounds?
87917.e: The germ that causes tetanus can get into a wound with soil. The vaccination protects against it.
87917.m: The tetanus vaccination protects you when wounds are dirty.

87918.q: How can you tell that a cut has become infected?
a: It turns red, hot and swollen
87918.e: An infected wound is red, warm, swollen and painful. Then you should show it to a doctor or nurse.
87918.m: An infected wound is red, warm and swollen.

87919.q: What belongs in every home first aid kit for small cuts?
87919.e: Plasters and bandages are good for treating small wounds. That is why they belong in every first aid kit.
87919.m: Plasters and bandages belong in the first aid kit.

87920.q: What does a scab on a wound form from?
87920.e: The blood in the wound becomes solid and dries. That makes a hard crust, the scab.
87920.m: A scab is dried blood on a wound.

87921.q: What job does a scab do?
87921.e: The scab covers the wound like a lid. That way less dirt gets in.
87921.m: A scab protects the wound like a lid.

87922.q: What is the best thing to do with a scab?
87922.e: If you pick off the scab, the wound can bleed again. Then it heals more slowly and a scar may be left.
87922.m: Leave a scab alone until it falls off.

87923.q: What grows under the scab while the wound heals?
87923.e: Under the crust the body makes new skin. When it is finished, the scab falls off by itself.
87923.m: New skin grows under the scab.

87924.q: What colour is a scab usually?
87924.e: A scab is made of dried blood. That is why it is dark red or brownish.
87924.m: A scab is usually dark red or brown.

87925.q: What finally happens to the scab when the wound has healed?
87925.e: When the new skin is finished, the protection is no longer needed. The scab then comes off by itself.
87925.m: A scab falls off when the wound has healed.

87926.q: What can be left if you keep picking off a scab?
87926.e: Picking it hurts the wound again and again. Then a scar can be left behind.
87926.m: A picked scab can leave a scar.

87928.q: What is the scientific word for platelets?
87928.e: The scientific word for platelets is thrombocytes. They help bleeding to stop.

87929.q: What do platelets do when you hurt yourself?
87929.e: Platelets rush to the wound and stick together there. That way they close the hole in the blood vessel.

87930.q: Which blood cells are the smallest?
a: They are all the same size
87930.e: Platelets are even smaller than red blood cells. They are tiny plates without a nucleus.
87930.m: Platelets are the smallest blood cells.

87931.e: Like the other blood cells, platelets are made in the bone marrow. From there they pass into the blood.
87931.m: Platelets are made in the bone marrow.

87932.q: What is it called when blood becomes solid at a wound?
87932.e: In blood clotting, liquid blood becomes solid at the wound. Platelets play an important part in this.
87932.m: In blood clotting, blood becomes solid at the wound.

87933.q: What happens if someone has too few platelets?
87933.e: Without enough platelets, bleeding is slower to stop. These people also bruise more easily.
87933.m: Few platelets mean you bleed more easily.

87934.q: Does a platelet live longer or shorter than a red blood cell?
87934.e: A platelet only lives for about a week. A red blood cell, on the other hand, lives about four months.
87934.m: Platelets only live for about a week.

87935.q: What forms when lots of platelets stick together at a wound?
87935.e: The platelets stick together and form a small plug. It blocks the damaged blood vessel like a cork.
87935.m: Platelets form a plug at a wound.

88131.q: Which two elements is quartz made of?
88131.e: Quartz is made of silicon and oxygen, chemically SiO2. After oxygen, silicon is the most common element in the Earth’s crust.
88131.m: Quartz is made of silicon and oxygen.

88132.q: What is the purple variety of quartz called?
88132.e: Amethyst is quartz coloured purple by traces of iron and natural radiation. It is often used as a gemstone.

88133.q: What is the yellow variety of quartz called?
88133.e: Citrine is yellow to golden-brown quartz. Its name comes from the Latin word for lemon.

88134.q: What is the brown to almost black quartz that crystal hunters often find in the Swiss Alps called?
88134.e: Smoky quartz gets its colour from natural radioactive radiation in the rock. In the Alps it is a common find, along with clear quartz.
88134.m: Smoky quartz is brown quartz from the Alps.

88135.q: Why is there a small quartz crystal in many watches?
a: It stores a lot of electricity
88135.e: When an electric voltage is applied, a quartz crystal vibrates at a very precise rate. The watch counts these vibrations and so measures time.
88135.m: A vibrating quartz crystal keeps the beat in a quartz watch.

88136.q: Which mineral is pale sand on beaches and in rivers usually mostly made of?
88136.e: Quartz is hard and is hardly dissolved by water. So it is left over when other minerals have long since weathered away.
88136.m: Pale sand is usually made of grains of quartz.

88137.q: Because quartz has no cleavage, what does a broken surface of quartz look like?
88137.e: Quartz does not break along smooth planes but with curved, glassy surfaces. This kind of break is called conchoidal, like in glass.
88137.m: Quartz breaks with curved surfaces like glass.

88138.q: Which group of minerals is the most common in the Earth’s crust?
88138.e: Feldspars occur in a great many rocks, for example in gneiss, basalt and sandstone. They make up a large part of the Earth’s crust.
88138.m: Feldspars are the most common minerals in the Earth’s crust.

88139.q: What does the Mohs scale, on which feldspar also appears, measure?
88139.e: On the Mohs scale from 1 to 10, a harder mineral scratches a softer one. Feldspar has a hardness of 6.
88139.m: The Mohs scale compares the hardness of minerals.

88140.q: For which product is weathered feldspar an important raw material?
88140.e: Over a long time, water breaks feldspar down into a white clay called kaolin. It is a main ingredient of porcelain.
88140.m: Weathered feldspar gives a raw material for porcelain.

88141.q: What is feldspar mainly used for in industry?
88141.e: Feldspar melts when fired and binds the other ingredients together. That is why it is important for ceramics, tiles and glass.
88141.m: Feldspar is an important raw material for ceramics and glass.

88142.q: Which bluish shimmering gemstone is a feldspar?
88142.e: Moonstone is a feldspar with fine layers inside. They scatter the light and create a milky, bluish shimmer.

88143.q: What does the word part “spar” in the name feldspar mean?
88143.e: Miners used to call minerals that split easily along smooth surfaces “spar”. Feldspar has two such directions of splitting.
88143.m: Spar is an old word for minerals that split easily.

88144.q: What gives some granites a reddish colour?
88144.e: Granite is made of feldspar, quartz and mica. If the feldspar is pink, the whole rock looks reddish.
88144.m: Pink feldspar makes some granite reddish.

88145.q: How does the colourful sheen of some feldspars such as labradorite come about?
a: Light is reflected by fine layers in the crystal
They glow in the dark by themselves
88145.e: Labradorite contains fine layers. Light is reflected by them and overlaps, creating a metallic blue to green play of colours.
88145.m: Labradorite shimmers because light is reflected by fine layers.

88146.e: Mica has perfect cleavage in one direction. It can be split into flakes that are thinner than paper and bendy.
88146.m: Mica can be split into wafer-thin flakes.

88147.q: What does light-coloured mica look like in rock?
88147.e: Light-coloured mica is called muscovite. It shines silvery and is see-through in thin flakes.

88148.q: Why is the mica called biotite dark?
a: It contains a lot of iron
88148.e: Biotite contains a lot of iron and magnesium, so it is blackish brown. It is named after the French physicist Jean-Baptiste Biot.
88148.m: Biotite is the dark, iron-rich mica.

88149.q: What were large sheets of mica used for in Russia in the past?
88149.e: Large, see-through sheets of mica used to replace expensive glass in windows. That is where the name muscovite comes from, after “Muscovy glass”.
88149.m: In Russia, mica used to be used as window glass.

88150.q: Why is mica used in electrical engineering?
a: It insulates and can withstand heat
88150.e: Mica does not conduct electricity and can cope with high temperatures. So it is used as insulation, for example in toasters and hair dryers.
88150.m: Mica is a heat-resistant electrical insulator.

88151.q: Which group of rocks does glittering mica schist belong to?
88151.e: Mica schist forms when claystones are changed under pressure and heat. The lined-up mica flakes make it glitter.
88151.m: Mica schist is a changed, metamorphic rock.

88152.q: Why does mica split so easily?
a: It is built of flat layers that are only weakly joined
88152.e: In micas, the building blocks are joined into flat layers. Between the layers the bond is weak, which is why mica splits so well.
88152.m: Mica is built in layers and so splits well.

88153.q: Which mineral gives many cosmetics a glittering pearly shine?
88153.e: Finely ground mica reflects light from its smooth flakes. In eyeshadow and lipstick it is often listed as “mica” on the packaging.

88154.q: Calcite is the main mineral in which substance that also builds up in a kettle?
88154.e: Calcite is made of calcium carbonate, which is lime. Hard water leaves this white coating in the kettle.

a: You can scratch it with a knife
You can shape it like modelling clay
88155.e: Calcite is a rather soft mineral. You can easily scratch it with a pocket knife.
88155.m: Calcite is soft enough to be scratched by a knife.

88156.q: What happens if you put a drop of dilute hydrochloric acid on calcite?
88156.e: The acid breaks down the calcium carbonate, and carbon dioxide escapes in bubbles. Geologists use this test to recognise limestones.

88157.q: What do you see if you look at writing through a clear calcite crystal?
88157.e: Clear calcite splits a beam of light into two beams. This double refraction is especially clear in “Iceland spar”.

88158.q: Which mineral are limestone and marble mainly made of?
88158.e: Limestone often forms from the shells of sea creatures, and marble from changed limestone. Both are made mainly of the same mineral.
88158.m: Limestone and marble are mainly made of calcite.

88159.q: What are dripstones in caves such as the Hölloch in the Muota valley usually made of?
88159.e: Rainwater dissolves lime in the rock. When it drips down in the cave, the dissolved mineral comes out again and builds dripstones.
88159.m: Dripstones are usually made of calcite.

88160.q: What shape does calcite break into when it splits?
88160.e: Calcite splits in three directions that are not at right angles to each other. This creates pieces shaped like slanted cubes, called rhombohedra.
88160.m: Calcite splits into rhombohedra, or slanted cubes.

88161.q: What do mussels and snails build their shells from?
88161.e: Mussels and snails build their shells from calcium carbonate, which is lime. Shimmering mother-of-pearl is made of it too.

88162.q: Which elements is pyrite made of?
88162.e: Pyrite is an iron sulphide with the formula FeS2. It is the most common sulphide mineral.
88162.m: Pyrite is made of iron and sulphur.

88163.q: Why is pyrite also called “fool’s gold”?
a: It shines like gold but is not gold
It is more valuable than gold
It is only found on jesters’ caps
88163.e: Pyrite has a brassy yellow metallic shine. Inexperienced gold seekers therefore often mistook it for gold.
88163.m: Pyrite shines like gold but is not gold.

88164.q: Where does pyrite get its name from?
a: From the Greek word for fire
From the Latin word for gold
From the person who discovered it
88164.e: If you strike pyrite against steel or stone, sparks fly. That is why the Greeks named it after the word “pyr”, meaning fire.
88164.m: Pyrite is named after the Greek word for fire.

88165.q: In what shape do pyrite crystals very often grow?
88165.e: Pyrite often forms shiny cubes that look polished. There are also crystals with twelve five-sided faces.

88166.q: What streak colour does pyrite leave on an unglazed porcelain plate?
88166.e: Gold leaves a golden-yellow streak, but pyrite leaves a greenish-black one. So the two are easy to tell apart.
88166.m: Pyrite leaves a black streak, gold a yellow one.

88167.q: What do you find if you try to scratch pyrite and gold with a steel needle?
a: Pyrite is much harder than gold
Gold is much harder than pyrite
88167.e: Pyrite has a Mohs hardness of 6 to 6.5, gold only about 2.5 to 3. Gold is easy to scratch and bend; pyrite is not.
88167.m: Pyrite is much harder than real gold.

88168.q: Why do pieces of pyrite in collections sometimes crumble to powder?
88168.e: Pyrite slowly reacts with oxygen and moisture in the air. This produces acid and whitish crusts that destroy the pieces.

88169.q: Which substance was mainly obtained from pyrite in the past?
88169.e: Pyrite is made of iron and sulphur. In the past, sulphur for making sulphuric acid was obtained from it; today it mostly comes from oil and natural gas.
88169.m: Pyrite used to be an important source of sulphur.

88170.q: In what crystal shape does halite grow?
88170.e: Halite belongs to the cubic crystal system and often forms beautiful cubes. Even table salt is made of tiny cubes when you look through a magnifying glass.

88171.q: Which property makes halite different from most other minerals?
a: It burns with a bright flame
88171.e: Halite dissolves easily even in cold water. That is why it is almost only found at the surface in dry areas.

88172.q: How does rock salt form in nature?
88172.e: When seawater evaporates in an enclosed basin, the salt comes out. Over a long time, thick layers of salt form this way.
88172.m: Rock salt forms from evaporated salt water.

88173.q: In which canton is the Schweizerhalle saltworks?
88173.e: The Schweizerhalle saltworks is in Pratteln in the canton of Basel-Landschaft. It is one of the Swiss saltworks that supply Switzerland’s salt.
88173.m: The Schweizerhalle saltworks is in Basel-Landschaft.

88174.q: What does the Greek word “hals”, from which the name halite comes, mean?
88174.e: The name halite comes from the Greek word “hals” for salt. Words such as “halogens” also come from it.
88174.m: Halite is named after the Greek word for salt.

88175.q: Why can rock salt slowly rise underground and form salt domes?
a: It is lighter and can change shape
It is blasted up by volcanoes
88175.e: Salt is less dense than most rocks and flows very slowly under pressure. So over millions of years it can push upwards like a mushroom.
88175.m: Light salt that can change shape can rise underground.

88176.q: What do you call the rock that is made almost entirely of halite?
88176.e: A rock that is mostly made of halite is called rock salt. It is obtained in mines or by drilling.
88176.m: A rock made of halite is called rock salt.

88177.q: What unusual colour can halite get from natural radiation in the rock?
88177.e: Pure halite is colourless. Natural radiation can create faults in the crystal structure that colour it blue or purple.
88177.m: Halite can turn blue because of radiation.

88178.q: What can you scratch gypsum with?
88178.e: Gypsum has a hardness of 2 on the Mohs scale. A fingernail is a little harder and can therefore scratch it.
88178.m: You can scratch gypsum with your fingernail.

88179.q: What is firmly built into the crystal of gypsum?
88179.e: Gypsum is calcium sulphate containing water. The water is firmly built into the crystal.
88179.m: Gypsum contains water in its crystal.

88180.q: Why does plaster of Paris become hard again after it is mixed with water?
a: It takes up water and crystallises
88180.e: When gypsum is heated, it loses part of its crystal water. If you mix it with water, it takes it up again and forms firm, interlocking crystals.
88180.m: Plaster hardens because it builds water back in.

88181.q: What is the fine-grained, translucent kind of gypsum that figures are carved from called?
88181.e: Alabaster is very fine-grained gypsum. It is soft, easy to work and lets a little light through.

88182.q: What does selenite, a special form of gypsum, look like?
88182.e: Selenite (also called Maria glass) is large, crystal-clear gypsum crystals that can be split into sheets. Thin sheets of it used to be placed over holy pictures.

88183.q: Which rose-shaped crystal formations from desert areas are often made of gypsum with sand?
88183.e: In dry soils, gypsum crystals form as flat, petal-like blades. Trapped sand gives desert roses their colour.
88183.m: Desert roses are gypsum crystals with sand.

88184.q: How long are the largest gypsum crystals in the Cave of the Crystals at Naica in Mexico?
88184.e: In the Cave of the Crystals at Naica, the crystals grew in very warm, mineral-rich water. They are among the largest known crystals in the world.
88184.m: There are giant gypsum crystals in the Naica cave.

88185.q: What is plaster used for in hospital?
88185.e: A plaster cast is put on wet and then becomes hard. It keeps broken bones still until they have grown back together.
88185.m: A plaster cast supports broken bones.

88186.q: What do garnet crystals often look like?
88186.e: Garnets often form roundish crystals with twelve diamond-shaped faces. They look almost like little balls.
88186.m: Garnet crystals are roundish and have many faces.

88187.q: Which fruit does the name of the mineral garnet remind you of?
88187.e: Red garnet grains in rock look like the seeds of a pomegranate. Both names go back to the Latin word for grain.
88187.m: Garnet is named after the pomegranate.

88188.q: What is garnet often used for in industry?
a: As an abrasive for grinding and blasting
88188.e: Garnet is hard and breaks into sharp-edged grains. That is why it is used on sandpaper and in water-jet cutting.
88188.m: Hard garnet is used as an abrasive.

88189.e: The most common garnet, almandine, is deep red to purplish red. That is why many people only know garnet as a red stone.

88190.q: What are beautiful, clear garnets often used for?
88190.e: Clear garnets are cut and set in rings or necklaces. The rare green demantoid is especially valuable.

88191.q: In which kind of rock is garnet found especially often?
88191.e: Garnet often forms when rocks deep in the Earth are changed under high pressure and high temperature. Gneisses are typical examples.
88191.m: Garnet is typical of metamorphic rocks.

88192.q: Which present-day country does the famous “Bohemian garnet” come from?
88192.e: Bohemia is part of the Czech Republic. The fiery red garnet was mined there for centuries and made into jewellery.
88192.m: Bohemian garnet comes from the Czech Republic.

88193.q: From the point of view of mineralogy, what is garnet?
a: A rock made of many minerals
88193.e: The name garnet covers several minerals with the same crystal structure but different make-up. That is why there are garnets in many colours.
88193.m: Garnet is a whole group of minerals.

88194.q: Who created the hardness scale for minerals that is still used in schools today?
88194.e: The German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs taught in Graz and Vienna, among other places. The hardness scale bears his name.
88194.m: The hardness scale comes from Friedrich Mohs.

88195.q: What is the Mohs hardness scale used for?
a: Finding out the age of rock
88195.e: In 1812, Friedrich Mohs drew up a series of ten minerals. With it you can find the hardness of a mineral by scratching.
88195.m: The Mohs scale compares the hardness of minerals.

88196.q: How many levels does the Mohs hardness scale have?
88196.e: The scale goes from 1, the softest, to 10, the hardest reference mineral. Each level has its own mineral.
88196.m: The Mohs scale has ten levels.

88197.q: On what principle does the Mohs hardness scale work?
a: The harder mineral scratches the softer one
88197.e: You test which mineral can scratch which. A mineral scratches all minerals of lower hardness and is scratched by harder ones.
88197.m: On the Mohs scale, the harder mineral scratches the softer one.

88198.q: Which mineral can be scratched with just a fingernail?
88198.e: Gypsum has a Mohs hardness of 2. A fingernail is a little harder and can therefore scratch gypsum, but not quartz, topaz or diamond.
88198.m: Gypsum can be scratched with a fingernail.

88199.q: Which well-known gemstones are made of the very hard mineral corundum?
88199.e: Corundum has a Mohs hardness of 9. Red corundum is called ruby, blue corundum is called sapphire.
88199.m: Ruby and sapphire are coloured corundum.

88200.q: Which of these minerals can scratch quartz?
88200.e: Topaz has a hardness of 8 and so is harder than quartz, which has a hardness of 7. Talc, gypsum and calcite are much softer.

88201.q: Why is a pocket knife useful when identifying minerals?
a: You test whether it can scratch the mineral
You use it to measure weight
You use it to find the colour
You use it to measure temperature
88201.e: A knife blade scratches minerals up to about hardness 5, but none from hardness 6. This lets you roughly place a mineral.
88201.m: A pocket knife helps you test a mineral’s hardness.

88202.q: What is true about the gaps between the levels of the Mohs scale?
a: They are not the same size
Each level is twice as hard
Each level is ten times as hard
88202.e: The Mohs scale only gives an order. The step from 9 to 10, for example, is much bigger than the step from 1 to 2.
88202.m: The levels of the Mohs scale are not evenly spaced.

88203.q: What shape are crystals of table salt?
88203.e: If you look at grains of salt through a magnifying glass, you see tiny cubes. This is because of the regular structure of the salt crystal.

88204.q: Which mineral is rock crystal made of?
88204.e: Rock crystal is clear, see-through quartz. In the Swiss Alps, large six-sided rock crystals are often found.

88205.q: What are people who search for crystals in the Swiss Alps traditionally called?
88205.e: Strahler search cracks and clefts in the rock for rock crystals and other minerals. The job has a long tradition in cantons such as Uri and the Grisons. Säumer were mule drivers, Senner are alpine dairymen and Flösser were raftsmen.
88205.m: Crystal hunters in the Alps are called Strahler.

88206.q: How can you grow salt crystals at home?
88206.e: When the water evaporates slowly, the salt is left behind. The salt particles arrange themselves regularly and form crystals.
88206.m: Crystals grow from evaporating salt water.

88207.q: What is special about the inside of a crystal?
a: A hollow space in the middle
88207.e: In a crystal, atoms or ions are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern. This pattern is called a crystal lattice.
88207.m: A crystal has a regular structure inside.

88208.q: What do you call solid substances without a regular crystal structure, such as glass?
88208.e: In amorphous substances, the particles are disordered, like in a frozen liquid. Glass and opal are examples.
88208.m: Glass is amorphous, meaning it has no crystal lattice.

88209.q: How can you recognise a well-grown crystal from the outside?
a: By smooth, flat faces and straight edges
88209.e: Because the building blocks inside are arranged regularly, crystals grow with flat faces and sharp edges.
88209.m: Crystals have flat faces and straight edges.

88210.q: What is the science that studies the structure of crystals called?
88210.e: Crystallography studies the shape, symmetry and lattice of crystals. An important tool is X-ray diffraction.

88211.q: Which of these is made of crystals?
88211.e: Snowflakes are ice crystals with six arms. Glass, on the other hand, is amorphous; its particles are disordered.

88212.q: Where does the Swiss name “Strahler” for crystal hunters come from?
a: From “Strahl”, an old word for rock crystal
From the sun shining in the mountains
88212.e: Rock crystals used to be called “Strahlen”. So someone who looks for them is a Strahler, and the activity is called “strahlen”.
88212.m: Strahler are named after the old word “Strahl” for rock crystal.

88213.q: What do crystal hunters call a hollow in the rock where crystals have grown?
88213.e: In clefts in the Alps, hot, mineral-rich water slowly left crystals behind as it cooled. Crystal hunters look specifically for such clefts.
88213.m: Crystals grow in clefts in the rock.

88214.q: What often shows crystal hunters a possible crystal cleft in the rock?
88214.e: White bands of quartz in the rock show that mineral-rich water flowed there. A cleft may be hidden behind them.
88214.m: White quartz bands often give away a crystal cleft.

88215.q: What did two crystal hunters find on the Planggenstock in the canton of Uri in 2005?
a: A huge treasure of rock crystals
A gold mine from Roman times
88215.e: In 2005, Franz von Arx and Paul von Känel opened a cleft above Lake Göscheneralp. It contained almost two tonnes of rock crystal.
88215.m: A huge crystal treasure was found on the Planggenstock in 2005.

a: A piece of frozen glacier ice
88216.e: Rock crystal is colourless, see-through quartz. It is the most common find of crystal hunters in the Alps.

88217.q: Roughly how long is the largest single crystal from the Planggenstock find?
88217.e: The middle crystal of the largest group measures about 107 cm. Such giant crystals only grow in large, undisturbed clefts.
88217.m: The largest Planggenstock crystals are about a metre long.

88218.q: What do crystal hunters need in many cantons before they are allowed to search for crystals?
88218.e: The cantons have their own rules for crystal hunting. You often need a licence or permit and must follow rules to protect nature.
88218.m: Crystal hunters often need a permit from the canton.

88219.q: Why is crystal hunting in the high mountains dangerous?
a: Because of falling rocks and the risk of falling
Because of the noise of the crystals
88219.e: Crystal hunters climb on steep, often crumbly rock. Loose stones and falls are the greatest dangers.
88219.m: Falling rocks and falls are risks in crystal hunting.

88220.q: Why do crystal hunters in the high mountains search mainly in summer and autumn?
a: Then the rock is usually free of snow
88220.e: In winter and spring there is a lot of snow in the mountains, and clefts are covered. Only in summer and autumn can you reach the rock.
88220.m: Crystal hunters are out mainly in summer and autumn.

88221.q: In which canton is the Lengenbach mineral quarry?
88221.e: The quarry is in the municipality of Binn in Upper Valais. It is one of the best-known mineral sites in the world.
88221.m: The Lengenbach quarry is in Valais.

88222.q: In which valley is the Lengenbach quarry?
88222.e: The valley is a side valley of the Goms and is now a regional nature park. It is famous among mineral collectors worldwide.
88222.m: The Lengenbach quarry is in the Binn valley.

88223.q: Where do the crystals grow in the Lengenbach quarry?
a: In the water of a mountain lake
In the ice of a glacier
88223.e: The finds sit in a white rock that looks like grains of sugar. In its hollows, the crystals had room to grow.
88223.m: The Lengenbach crystals grew in hollows in the rock.

88224.q: What is the Lengenbach quarry known for worldwide?
a: For many minerals discovered there for the first time
For the largest gold deposit in Europe
For the deepest cave in the Alps
88224.e: More than 40 kinds of minerals were described for the very first time at Lengenbach. Some are still not known from anywhere else.
88224.m: Many minerals were first discovered at Lengenbach.

88225.q: What is special about some minerals from the Lengenbach quarry?
a: They are not known from anywhere else in the world
They are made of pure gold
88225.e: At Lengenbach, for example, more than 30 rare thallium minerals are known, many of them only from here. This has made the site world-famous.
88225.m: Some minerals exist only at Lengenbach.

88226.q: What colour is the arsenic mineral realgar from the Lengenbach quarry?
88226.e: Realgar is a bright red arsenic sulphide. At Lengenbach it forms striking red bands in the pale rock.
88226.m: Realgar is a red arsenic mineral.

88227.q: Roughly how many different kinds of minerals are known from the Lengenbach quarry?
88227.e: A study in 2018 counted about 160 kinds of minerals from the quarry; today there are about 170. For such a small quarry, that is extraordinarily many.
88227.m: About 160 kinds of minerals are known from Lengenbach.

88228.q: What is the digging in the Lengenbach quarry for?
88228.e: Early mining in the 18th century hardly paid off. Since 1958, working groups have been recovering mineral specimens there without a break for science and collectors.
88228.m: At Lengenbach, minerals are sought for research and collections.

88229.q: What may visitors do at the “Klopfplatz” in front of the Lengenbach quarry?
88229.e: In summer, rock from the quarry is put out there. With a hammer and a magnifying glass you can search it yourself for small crystals.
88229.m: At the Klopfplatz you may search for minerals yourself.

88230.q: Between which atoms does an ionic bond typically form?
88230.e: Metal atoms give up electrons easily, and non-metal atoms take them in. The charged particles that form attract each other.
88230.m: An ionic bond usually joins a metal to a non-metal.

88231.q: Which force holds the oppositely charged ions together in an ionic bond?
88231.e: Positive and negative charges attract each other. This electrical attraction between the ions is the ionic bond.
88231.m: Opposite charges attract and hold ions together.

88232.q: What is a positively charged ion called?
88232.e: An atom that gives up electrons has more protons than electrons, so it is positively charged. In electrolysis, these ions move to the negative cathode.
88232.m: Positively charged ions are called cations.

88233.q: What is a negatively charged ion called?
88233.e: If an atom takes in extra electrons, it is negatively charged. In electrolysis, these ions move to the positive anode.
88233.m: Negatively charged ions are called anions.

88234.q: What charge does a magnesium atom get when it gives up its two outer electrons?
88234.e: Each electron given up takes a negative charge with it. After giving up two electrons, two positive charges are left over.
88234.m: Giving up electrons makes an atom positively charged.

88235.q: What is the charge of a sulphide ion, that is, a sulphur ion?
88235.e: A sulphur atom has six outer electrons and takes in two more. This gives it a double negative charge.
88235.m: Sulphur forms sulphide ions with a double negative charge.

88236.q: What is the regular arrangement of ions in a solid salt called?
88236.e: In a solid salt, the ions sit in turn in a regular pattern. This three-dimensional pattern is called an ionic lattice.
88236.m: Solid salts are made of a regular ionic lattice.

88237.q: Why do ionic compounds shatter when struck hard instead of changing shape?
a: Ions with the same charge end up side by side and repel each other
88237.e: If a blow shifts the layers of the lattice, ions with the same charge are suddenly next to each other. They repel each other and the crystal breaks.
88237.m: Ionic crystals are brittle because like charges repel.

88238.q: What is the formula of magnesium oxide, a compound of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻?
88238.e: The two positive charges of the magnesium ion exactly balance the two negative charges of the oxide ion. That is why the ions are in a ratio of 1 to 1.
88238.m: In an ionic compound the charges balance overall.

88239.q: How does a covalent bond form?
a: Two atoms share a pair of electrons
One atom gives another an electron
Metal atoms form an electron gas
88239.e: In a covalent bond, electrons belong to both atoms together. Each atom usually adds one electron to the shared pair.
88239.m: In a covalent bond, atoms share electrons.

88241.q: Between which atoms do covalent bonds typically occur?
a: Between metal and noble gas atoms
88241.e: Non-metal atoms all attract electrons fairly strongly. None of them gives up its electrons completely, so they share them.
88241.m: Non-metals usually join each other with covalent bonds.

88242.q: How many shared pairs of electrons does a double bond have?
88242.e: In a double bond, two atoms share two pairs of electrons, so four electrons in total.
88242.m: A double bond is made of two shared pairs of electrons.

88243.q: Which bond joins the two atoms in the oxygen molecule O₂?
88243.e: Each oxygen atom has six outer electrons and needs two more. That is why the two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
88243.m: In the oxygen molecule the atoms are joined by a double bond.

88244.q: What kind of particle forms when a few non-metal atoms join through covalent bonds?
88244.e: Atoms joined by covalent bonds form a closed unit such as H₂O or CO₂. These units are called molecules.
88244.m: Covalent bonds hold the atoms together in molecules.

88245.q: What is a covalent bond with three shared pairs of electrons called?
88245.e: A triple bond is very strong. It is found, for example, in the nitrogen molecule N₂.
88245.m: Three shared pairs of electrons make a triple bond.

88246.q: How many covalent bonds does a hydrogen atom form?
88246.e: Hydrogen has only one electron. With one shared pair of electrons, its shell is already full.
88246.m: A hydrogen atom always forms just one bond.

88247.q: In which substance are all the atoms joined by covalent bonds into a giant lattice?
88247.e: In diamond, every carbon atom is firmly joined to four neighbours. This continuous lattice of atoms makes it extremely hard.
88247.m: Diamond is a giant lattice of covalent bonds.

88248.q: What is the model called that describes the freely moving electrons in a metal?
88248.e: The outer electrons of the metal atoms do not belong to any one atom. They move like a gas between the positively charged metal particles.
88248.m: In a metal, the outer electrons move like an electron gas.

88249.e: Electric current is flowing charge. When a voltage is applied, the mobile electrons in the metal can easily move in one direction.
88249.m: Metals conduct electricity thanks to their mobile electrons.

88250.q: Why can metals be hammered and bent without breaking?
a: The layers of metal slide past each other without the bond breaking
Metals contain a lot of air
88250.e: The mobile electrons hold the metal particles together even after they have shifted. So the metal changes shape instead of breaking.
88250.m: Metals can be shaped because the metallic bond survives the shift.

88251.q: Which property of a metal's surface is also explained by the freely moving electrons?
88251.e: The mobile electrons at the surface reflect almost all the light that hits them. That is why freshly polished metals shine.
88251.m: Metals shine because their electrons reflect the light.

88252.q: What is a mixture of two or more metals, such as bronze, called?
88252.e: Melting metals together makes a new metal mixture with different properties. Bronze is often harder than its ingredients.
88252.m: A mixture of metals is called an alloy.

88253.q: Which metals is brass made of?
88253.e: Brass is a golden yellow alloy of copper and zinc. It is used, for example, for door handles and brass instruments.
88253.m: Brass is made from copper and zinc.

88254.q: Why are metals especially good at conducting heat?
a: The mobile electrons pass on energy quickly
88254.e: The freely moving electrons take in movement energy and carry it quickly through the whole metal. That is why a metal spoon in tea soon gets hot.
88254.m: Metals conduct heat well because their electrons carry energy.

88255.q: What are the positively charged particles called that remain in the metal lattice when the outer electrons are set free?
88255.e: When a metal atom gives its outer electrons to the shared electron gas, the rest of the atom is left with a positive charge. This remainder is called an atomic core.
88255.m: In a metal lattice, positive atomic cores sit in an electron gas.

88256.q: Which particles is a salt made of?
88256.e: In salts, positively and negatively charged particles take turns. Overall a salt is electrically neutral.
88256.m: Salts are made of cations and anions.

88257.q: What is the salt with the formula MgSO₄, also known as Epsom salt?
88257.e: Mg stands for magnesium and SO₄ for the sulphate group. The salt tastes bitter and is used, for example, in bath salts.

88258.q: Which salt is the main ingredient of gypsum?
88258.e: Gypsum is calcium sulphate with built-in water of crystallisation. It is used for walls, plaster casts and models.
88258.m: Gypsum is made of calcium sulphate.

88259.q: Why do salts usually have very high melting points?
a: The attraction between the ions is very strong
Salts contain a lot of water
Salts are made of light gases
88259.e: To melt a salt, you have to overcome the strong attraction in the ionic lattice. That needs a lot of energy and high temperatures.
88259.m: Salts only melt at high temperatures.

88260.q: What are the salts of hydrochloric acid called?
88260.e: Hydrochloric acid is a solution of hydrogen chloride (HCl). Its acid group is the chloride ion Cl⁻.
88260.m: The salts of hydrochloric acid are called chlorides.

88261.q: What are the salts of sulphuric acid called?
88261.e: The acid group of sulphuric acid is the sulphate ion. One example is copper sulphate.
88261.m: The salts of sulphuric acid are called sulphates.

88262.q: Which salt is often used as a fertiliser because it gives plants potassium?
88262.e: Plants need potassium as an important nutrient. Potassium chloride is mined for this and sold as potash fertiliser.
88262.m: Potassium chloride is an important potash fertiliser.

88263.q: What colour are copper sulphate crystals that contain water of crystallisation?
88263.e: Copper sulphate with water of crystallisation forms bright blue crystals. Without water, the salt is white.
88263.m: Copper sulphate containing water is blue.

88264.q: What is sodium chloride called in everyday life?
88264.e: Sodium chloride is the salt we use to season food. It is called table salt or cooking salt.
88264.m: Sodium chloride is our table salt.

88265.q: What happens to table salt in a hot frying pan?
88265.e: Table salt only melts at very high temperatures of about 800 degrees. So in the pan it stays solid.
88265.m: Table salt only melts at very high temperatures.

88266.q: What shape are table salt crystals under a magnifying glass?
88266.e: The ions in table salt are arranged in a regular, cube-shaped lattice. That is why the crystals look like little cubes.

88267.q: In what ratio are sodium and chloride ions found in table salt?
88267.e: A sodium ion has a single positive charge, a chloride ion a single negative charge. For the crystal to be neutral, there must be equal numbers of both.
88267.m: Table salt contains as many sodium ions as chloride ions.

88268.q: Why is it easier to float in the very salty Dead Sea than in a lake?
a: The salt water has a higher density
There are waves in the Dead Sea
88268.e: Dissolved salt makes water denser. Denser water holds the body up better, so you float almost by yourself.
88268.m: Salt water holds you up better because it is denser.

88269.q: What happens if you throw a piece of pure sodium into water?
a: It reacts violently and hydrogen forms
It simply sinks to the bottom
88269.e: Sodium is a very reactive alkali metal. With water it forms sodium hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas, often with hissing and sometimes even with fire.
88269.m: Pure sodium reacts violently with water.

88270.q: What is the most salt per day that the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends for adults?
88270.e: The WHO recommends that adults eat less than 5 grams of salt per day, about one teaspoon. Too much salt can raise blood pressure.
88270.m: Adults should eat less than 5 grams of salt per day.

88271.q: What happens to the ions when table salt dissolves in water?
a: They are surrounded by water molecules and spread out
They join up to form molecules
They break down into protons and neutrons
88271.e: The water molecules pull the ions out of the lattice and gather around them. This process is called hydration.
88271.m: When salt dissolves, the ions are surrounded by water molecules.

88272.q: What is left when salt water evaporates completely?
88272.e: When it evaporates, only the water escapes. The dissolved salt is left behind as crystals. This is how sea salt is made.
88272.m: When salt water evaporates, the salt is left behind.

88273.q: What does the electronegativity of an atom describe?
a: How strongly it attracts electrons in a bond
How many protons it has in its nucleus
88273.e: Electronegativity is a measure of how strongly an atom pulls the shared pair of electrons in a bond towards itself.
88273.m: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts bonding electrons.

88274.q: What does it mean if an atom has a high electronegativity?
a: It has a great many neutrons
88274.e: Electronegativity tells you how strongly an atom pulls the electrons in a bond towards itself. The higher the value, the stronger the pull.
88274.m: High electronegativity means a strong pull on bonding electrons.

88279.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity of all?
88279.e: Fluorine attracts electrons in a bond more strongly than any other element. It is at the top right of the periodic table.
88279.m: Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

88280.q: What is the difference in electronegativity in a bond between two identical atoms, for example in H₂?
88280.e: Two identical atoms have exactly the same electronegativity. So the difference is zero, and the pair of electrons sits exactly in the middle.
88280.m: Identical atoms pull the bonding pair equally strongly.

88281.q: What does a molecular formula tell you?
a: Which atoms and how many of each are in a molecule
How the atoms are arranged in space
How heavy a kilogram of the substance is
At what temperature the substance boils
88281.e: The molecular formula lists all the atoms in a molecule, for example H₂O. It says nothing about how the atoms are linked.
88281.m: The molecular formula counts the atoms in a molecule.

88282.q: What is the molecular formula of methane, the main part of natural gas?
88282.e: A methane molecule is made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. It is the simplest hydrocarbon.

88283.q: How many atoms are in one molecule of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆)?
88283.e: You count 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms. 6 + 12 + 6 makes 24 atoms.
88283.m: Adding up the numbers in the molecular formula gives the number of atoms.

88284.q: What is the molecular formula of ammonia?
88284.e: An ammonia molecule is made of one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms. It has a sharp smell and is used for fertiliser.

88285.q: Which substance has the molecular formula C₂H₆O?
88285.e: Ethanol, the alcohol in drinks, is made of 2 carbon, 6 hydrogen and one oxygen atom. It is found in wine and beer.
88285.m: The alcohol in drinks has the molecular formula C₂H₆O.

88286.q: How many atoms in total are in one molecule of sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)?
88286.e: H₂SO₄ contains 2 hydrogen atoms, 1 sulphur atom and 4 oxygen atoms. 2 + 1 + 4 makes 7.
88286.m: No number after a symbol means one atom.

88287.q: What is the formula of carbon dioxide?
88287.e: Carbon dioxide has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. The prefix ‘di’ means two.
88287.m: Carbon dioxide has the formula CO₂.

88288.q: What does the small 2 in the formula H₂O mean?
a: A molecule contains two hydrogen atoms
The molecule has a double charge
88288.e: The small number applies to the symbol directly in front of it. So a water molecule has two H atoms and one O atom.
88288.m: Small numbers count the atoms of the symbol in front.

88290.q: What does a structural formula show in addition to the molecular formula?
a: How the atoms are joined to each other
How many neutrons the atoms have
88290.e: In the structural formula you can see which atom is bonded to which. This lets you tell apart substances with the same molecular formula.
88290.m: The structural formula shows how the atoms are linked.

88291.q: What does a line between two atoms in a structural formula mean?
88291.e: In the structural formula, each line stands for a shared pair of electrons, that is, a bond. This shows which atoms are joined.
88291.m: A line in a structural formula is a bond.

88292.q: How many bond lines does the structural formula of ethane (C₂H₆) show?
88292.e: Each of the six hydrogen atoms is attached to a carbon atom by a line. There is also a line between the two carbon atoms: 6 + 1 makes 7.
88292.m: In a structural formula, each line stands for a single bond.

88293.q: What is the structural formula of carbon dioxide?
88293.e: The carbon atom sits in the middle and has a double bond to each oxygen atom. The molecule is straight.
88293.m: In carbon dioxide, the carbon is in the middle.

88294.q: What shape is a water molecule?
88294.e: The two lone pairs of electrons on the oxygen push the two hydrogen atoms together. That is why the molecule is bent like a V.

88295.q: How many bond lines come from each carbon atom in a structural formula?
88295.e: Carbon has four outer electrons, so it forms four bonds. A double bond counts as two lines.
88295.m: Carbon always has four bonds in structural formulas.

88296.q: Which molecular formula belongs to the structural formula H-O-O-H?
88296.e: You count two hydrogen and two oxygen atoms. The substance is called hydrogen peroxide and is used for bleaching.
88296.m: You can count the molecular formula from the structural formula.

88298.q: Where do hydrogen bonds act in liquid water?
a: Between the water and the air
88298.e: A hydrogen atom of one molecule is attracted by the oxygen atom of a neighbouring molecule. That way the molecules loosely cling together.
88298.m: Hydrogen bonds link water molecules to each other.

88299.q: What is the weak attraction called that makes water molecules stick to each other?
88299.e: The hydrogen atom of one water molecule is attracted by the oxygen atom of a neighbouring molecule. This attraction is called a hydrogen bond.
88299.m: Water molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds.

88300.q: Why does ice float on liquid water?
a: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules further apart
Ice contains trapped bubbles of nitrogen
Ice is repelled magnetically by water
88300.e: When water freezes, the hydrogen bonds arrange the molecules into an open lattice with gaps. That is why ice has a lower density than water.
88300.m: Ice is lighter than water because its lattice has gaps.

88301.q: At what temperature does water have its greatest density?
88301.e: Water is densest at around 4 °C. That is why in winter water at 4 degrees gathers at the bottom of lakes, and fish survive there.

88302.q: What holds the two strands of DNA together?
88302.e: The bases of the two strands face each other in pairs and are joined by two or three hydrogen bonds. This allows the DNA to be separated for copying.
88302.m: Hydrogen bonds hold the DNA double helix together.

88303.q: How strong is a hydrogen bond compared with a covalent bond?
88303.e: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules and is only a small fraction as strong as a covalent bond. That is why it is easy to break.
88303.m: Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds.

88304.q: Why can pond skaters walk on the surface of water?
a: Hydrogen bonds create a high surface tension
The water is frozen at the surface
The insects are lighter than air
There is low pressure under the surface
88304.e: At the surface, the water molecules pull strongly together through hydrogen bonds. This forms a kind of thin skin that can carry small animals.
88304.m: Hydrogen bonds give water a high surface tension.

88305.q: What happens to the hydrogen bonds when water boils?
88305.e: When water boils, the molecules get so much energy that the hydrogen bonds break. The molecules separate and fly off as steam.
88305.m: When water boils, the hydrogen bonds between the molecules break.

a: A molecule with a positive end and a negative end
A molecule made of exactly two atoms
A molecule that is always a gas
88306.e: If one atom attracts the bonding electrons more strongly, a negative part forms there. If the centres of charge are apart, the molecule has two poles.
88306.m: A dipole has a positive end and a negative end.

88307.q: Which well-known molecule is a dipole?
88307.e: In the water molecule, oxygen attracts the electrons more strongly than hydrogen. Molecules made of two identical atoms have no poles.

88308.q: Which simple experiment shows that water is made of dipole molecules?
a: A thin stream of water is bent by a rubbed plastic rod
Water gets cold in the fridge
An ice cube melts in your hand
88308.e: The rubbed rod is electrically charged. The water molecules turn the matching end towards it, and the stream bends.
88308.m: A charged rod bends a stream of water.

88309.q: Which end of a water molecule is partly negatively charged?
88309.e: Oxygen attracts the bonding electrons more strongly than hydrogen. That is why there is a partial negative charge on the oxygen.
88309.m: In the water molecule, oxygen is the negative pole.

88311.q: Why do oil and water not mix?
a: Water is polar, oil is non-polar
Water is always colder than oil
88311.e: Because of their poles, water molecules cling tightly together and do not let the non-polar oil molecules in between. The rule is: like dissolves like.
88311.m: Polar and non-polar substances do not mix well.

88312.q: What does the prefix ‘di’ in the word dipole mean?
88312.e: ‘Di’ comes from Greek and means two. So a dipole has two poles.
88312.m: A dipole is a particle with two poles.

88313.q: What are substances called that mix well with water or dissolve in it?
88313.e: Hydrophilic means ‘water-loving’. Such substances are usually polar and are surrounded well by water molecules.

88314.q: How many electrons does a nitrogen atom share with bonding partners to reach the octet?
88314.e: Nitrogen has five outer electrons and needs three more. That is why it forms three bonds in molecules such as NH₃.

88315.q: How many electrons does an oxygen atom take in to get a full outer shell?
88315.e: Oxygen has six outer electrons. With two extra electrons it reaches eight, the same arrangement as the noble gas neon.
88315.m: Oxygen needs two electrons for a full octet.

88316.q: How many electrons does a sodium atom give up to reach the electron arrangement of a noble gas?
88316.e: Sodium has only one electron in its outermost shell. If it gives this up, the full shell underneath becomes the new outer shell.
88316.m: Sodium gives up one electron and so becomes stable.

88317.q: Which element is an exception and aims for only two electrons in its outer shell?
88317.e: Hydrogen has only the first shell, and only two electrons fit into it. With two it reaches the arrangement of helium.
88317.m: Hydrogen is already happy with two electrons.

88318.q: How many electrons does a calcium atom give up to reach the electron arrangement of a noble gas?
88318.e: Calcium has two electrons in its outermost shell. If it gives up both, the ion Ca²⁺ forms, with the arrangement of argon.
88318.m: Calcium becomes an ion with a double positive charge.

88319.q: According to the octet rule, how many electrons do most atoms want in their outermost shell?
88319.e: ‘Octet’ means a group of eight. With eight outer electrons, atoms have a stable arrangement like the noble gases.
88319.m: Most atoms aim for eight outer electrons.

88320.q: Which noble gas has the same electron arrangement as the chloride ion Cl⁻?
88320.e: The chloride ion has 18 electrons. The noble gas that comes directly after chlorine in the periodic table has exactly as many.
88320.m: Ions often reach the electron arrangement of a noble gas.

88321.q: How can you tell the number of outer electrons of a main group element from the periodic table?
a: From the number of the main group
From the number of the period
From the colour of the box
88321.e: All elements in a main group have the same number of outer electrons. Carbon is in main group 4 and has four.
88321.m: The main group number shows the number of outer electrons.

88322.q: What do you draw as dots or lines around the element symbol in a Lewis formula?
88322.e: The Lewis formula shows the outer electrons, also called valence electrons. A dot is one electron, a line is a pair of electrons.
88322.m: The Lewis formula shows an atom's outer electrons.

88323.q: How many electrons does a single line in a Lewis formula stand for?
88323.e: A line stands for a pair of electrons. A single electron, on the other hand, is drawn as a dot.
88323.m: A line in a Lewis formula stands for two electrons.

88324.q: How many lone pairs of electrons does the oxygen atom in a water molecule have?
88324.e: Oxygen has six valence electrons. It uses two of them for the bonds to the H atoms, and the other four form two lone pairs.
88324.m: The oxygen in water carries two lone pairs of electrons.

88325.q: How many lone pairs of electrons does the nitrogen atom in an ammonia molecule have?
88325.e: Nitrogen has five valence electrons. It needs three for the bonds to the H atoms, and the remaining two form a lone pair.
88325.m: In ammonia, the nitrogen has one lone pair of electrons.

88326.q: How many lone pairs of electrons does each atom in the chlorine molecule Cl₂ carry?
88326.e: Each chlorine atom has seven valence electrons. One goes into the shared bond, and the other six form three lone pairs.
88326.m: Each chlorine atom in Cl₂ has three lone pairs of electrons.

88327.q: How many valence electrons must you share out in total in the Lewis formula of methane (CH₄)?
88327.e: Carbon brings four, and the four hydrogen atoms bring one each. 4 + 4 makes 8 electrons, so four bond lines.
88327.m: For a Lewis formula, first add up all the valence electrons.

88328.q: What other name is the Lewis formula known by?
88328.e: Because it shows the valence electrons as dots or as lines for pairs, it is also called an electron dot formula or electron formula.
88328.m: The Lewis formula is also called the electron dot formula.

88329.q: What does a Lewis formula show in addition to a simple structural formula?
a: The number of neutrons in the nucleus
88329.e: In a Lewis formula you draw the non-bonding electron pairs as well as the bonds. That way you can see, for example, the two lone pairs on the oxygen in water.
88329.m: A Lewis formula also shows the lone pairs of electrons.

a: It sets which number stands for which character
It connects the computer to the internet
88528.e: ASCII is an American standard. Every letter, digit and punctuation mark gets a number so that the computer can store text.
88528.m: ASCII is an old American standard for encoding characters.

88529.q: In ASCII code, “A” has the code 65 and “B” has the code 66. What code does “D” have?
88529.e: In ASCII the capital letters follow each other directly: A = 65, B = 66, C = 67, D = 68.
88529.m: In ASCII code every letter is a number.

88530.q: In ASCII code, the digit “0” has the code 48. What code does the digit “3” have?
88530.e: The digits 0 to 9 have the codes 48 to 57. So the digit 3 has 48 + 3 = 51. For the computer, the character “3” is not the same as the number 3.
88530.m: A digit as a character has a different code from its number value.

88531.q: In ASCII code, “A” has the code 65 and “a” has the code 97. By how much do the two codes differ?
88531.e: 97 minus 65 is 32. This gap applies to all letters; for example, “B” has the code 66 and “b” the code 98.
88531.m: In ASCII, small letters always have a code 32 higher than capital letters.

88532.q: Does the space have its own number in ASCII code?
a: Yes, the space has its own code too
No, it is left out when saving
No, it is saved as the letter A
88532.e: The space has the number 32 in ASCII code. For the computer it is a character like any other.
88532.m: Even a space is a character with its own code for the computer.

88533.q: Roughly when was ASCII code created?
88533.e: The first version of ASCII appeared in 1963 in the USA, in the early days of computers. It was revised several times later.
88533.m: ASCII dates from the early sixties.

88534.q: Which character is not included in the original ASCII code?
88534.e: ASCII only contains the English letters, without umlauts. For “ä”, “ö” and “ü” other codes were needed later.
88534.m: German umlauts are missing from the original ASCII code.

88535.q: What are invisible ASCII characters like the line break or the tab called?
88535.e: Control characters are commands such as a line break or a tab. You do not see them as characters on the screen. In ASCII code they have the numbers 0 to 31.
88535.m: Control characters are invisible commands such as a line break.

88536.q: In ASCII code “A” = 65 and “a” = 97. Which word do the codes 72 and 105 make?
88536.e: 72 is 65 + 7, so the eighth capital letter, H. 105 is 97 + 8, so the ninth small letter, i. Together they make “Hi”.
88536.m: With an ASCII table you can turn sequences of numbers back into text.

88537.q: What is the aim of Unicode?
a: To give every written character in the world a code
To make pictures smaller without loss
88537.e: Unicode is meant to cover all the scripts in the world, from Latin to Arabic to Chinese. This means texts can be exchanged in any language.
88537.m: Unicode is a shared character code for all the languages of the world.

88538.q: What does every character get in Unicode?
88538.e: Every character, whether a letter, a digit or an emoji, has its own number in Unicode. This way every computer knows which character is meant.
88538.m: In Unicode every character has its own number.

88539.q: Which popular picture symbols are also part of the Unicode standard?
88539.e: Emojis are characters defined in the Unicode standard. That is why you can send them between different devices.
88539.m: Emojis are characters from the Unicode standard.

88540.q: Roughly how many characters does Unicode include (as of 2025)?
88540.e: Characters are added with every new version. Version 17.0 from 2025 contains about 160,000 characters.
88540.m: Unicode keeps growing with every new version.

88541.q: Which characters make up the first 128 code points of Unicode?
a: The same characters as in ASCII code
88541.e: Unicode was built so that the first 128 characters match ASCII. This keeps old texts readable.
88541.m: Unicode is backwards compatible with the old ASCII code.

88542.q: What do you often see when a text is opened with the wrong character encoding?
a: A strange jumble of characters instead of umlauts
88542.e: If UTF-8 is read wrongly, for example, something like “Ã¤” appears instead of “ä”. The bytes are then matched to other characters.
88542.m: A jumble of characters appears when sender and receiver use different encodings.

a: An encoding that stores Unicode characters as bytes
88543.e: UTF-8 sets how Unicode characters are stored in bytes. Today it is the most common encoding on the internet.
88543.m: UTF-8 is the most common way of storing Unicode texts.

88544.q: Which organisation looks after the Unicode standard?
88544.e: The Unicode Consortium is a non-profit organisation. For example, it decides which new emojis are added.
88544.m: The Unicode Consortium decides on new Unicode characters.

88545.q: What base does the hexadecimal system have?
88545.e: “Hexadecimal” means sixteen. So you need sixteen different digits.
88545.m: The hexadecimal system is a place value system with sixteen digits.

88546.q: What value does the hexadecimal digit F have?
88546.e: After 0 to 9 come A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14 and F = 15.
88546.m: In the hexadecimal system the letters A to F stand for the values ten to fifteen.

88547.q: Which decimal number matches the hexadecimal number 1F?
88547.m: In hexadecimal numbers, every place is worth sixteen times as much as the place to its right.

88548.q: How do you write the decimal number 255 in the hexadecimal system?
88548.e: FF means 15·16 + 15 = 255. That is the largest two-digit hexadecimal number.
88548.m: With two hexadecimal digits you can write values from zero to two hundred and fifty-five.

88549.q: What colour does the web colour code #FF0000 have?
88549.e: A colour code consists of three pairs for red, green and blue. With #FF0000 red is fully on, and green and blue are 00.
