a: Because the tap water there is harder
Because the air there is damper
Because the appliances there are older
89254.e: Water that flows through limestone takes up many calcium and magnesium ions and is hard. Hard water leaves more limescale.
89254.m: Hard water leaves more limescale than soft water.

89255.q: What does it mean when tap water is ‘hard’?
a: It contains a lot of dissolved lime
89255.e: Hard water contains many dissolved calcium and magnesium particles. When it is heated, these form limescale.
89255.m: Hard water contains a lot of dissolved lime.

89256.q: Which kitchen ingredient can you use for descaling?
89256.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid. This dissolves limescale, for example on shower heads or taps.
89256.m: Vinegar descales because it contains acetic acid.

89257.q: Why should you descale a coffee machine regularly?
a: Limescale blocks the pipes and makes heating less efficient
89257.e: Limescale builds up on heating elements and in thin pipes. The appliance then needs more energy and can get blocked.
89257.m: Limescale blocks appliances and wastes energy.

89258.q: Why should you not mix descaler with cleaners containing chlorine?
89258.e: Acids release poisonous chlorine gas from cleaners containing chlorine. That is why such products must never be used together.
89258.m: Never mix acidic cleaners with chlorine cleaners.

89259.q: Which organ does the acidic food mixture go to directly after the stomach?
89259.e: After the stomach comes the small intestine. There the acid is neutralised and the food is digested further.
89259.m: After the stomach, the food mixture goes into the small intestine.

89260.q: Which pH is typical for stomach juice when the stomach is empty?
89260.e: In an empty stomach, the stomach juice is strongly acidic. After eating, the pH rises a little because the food buffers the acid.
89260.m: Stomach juice is strongly acidic in an empty stomach.

89261.q: What is one of the jobs of stomach acid?
a: It kills many germs in food
89261.e: The strongly acidic conditions in the stomach kill many bacteria that enter the body with food. It also helps with digestion.
89261.m: Stomach acid protects against many germs from food.

89262.q: Which nutrient is partly digested in the stomach with the help of acid and the enzyme pepsin?
89262.e: Stomach acid activates the enzyme pepsin. Pepsin splits proteins into smaller pieces.
89262.m: The digestion of proteins begins in the stomach.

89263.q: Why does the stomach not digest itself?
a: A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall
The stomach wall is made of metal
The acid is neutral in the stomach
The stomach completely renews itself every second
89263.e: The stomach lining makes a thick mucus that covers the wall. It keeps the acid away from the cells.
89263.m: A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.

a: Stomach acid gets into the gullet
Too much water in the gut
89264.e: When acidic stomach contents flow back into the gullet, they irritate its lining. You feel a burning behind the breastbone.
89264.m: With heartburn, stomach acid rises into the gullet.

89265.q: What kind of substance helps against too much stomach acid?
89265.e: Basic substances neutralise acids. That is why remedies for heartburn contain basic compounds.

89266.q: Where in the body is the acidic stomach juice made?
89266.e: Special cells in the stomach lining, the parietal cells, release hydrochloric acid. Other cells make mucus and enzymes.
89266.m: Stomach acid is made by cells in the stomach lining.

89267.q: Below roughly what pH do we speak of acid rain?
89267.e: Even clean rain is slightly acidic because carbon dioxide dissolves in it; its pH is about 5.6. If it is lower, we speak of acid rain.
89267.m: Rain with a pH below about 5.6 counts as acid rain.

89268.q: Which gas from burning coal and heating oil contributes especially to acid rain?
89268.e: Coal and heating oil contain sulphur. Burning them produces sulphur dioxide, which turns into sulphuric acid in the air.
89268.m: Sulphur dioxide from coal and oil causes acid rain.

89269.q: Which gases from car engines also contribute to acid rain?
89269.e: In hot engines, nitrogen and oxygen react to form nitrogen oxides. In the air these form nitric acid.
89269.m: Nitrogen oxides from engines form nitric acid in the air.

89270.q: Which damage caused by acid rain did people in Switzerland debate especially hotly in the 1980s?
89270.e: In the 1980s, people argued intensely about damage to trees under the slogan ‘forest dieback’. Acid rain counted as an important cause.
89270.m: Acid rain started the debate about forest dieback in the 1980s.

89271.q: Why are marble statues worn away especially badly by acid rain?
a: Marble is made of lime, which is dissolved by acids
Marble dissolves in water like sugar
89271.e: Like limestone, marble is made of calcium carbonate. Acids slowly dissolve it, so statues lose their details.
89271.m: Acid rain eats away buildings made of limestone and marble.

89272.q: Which measure greatly reduced acid rain in Europe?
a: Filters that remove sulphur from exhaust gases
89272.e: Flue gas desulphurisation in power stations and low-sulphur fuels greatly cut the release of sulphur dioxide. Since then rain has been much less acidic.
89272.m: Removing sulphur from exhaust gases has greatly reduced acid rain.

89274.q: What can happen to fish in lakes that have become very acidic from acid rain?
a: They can die because the water is too acidic
89274.e: Many kinds of fish can only cope with slightly acidic water. In very acidic lakes in Scandinavia, whole fish populations died for this reason.

89275.q: How can you tell that an acid is reacting with limestone?
a: It fizzes and forms gas bubbles
The stone gets hot and glows
89275.e: The reaction produces a gas. The bubbles make the acid fizz on the stone.
89275.m: Limestone fizzes when it comes into contact with acid.

89276.q: How do geologists test in the field whether a rock contains lime?
a: They drip dilute hydrochloric acid on it
They put it in salt water
They hold a magnet to it
89276.e: If the rock fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid, it contains calcium carbonate. This is called the acid test.
89276.m: Dilute hydrochloric acid is used to test rock for lime.

89277.q: What is the chemical formula of calcium carbonate, the main part of limestone?
89277.e: Calcium carbonate is made of calcium ions and carbonate ions (CO3). This gives the formula CaCO3.
89277.m: Limestone is mainly calcium carbonate, with the formula CaCO3.

89278.q: What happens to the shell of a raw egg if you leave the egg in vinegar for a day?
89278.e: Eggshells are mainly calcium carbonate. The acetic acid dissolves the shell, and only the soft skin is left.
89278.m: Vinegar dissolves eggshells, which contain lime.

89279.q: Which rock forms when limestone is changed deep in the Earth by heat and pressure?
89279.e: Under great heat and high pressure, limestone is changed into marble. That is why marble, like limestone, is made of calcium carbonate.

a: Water containing carbonic acid slowly dissolves the limestone
Volcanoes blast holes in the rock
89280.e: Rainwater takes in carbon dioxide and becomes slightly acidic. Over a long time it dissolves the lime and forms hollow spaces.
89280.m: Slightly acidic water dissolves limestone and so forms caves.

89281.q: Which of these substances is also mainly made of calcium carbonate?
89281.e: Chalk, limestone and marble are all mainly made of calcium carbonate. Granite and quartz, on the other hand, are mainly made of silicates.
89281.m: Like limestone, chalk is made of calcium carbonate.

89282.q: Which household product removes limescale from a kettle?
89282.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid. The acid dissolves the limescale, and bubbles of carbon dioxide form.
89282.m: Acids such as vinegar dissolve limescale.

89283.q: Which fruits contain especially large amounts of citric acid?
89283.e: Citrus fruits such as lemons and limes contain a lot of citric acid. It gives them their sour taste.
89283.m: Lemons and limes are rich in citric acid.

89284.q: What is citric acid often used for in the home?
89284.e: Citric acid dissolves limescale. That is why it is used to descale kettles and coffee machines.

89285.q: What does pure citric acid look like at room temperature?
89285.e: Pure citric acid is a colourless to white solid. You buy it as a powder, for example for descaling.
89285.m: Pure citric acid is a white powder.

89286.q: With which living thing is most citric acid made industrially today?
89286.e: Today citric acid is mainly made from sugar using the mould Aspergillus niger. Lemons alone could not meet the demand.
89286.m: Citric acid is made industrially with moulds.

89287.q: What are the salts of citric acid called?
89287.e: The salts and esters of citric acid are called citrates. One example is sodium citrate, which is found in foods.
89287.m: The salts of citric acid are called citrates.

89288.q: What is the citric acid cycle in our cells for?
89288.e: In the citric acid cycle, cells get energy from nutrients. Citric acid is an important substance along the way.
89288.m: The citric acid cycle supplies cells with energy.

89289.q: Why can citric acid remove limescale from a kettle?
a: The acid makes the limescale magnetic
The acid makes the limescale invisible
89289.e: Acids react with limescale. The limescale dissolves and can be rinsed away.
89289.m: Acids such as citric acid dissolve limescale.

89290.q: Where did citric acid come from in the past, before people made it with moulds?
89290.e: In the 18th century, citric acid first came from lemon juice. Today it is mainly made from sugar using moulds.
89290.m: Citric acid was first obtained from lemon juice.

89291.q: Where is ammonia often used as a refrigerant?
a: In artificial ice rinks and large cold stores
89291.e: In large cooling systems such as artificial ice rinks, ammonia is a proven refrigerant. Because it is poisonous, it is hardly used in small household appliances.
89291.m: Large cooling systems such as ice rinks are often cooled with ammonia.

89292.q: What does ammonia gas smell like?
89292.e: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a very sharp smell. You may know the smell from badly aired stables.
89292.m: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a sharp smell.

89293.q: What is a solution of ammonia in water like?
a: Different depending on the time of day
89293.e: In water, ammonia takes up a hydrogen ion. This produces hydroxide ions and the solution becomes alkaline.
89293.m: Ammonia forms an alkaline solution with water.

89294.q: What is the well-known process for making ammonia on a large scale called?
89294.e: At the beginning of the 20th century, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed a process for making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
89294.m: Ammonia is made by the Haber-Bosch process.

89295.q: What is most of the ammonia produced used for?
89295.e: Nitrogen fertiliser is made from ammonia. Without this fertiliser, far fewer people in the world could be fed.
89295.m: Ammonia is the raw material for nitrogen fertiliser.

89296.q: What was the old name for a solution of ammonia in water, often used in the past as a cleaning agent?
89296.e: Spirit of hartshorn is ammonia dissolved in water. Ammonia solution is used, for example, in glass cleaners.
89296.m: Spirit of hartshorn is a solution of ammonia in water.

89297.q: Which ion forms when ammonia takes up a hydrogen ion?
89297.e: Ammonia (NH3) takes up a hydrogen ion and becomes the ammonium ion (NH4+). Ammonium salts are found in many fertilisers.
89297.m: Ammonia and a hydrogen ion make the ammonium ion.

89298.q: Is ammonia gas lighter or heavier than air?
89298.e: Ammonia has a lower density than air. That is why escaping ammonia rises upwards.
89298.m: Ammonia gas is lighter than air.

89496.q: Which data does the Swiss Data Protection Act protect?
89496.e: The Data Protection Act sets out how information relating to a specific or identifiable person is handled. This includes things like name, address or photos.
89496.m: The Data Protection Act protects information about people.

89497.q: Under the Swiss Data Protection Act, what must a company do if it collects data about you?
a: Report the data to your school
89497.e: Companies have a duty to inform. They must say which data they collect and what they use it for.
89497.m: Anyone who collects personal data must inform the people concerned.

89498.q: What is the job of the FDPIC in Switzerland?
89498.e: FDPIC stands for Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner. It checks whether authorities and companies comply with the Data Protection Act and advises the public.
89498.m: The FDPIC watches over data protection in Switzerland.

89499.q: Which of these details counts as particularly sensitive under the Data Protection Act?
89499.e: Particularly sensitive data includes data about health, religion, political views, as well as genetic and biometric data. Stricter rules apply to it.
89499.m: Health data is particularly sensitive personal data.

89500.q: Under the Data Protection Act, what can you ask of a company that stores data about you?
a: Information about which data it has on you
A payment for every detail stored
The deletion of all data of all customers
89500.e: Everyone has a right of access. The company must say which data it processes about that person and why.
89500.m: You may ask which data a company has stored about you.

89501.q: What does it usually cost to ask a company which data it has about you?
a: Nothing, the information is usually free
A fee for each detail stored
You have to buy a yearly subscription
89501.e: The right of access is meant to be open to everyone. That is why the information is free in principle and usually has to be given within 30 days.
89501.m: Information about your own data is usually free.

89502.q: What can happen if someone deliberately breaks the Swiss Data Protection Act?
a: They can get a large fine
They only have to change their password
89502.e: For deliberate breaches there are fines of up to 250,000 francs. It is mainly the responsible people who are fined.
89502.m: Breaking data protection rules can be expensive.

89503.q: What does “privacy by default” mean in the Data Protection Act?
a: The most privacy-friendly setting is switched on from the start
All data is public by default
You have to choose a new password every year
Apps may only be used in Switzerland
89503.e: Default settings must be chosen so that only as little data as necessary is processed. Anyone who wants to share more has to set this up themselves.
89503.m: An app's basic settings should give away as little data as possible.

89504.q: What must a company do if personal data is stolen from it and this creates a high risk for the people concerned?
a: Report the incident to the FDPIC
Only inform the police in another country
89504.e: If there is a data security breach likely to cause a high risk, it must be reported to the FDPIC. The FDPIC should be informed as quickly as possible.
89504.m: A company must report serious data breaches to the FDPIC.

89505.q: Which English word does “phishing” come from?
89505.e: The fraudsters “fish” for passwords. The “ph” instead of “f” is a nod to earlier hacker spellings.
89505.m: In phishing, fraudsters fish for passwords.

89506.q: An email seems to come from your bank and asks for your password. What is correct?
a: Genuine banks never ask for passwords by email
You reply straight away with the password
You send only half of the password
You forward the email to all your friends
89506.e: Banks and other genuine companies never ask for passwords by email, text message or telephone. A request like this is almost always an attempt at fraud.
89506.m: No genuine company asks for your password by email.

89507.q: What is the best way to check where a link in a suspicious email really leads?
a: Hover the mouse over it without clicking and look at the address
89507.e: When you hover over it, the email program shows the real destination address. If it differs from the official address, be careful.
89507.m: Before clicking, you check where a link really leads.

89508.q: A phishing email knows your name and your school. Why is it particularly dangerous?
a: It can set the computer on fire
It definitely comes from the school
89508.e: Fraudsters collect information about their victim beforehand. A personal message seems believable, so it is easier to fall for it. This is called spear phishing.
89508.m: Personal phishing emails are especially hard to spot.

89509.q: Which federal office in Switzerland can you report cyber attacks such as phishing to (as of 2026)?
a: The Federal Office for Cyber Security
The Federal Office of Public Health
89509.e: The Federal Office for Cyber Security (NCSC) receives reports of cyber incidents. It grew out of the National Cyber Security Centre at the beginning of 2024.
89509.m: In Switzerland you can report cyber incidents to the Federal Office for Cyber Security.

89510.q: What is the general term for harmful programs?
89510.e: Malware is short for “malicious software”, meaning harmful software. Viruses, worms and Trojans all belong to it.
89510.m: Malware is the umbrella term for harmful programs.

89511.q: What is a harmful program called that spreads by itself over networks without attaching itself to a file?
89511.e: A computer worm uses networks and security gaps to copy itself from computer to computer. A virus, on the other hand, needs a host file.
89511.m: A worm spreads by itself over networks.

a: It secretly spies on data and behaviour
89512.e: Spyware collects information without the user knowing, such as websites visited or login details, and sends it to third parties.

89513.e: A keylogger stores every key press. This lets attackers read passwords and messages.
89513.m: A keylogger records every key press.

89514.q: What is a network of many infected computers controlled remotely by an attacker called?
89514.e: The owners of the devices often notice nothing. Botnets are used, for example, for spam or for overload attacks on websites.
89514.m: A botnet consists of many remotely controlled, infected devices.

89515.q: Which kind of harmful program mainly shows unwanted advertising?
89515.e: Adware (from “advertising”) shows advert windows without being asked. It is often installed together with free programs.
89515.m: Adware floods the device with advertising.

89516.q: How does harmful software most often get onto smartphones?
a: Through apps from unsafe sources outside the official app stores
By charging with your own charger
89516.e: Apps from unknown sources are not checked and can contain harmful code. Official stores check apps, though not perfectly.
89516.m: You should only install apps from official stores.

89517.q: Why is a harmful program like a rootkit particularly hard to detect?
a: It hides deep in the operating system
It is always marked in red
It shows itself as an advert every day
89517.e: A rootkit changes parts of the operating system so that harmful programs stay invisible. That is why even antivirus programs find it hard to detect.
89517.m: A rootkit hides harmful software deep in the system.

89518.q: What does a computer virus need in order to spread?
a: A host file or a program to attach itself to
89518.e: Like a biological virus, a computer virus needs a host. It copies itself into other files and becomes active when they are opened.
89518.m: A computer virus needs a host file.

89519.q: Why is a computer virus called that?
a: Because it multiplies like a biological virus and infects other files
Because it only appears when you are ill
Because it comes from a laboratory
Because it gives the computer a cold
89519.e: The name describes its behaviour: the program copies itself and “infects” other programs. The term became well known in the 1980s.
89519.m: A computer virus infects other files like a real virus.

89520.q: What is the protective program called that searches files for known viruses?
89520.e: An antivirus program compares files with the identifying features of known harmful programs and watches for suspicious behaviour.
89520.m: An antivirus program finds and removes harmful software.

89521.q: Why does an antivirus program need to be updated regularly?
a: Because new viruses are appearing all the time
Because otherwise it gets too loud
Because otherwise there are no more emails
89521.e: The program mainly recognises pests whose features (signatures) it knows. Without new signatures, new viruses go undetected.
89521.m: Virus protection only works with up-to-date signatures.

89522.q: Why should you not enable macros in Word or Excel files from strangers?
a: They use too much printer ink
89522.e: Macros are small programs inside documents. Attackers often hide viruses in them, which start working when enabled.
89522.m: You should not enable macros in documents from strangers.

89523.q: What was the name of the computer worm from 2000 that spread by email as a love letter?
89523.e: The attachment was called LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU. Anyone who opened it sent the pest on to all their contacts; millions of computers were affected.
89523.m: The ILOVEYOU pest spread as a love letter in 2000.

89524.q: How did the first PC viruses in the 1980s mainly spread?
89524.e: At that time most computers were not connected to the internet. Viruses such as Brain from 1986 travelled on floppy disks from computer to computer.
89524.m: The first PC viruses spread on floppy disks.

89525.q: What should you do if an antivirus program raises the alarm on the school computer?
a: Tell the teacher or the IT support
Send the suspicious file to friends
89525.e: Experts can check whether the file is really dangerous and remove it. Trying things out yourself can make the damage worse.
89525.m: If there is a virus alarm, you get help from experts.

89526.q: What is a Trojan in computing?
a: A program that looks useful but secretly does damage
89526.e: A Trojan disguises itself, for example, as a free game or a utility. In the background, however, it carries out harmful functions.
89526.m: A Trojan disguises itself as a useful program.

89527.q: Which legend is the Trojan named after?
a: The wooden horse in the battle for Troy
The building of the Tower of Babel
The wanderings in the Minotaur's labyrinth
89527.e: In the Greek legend, warriors hid inside a wooden horse that the Trojans themselves pulled into their city. In the same way, the computer Trojan gets into the system unnoticed.
89527.m: The Trojan is named after the wooden horse of Troy.

89528.q: What makes a Trojan different from a computer virus?
a: A Trojan usually does not copy itself
A Trojan does not need an operating system
89528.e: A virus copies itself into other files. A Trojan, on the other hand, is installed by the victim themselves, because they think it is useful.
89528.m: A Trojan is usually installed by the victim themselves.

89529.q: What can a Trojan with a backdoor allow an attacker to do?
89529.e: A backdoor opens a secret way in. The attacker can then steal files, start programs or switch on the webcam.
89529.m: Through a backdoor an attacker can control the computer remotely.

89530.q: What is the best way to protect yourself from Trojans?
a: Only download programs from trustworthy sources
Install as many free programs as possible
Save all files on the desktop
89530.e: Trojans often hide in cracked games or dodgy downloads. Official websites and app stores are much safer.
89530.m: Only download software from trustworthy sources.

89531.q: What do Trojans most often disguise themselves as?
89531.e: Free offers tempt people to install a file without checking it. Illegal copies of paid games in particular often contain harmful code.
89531.m: Free offers from dodgy sources often contain Trojans.

89532.q: What is a Trojan called that secretly downloads more harmful programs from the internet?
89532.e: A downloader is small and inconspicuous at first. After installation it fetches more pests such as spyware or ransomware onto the device.
89532.m: A downloader Trojan fetches more pests.

89533.q: What is a Trojan called that specifically targets login details for online banking?
89533.e: Banking Trojans intercept login details or change payment orders without anyone noticing. Swiss bank customers have also been targets of such attacks.
89533.m: Banking Trojans are after the money in bank accounts.

a: It encrypts data and demands a ransom
89534.e: A ransom is money demanded to release something. The victims are supposed to pay to be able to read their data again.
89534.m: Ransomware demands a ransom for encrypted data.

89535.q: In what form do ransomware blackmailers usually demand the ransom?
a: In cash at the bank counter
89535.e: Cryptocurrencies are hard to trace. That is why attackers usually demand payment in Bitcoin or similar currencies.

89536.q: What do experts and authorities recommend if you become a victim of ransomware?
a: Do not pay the ransom and report the incident
89536.e: There is no guarantee that the data will come back after paying. Payments also fund further attacks.
89536.m: With ransomware you should not pay but report the attack.

89537.q: What happened in May 2017 in the attack with the ransomware “WannaCry”?
a: Hundreds of thousands of computers were encrypted, including in hospitals
The whole internet was switched off for a week
All mobile phones were repaired for free
Only a single computer was affected
89537.e: WannaCry used a security gap in Windows and spread by itself. Computers in over 150 countries were affected, including hospitals in Great Britain.
89537.m: WannaCry was one of the biggest ransomware attacks in 2017.

89538.q: What should you do if you notice that ransomware is encrypting files right now?
a: Disconnect the device from the network immediately
89538.e: If the device is disconnected from the network, the harmful software cannot spread to other devices on the network. After that you get expert help.
89538.m: If ransomware strikes, you disconnect the device from the network immediately.

89539.q: What is the blackmail called in which attackers encrypt data and also threaten to publish it?
89539.e: The attackers copy the data before encrypting it. This is meant to push even people who have a backup into paying.
89539.m: In double extortion, attackers also threaten to publish the data.

89540.q: Which organisations often become victims of ransomware because they urgently depend on their data?
89540.e: When hospitals or administrations can no longer work, the pressure to pay is very high. Municipalities and companies in Switzerland have also been affected.
89540.m: Ransomware often hits organisations that cannot work without their data.

89541.q: How does ransomware often get onto a computer?
89541.e: Many attacks start with an email whose attachment looks like a bill. If you open it, the harmful software starts.
89541.m: You do not open unexpected email attachments.

a: You log in with two different kinds of proof
You need two passwords that are the same
Two people have to log in together
You log in twice a day
89542.e: As well as the password, you need a second proof of a different kind, such as a code on your mobile phone. A stolen password alone is then not enough.
89542.m: Two-factor authentication requires two different kinds of proof.

89543.q: Which category of factors does a password belong to?
89543.e: A password is something you know. A mobile phone that a code is sent to, on the other hand, belongs to the category of possession.
89543.m: A password is a factor from the knowledge category.

89544.q: Which category of factors does a fingerprint belong to?
89544.e: Biometric features such as a fingerprint or a face are firmly linked to the person.
89544.m: A fingerprint is a biometric feature.

89545.q: Which combination is genuine two-factor authentication?
a: Password and a code from an app on your phone
89545.e: Password, date of birth and username all belong to the knowledge category. Only a factor from another category, such as the phone as possession, makes it two factors.
89545.m: The two factors must come from different categories.

89546.q: How long is a code from an authenticator app typically valid?
89546.e: Such one-time codes are calculated from a secret key and the current time. They usually change every 30 seconds.
89546.m: Codes from authenticator apps expire after a short time.

89547.q: What does the abbreviation 2FA stand for?
89547.e: 2FA is the common short form for two-factor authentication.
89547.m: The abbreviation 2FA stands for two-factor authentication.

89548.q: You get a 2FA code by text message, although you did not want to log in at all. What does this probably mean?
a: Someone knows your password and is trying to log in
89548.e: The code is only sent after the correct password has been entered. You should not give the code to anyone and should change your password immediately.
89548.m: An unexpected login code is a sign of a stolen password.

89549.q: What are the recovery codes for that you get when setting up 2FA?
a: For logging in if you lose your phone
89549.e: Without the second factor you would otherwise no longer get into your account. You keep the codes in a safe place, separate from your phone.
89549.m: Recovery codes save your access if your phone is missing.

89550.q: What is a small device for the USB port that serves as a second factor called?
89550.e: A security key belongs to the possession category. It confirms the login at the press of a button and is well protected against phishing.
89550.m: A security key is a device that serves as a second factor.

89551.q: What does a password manager do?
a: It stores many passwords encrypted in one place
It gives passwords away to friends
It deletes all passwords every day
It makes all passwords the same
89551.e: The password manager is like a digital safe. You can use a different, strong password for every account without having to remember them all.
89551.m: A password manager is a safe for passwords.

89552.q: What is the one password that opens a password manager called?
89552.e: The master password protects all the other stored passwords. It must be especially strong and must never be forgotten.
89552.m: The master password opens the password manager.

89553.q: Why should you not use the same password for all accounts?
a: If it is stolen once, all accounts are in danger
Because it would get too long
Because websites technically do not allow it
89553.e: Attackers try stolen passwords on many services. With different passwords the damage stays limited to one account.
89553.m: Every account needs its own password.

89554.q: What help do many password managers offer when creating new accounts?
a: They write the password on a piece of paper
They always use your date of birth
89554.e: The built-in password generator mixes capital and small letters, digits and special characters. Passwords like these are almost impossible to guess.
89554.m: A password generator creates strong random passwords.

89555.q: How does a password manager help against phishing sites?
a: It only fills in passwords automatically on the real web address
89555.e: The manager remembers the address a password belongs to. On a fake site with a different address it does not offer it.
89555.m: If the password manager fills nothing in, the site may be fake.

89556.q: How are the passwords stored in a good password manager?
a: On a note in your desk
89556.e: Without the master password the stored data is unreadable. Even if someone steals the file, they cannot do much with it.
89556.m: A password manager stores passwords encrypted.

89557.q: What is especially important with a password manager?
a: Choosing a strong master password and also protecting it with 2FA
Keeping the master password as short as possible
Telling all your friends the master password
Sticking the master password on the screen
89557.e: Anyone who knows the master password has access to all accounts. A long sentence as a password and a second factor make the safe secure.
89557.m: The master password needs to be especially well protected.

89558.q: What minimum password length do experts recommend for important accounts (as of 2026)?
89558.e: Every extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords. The Federal Office for Cyber Security recommends at least 12 characters.
89558.m: Long passwords are much harder to crack than short ones.

a: It controls which data may go into and out of a network
89559.e: A firewall checks data traffic according to set rules. Unwanted connections are blocked.
89559.m: A firewall filters data traffic according to rules.

89560.q: What does the word “firewall” literally mean?
89560.e: Just as a fireproof wall stops a fire, the firewall is meant to stop attacks from the internet.
89560.m: A firewall works like a fireproof wall for computers.

89561.q: Where at home is there often a firewall that protects the whole home network?
89561.e: The router connects the home network to the internet. Many routers have a built-in firewall that rejects unwanted connections from outside.
89561.m: The router often protects the home network with a firewall.

89562.q: What is a firewall called that runs directly on your own computer?
89562.e: A personal firewall is a program on the device itself. It can even allow or block internet access for individual programs.
89562.m: A personal firewall protects a single computer.

89563.q: How does a firewall decide whether to allow a connection?
a: By set rules, for example about addresses and ports
By the colour of the screen
By the time of the last update
By the name of the user at the screen
89563.e: The rules set which senders, receivers and ports are allowed. Everything else is rejected.
89563.m: A firewall works with rules for addresses and ports.

89564.q: Does a firewall alone protect you from all dangers on the internet?
a: No, it is only part of the protection
No, it has no effect at all
89564.e: A firewall does not stop, for example, a phishing email that you open yourself. Updates, virus protection and care are just as important.
89564.m: A firewall does not replace care and updates.

89565.q: What is a port in connection with a firewall?
a: A number that identifies a particular service on a device
89565.e: A computer uses port numbers to tell different services apart, such as websites or email. The firewall can open or close individual ports.
89565.m: Ports are numbers for different network services.

89566.q: Why should you not simply switch off the firewall on your computer?
a: Because the computer can then be attacked more easily
Because the screen would go black
Because the keyboard would stop working
89566.e: Without a firewall, attackers can reach open services on the computer directly. This is especially dangerous on public Wi-Fi networks.
89566.m: It is best to leave the firewall switched on at all times.

89567.q: What is a cookie on the internet?
a: A small text file that a website stores in the browser
A harmful program that deletes files
89567.e: Cookies store, for example, that you are logged in or what is in your shopping basket. On your next visit the browser sends them back to the website.
89567.m: A cookie is a small file that lets a website remember you.

89568.q: Why are cookies useful in an online shop?
a: So that the shopping basket is kept as you click on
So that the shop delivers faster
So that the computer starts faster
89568.e: Without cookies, the website would forget what you had chosen with every new click. The cookie remembers the shopping basket.
89568.m: Cookies remember things like the contents of your shopping basket.

89569.q: What are cookies called that do not come from the website you are visiting but from another company, for example for advertising?
89569.e: Third-party cookies come, for example, from advertising networks that are built into many sites. This allows browsing behaviour to be tracked across many websites.
89569.m: Third-party cookies are often used to track browsing behaviour.

89570.q: What happens to a session cookie?
a: It is deleted when you close the browser
It is sent to all your contacts
89570.e: Session cookies only apply for one visit. Persistent cookies, on the other hand, have an expiry date that can be far in the future.
89570.m: A session cookie disappears when you close the browser.

89571.q: What can you do to get rid of stored cookies?
a: Delete them in the browser settings
89571.e: In every browser you can delete cookies one by one or all at once. Afterwards, though, you have to log in again on websites.
89571.m: Cookies can be deleted in the browser settings.

89572.q: What does a cookie banner on a website ask you?
a: Whether you agree to certain cookies
89572.e: Many websites ask for permission before they set cookies for statistics or advertising. You can often allow only the necessary cookies.
89572.m: With cookie banners you can often allow only necessary cookies.

a: In the browser on your own device
89573.e: A website puts cookies in the browser on your computer or phone. On your next visit the browser sends them back to the website.
89573.m: Cookies are kept in the browser on your own device.

89574.q: Can cookies themselves run programs on your computer like a virus?
a: No, they only contain stored text data
Yes, they format the hard drive
89574.e: Cookies are pure data and not executable code. The main problem is that they can be used to track browsing behaviour.
89574.m: Cookies are not programs but stored data.

a: The traces you leave on the internet
The size of your shoes in an app
A step counter on your wrist
89575.e: It includes posts, photos, comments, searches and websites you have visited. Much of it stays stored for a long time.
89575.m: Everything you do online leaves traces.

89576.q: What is part of your active digital footprint?
a: A photo that you post yourself on social media
Data that a website secretly collects about you
The location your phone reports in the background
The IP address that a server stores
89576.e: You leave active traces on purpose, for example through posts, comments or reviews.
89576.m: What you post yourself is part of your active digital footprint.

89577.q: What is part of your passive digital footprint?
a: Data that websites automatically collect about you while you browse
89577.e: Websites and apps store, for example, which pages you visit and for how long. This often happens without you noticing.
89577.m: Passive traces are created without you consciously sharing anything.

89578.q: Why should you think carefully before posting a photo?
a: Because pictures can be copied and hardly ever disappear completely
Because photos on the internet are deleted automatically after an hour
Because only adults can see photos
89578.e: Others can save pictures, forward them or take screenshots. Even if you delete the original, copies can still exist.
89578.m: Once something is on the internet, it can hardly be fully taken back.

89579.q: Which hidden information can a mobile phone photo contain that gives something away about you?
a: The place it was taken as GPS coordinates
The height of the person taking the photo
89579.e: The metadata (EXIF) of a photo can include the date, time and GPS location. You can switch off the camera's location function.
89579.m: Photos can secretly reveal where they were taken.

89580.q: Who sometimes looks at your digital footprint when you apply for something?
a: No one, it is technically impossible
89580.e: Some companies search for applicants' names on the internet. Embarrassing or hurtful posts can make a bad impression.
89580.m: Future apprenticeship companies can also see your online traces.

89581.q: What helps keep your own digital footprint small?
a: Checking privacy settings in apps and sharing little personal information
Installing as many apps as possible
Giving your date of birth everywhere
89581.e: In the settings you can decide who sees posts and which data an app gets. Less shared information means fewer traces.
89581.m: Good privacy settings make your digital footprint smaller.

89582.q: How can you easily check what can be found about you publicly on the internet?
a: Type your own name into a search engine
89582.e: A search for your own name shows which pictures, profiles or posts can be found publicly. This is also called “egosurfing”.
89582.m: If you search for your name, you see part of your digital footprint.

89583.q: What is advertising called that is chosen for you based on your previous traces on the internet?
89583.e: An interest profile is built from pages visited, searches and clicks. You are then shown advertising that matches it.
89583.m: Your digital footprint decides which adverts you see.

89584.q: Why are software updates important for security?
89584.e: With updates, manufacturers fix errors that attackers could exploit. Anyone who does not update stays open to attack.

89585.q: What is a small update that fixes a particular error called?
89585.e: A patch is a piece of material used to mend a hole. A software patch mends a hole in the program, so to speak.
89585.m: A patch mends an error in a program.

89586.q: What is a security gap called that attackers exploit before the manufacturer knows about it or has a patch?
89586.e: The manufacturer had “zero days” to close the gap. Gaps like this are especially dangerous and valuable to attackers.
89586.m: A zero-day vulnerability is not yet closed when attackers use it.

89587.q: Which setting helps you not to miss important updates?
a: Never connecting the device to the internet
89587.e: Automatic updates are installed as soon as they are available. This way the device is quickly protected again.
89587.m: Automatic updates keep devices up to date without any effort.

89588.q: Microsoft usually releases security updates on a fixed day each month. Why?
a: So that companies can prepare for installing them
Because computers only have power on that day
To make things easier for attackers
Because otherwise updates would cost nothing
89588.e: This fixed date is called “Patch Tuesday” and is usually the second Tuesday of the month. This lets companies plan when to update their computers.
89588.m: Microsoft usually delivers security updates on the second Tuesday of the month.

89589.q: What does it mean when an operating system no longer gets “support”?
a: It no longer gets security updates
It is automatically replaced for free
It can no longer show photos
89589.e: After support ends, newly discovered gaps are no longer closed. Systems like this should be replaced or upgraded.
89589.m: Without support there are no more security updates.

89590.q: Where should you get updates for programs from?
a: Directly from the manufacturer or through the built-in update function
Through a link in an unknown email
From a random website with adverts
From a USB stick you found
89590.e: Fake update messages are a popular trick for spreading harmful software. Only official update routes are safe.
89590.m: Real updates come directly from the manufacturer.

89591.q: Since October 2025 Windows 10 no longer gets free security updates. What does this mean?
a: Newly discovered security gaps stay open
The computer no longer switches on
89591.e: After support ends, Microsoft no longer closes new gaps for free. A system like this should be upgraded or replaced.
89591.m: Regular support for Windows 10 ended in October 2025.

89771.q: Through which sheet of muscle between the chest and the belly does the food pipe pass?
89771.e: The diaphragm separates the chest from the belly. The food pipe goes through an opening in the diaphragm to the stomach.
89771.m: The food pipe passes through the diaphragm.

89772.q: What does the food pipe look like?
89772.e: The food pipe is a long, soft tube. It connects the throat with the stomach.
89772.m: The food pipe is a soft tube.

89773.q: What pushes food down the food pipe?
89773.e: The muscles of the food pipe squeeze together like a wave. That way they push each mouthful down bit by bit.
89773.m: Muscles in the food pipe push food down.

89774.q: Does food still reach your stomach if you swallow while doing a handstand?
a: No, it stays in your throat
89774.e: The food pipe does not only work with gravity. Its muscles push food into the stomach even when you are upside down.
89774.m: The food pipe pushes food into the stomach even upside down.

89775.q: Roughly how long is an adult's food pipe?
89775.e: In adults the food pipe is about 25 centimetres long. That is roughly as long as a school ruler.
89775.m: An adult's food pipe is about 25 centimetres long.

89776.q: Which tube lies in the neck directly in front of the food pipe?
89776.e: There are two tubes in the neck, one behind the other. At the front is the windpipe for air, behind it the food pipe for food.
89776.m: The windpipe lies in front of the food pipe in the neck.

89777.q: What is the burning feeling called when stomach juice rises into the food pipe?
89777.e: Sometimes sour stomach juice flows back into the food pipe. This burns behind the breastbone and is called heartburn.
89777.m: Sour stomach juice in the food pipe causes heartburn.

89778.q: Roughly how long does a mouthful take to get from the mouth to the stomach?
89778.e: The mouthful slides quickly down the food pipe. After a few seconds, about ten at most, it is already in the stomach.
89778.m: A mouthful reaches the stomach in a few seconds.

89779.e: Saliva comes from the salivary glands. They are in front of the ears, under the tongue and under the jaw.

89780.q: Why do we need saliva when we eat?
89780.e: Saliva makes food soft and slippery. That makes each mouthful easier to swallow.

89781.q: What is saliva mostly made of?
89781.e: Saliva is almost all water. Only a few other substances are dissolved in it.

89782.q: Roughly how much saliva does an adult make in a day?
89782.e: An adult makes about half a litre to one and a half litres of saliva a day. Most of it is swallowed without noticing.
89782.m: We make about a litre of saliva every day.

89783.q: Why does bread taste sweeter if you chew it for a long time?
89783.e: Saliva contains a substance that breaks down the starch in bread into sugar. That is why bread chewed for a long time tastes slightly sweet.
89783.m: Saliva starts digesting food in the mouth.

89784.q: What often happens in your mouth when you smell tasty food?
89784.e: Just the smell of food tells the salivary glands to get to work. People then say: “It makes my mouth water.”
89784.m: The smell of food makes saliva flow.

89785.q: How does saliva help our teeth?
a: It rinses away bits of food
89785.e: Saliva rinses small bits of food off the teeth. It also helps protect the teeth from acid.
89785.m: Saliva rinses and protects the teeth.

89786.q: When does the body make especially little saliva?
89786.e: At night the salivary glands make only a little saliva. That is why your mouth is often dry in the morning.
89786.m: The body makes little saliva during sleep.

89787.q: What is saliva also called in everyday language?
89787.e: In everyday life saliva is also called spit. The word comes from “to spit”.

89788.q: Which teeth do you use to bite a piece off an apple?
89788.e: The incisors at the front are flat and sharp. You use them to bite pieces off.

89789.q: Which teeth do you use to grind up food?
89789.e: The molars at the back of the mouth are broad. They grind food like a mill.

89790.q: Which part of the body pushes food between the teeth while you chew?
89790.e: The tongue is a strong muscle. It keeps turning the food and pushing it back between the teeth.
89790.m: The tongue pushes food to the teeth.

89791.q: Which bone moves up and down when you chew?
89791.e: When you chew, only the lower jaw moves. The upper jaw is fixed firmly to the skull.
89791.m: The lower jaw moves when you chew.

89792.q: Which part of the jaw moves up and down when you chew?
89792.e: When you chew, only the lower jaw moves. Strong muscles in the cheek pull it up powerfully.
89792.m: The lower jaw moves when you chew.

89793.q: What shouldn't you do while chewing with a full mouth?
89793.e: If you talk with your mouth full, it is easier to choke. It is also rude.
89793.m: Don't talk with your mouth full.

89794.q: What do food and saliva become when you chew?
89794.e: The teeth break the food into small pieces and the saliva makes it wet. This turns it into a soft mush that is easy to swallow.
89794.m: Chewing turns food into a soft mush.

89795.q: What do you notice more easily if you eat slowly and chew well?
89795.e: The feeling “I'm full” comes a little late. If you eat slowly, you notice it in time and don't eat too much.
89795.m: If you eat slowly, you notice better when you are full.

89796.q: What helps if a dry mouthful is hard to swallow?
89796.e: Water makes the mouthful moist and slippery. Then it slides down the throat more easily.
89796.m: A sip of water helps you swallow.

89797.q: What do you usually do when food goes down the wrong way?
89797.e: When something gets into the windpipe, the body coughs hard. That pushes the food back out.
89797.m: Coughing gets food that went down the wrong way back out.

89798.q: Can you swallow and breathe in at the same time?
89798.e: When you swallow, the windpipe is closed for a moment. That is why your breathing stops briefly.
89798.m: Breathing pauses briefly when you swallow.

89799.q: Which part of the body pushes a mouthful back into the throat when you swallow?
89799.e: The tongue presses the mouthful against the roof of the mouth and pushes it backwards. Then swallowing begins.
89799.m: The tongue pushes the mouthful back for swallowing.

89800.q: What do we say when food gets into the windpipe while swallowing?
a: It went down the wrong way
89800.e: People say: “It went down the wrong way.” The body then tries to get the food out of the windpipe quickly.
89800.m: When food gets into the windpipe, it has gone down the wrong way.

89801.q: What should small children not put in their mouths because they could swallow it?
89801.e: Small hard things like marbles can get stuck in the throat. That is why they don't belong in the mouth.
89801.m: Small toys don't belong in the mouth.

89802.q: Do you swallow even when you are not eating?
89802.e: We swallow our saliva again and again all day long. It usually happens all by itself.
89802.m: We keep swallowing saliva even without food.

89803.q: What can you see bobbing in the neck when someone swallows?
89803.e: When you swallow, the voice box is pulled up for a moment. In many people you can see this clearly in the neck.
89803.m: The voice box moves up when you swallow.

89804.q: What can give you tummy ache?
89804.e: If you eat too much, your stomach is very full. That can press and hurt.
89804.m: Eating too much can give you tummy ache.

89805.q: What often helps with a mild tummy ache?
89805.e: Warmth relaxes the tummy. A hot-water bottle or a warm cushion often helps with a mild tummy ache.
89805.m: Warmth is good for the tummy.

89806.q: What do people often drink when they have tummy ache?
89806.e: Fennel tea and camomile tea are mild and warm. Many people drink them when their tummy hurts.
89806.m: Fennel tea is a popular tea for tummy ache.

89807.q: Who should you tell if your tummy hurts badly?
89807.e: With a bad tummy ache, an adult should help. If needed, you go to the doctor.
89807.m: With a bad tummy ache, get an adult.

89808.q: What is it called when you can't go to the toilet for a long time and your tummy feels tight?
89808.e: With constipation, poo stays in the gut too long and becomes hard. That can give you tummy ache.
89808.m: Constipation can give you tummy ache.

89809.q: What helps keep poo nice and soft?
89809.e: Water, vegetables and fruit keep poo soft. Exercise helps the gut as well.
89809.m: Drinking plenty and eating vegetables keeps poo soft.

89810.q: On which side does the tummy usually hurt with appendicitis?
89810.e: The appendix is in the lower right of the belly. When it is inflamed, it usually hurts there, and you must see a doctor.
89810.m: With appendicitis, the lower right of the belly usually hurts.

89811.q: What can also give you tummy ache without you being ill?
89811.e: Fear or excitement, for example before a test, can also make your tummy feel tight. The tummy and feelings are connected.
89811.m: Worries can also give you tummy ache.

89812.q: Where does food go after the stomach?
89812.e: From the stomach the mushy food goes into the gut. There it is digested further.
89812.m: After the stomach comes the gut.

89813.q: What is the first, long and thin part of the gut called?
89813.e: First comes the small intestine. It is much longer than the large intestine, but narrower.
89813.m: The small intestine comes straight after the stomach.

89814.q: Is an adult's gut longer or shorter than the person is tall?
89814.e: The gut is several metres long. It lies neatly folded up in the belly.
89814.m: The gut is several metres long and lies folded in the belly.

89815.q: What does the small intestine take from food into the blood?
89815.e: In the small intestine the nutrients from food pass into the blood. That way they reach every part of the body.
89815.m: The small intestine passes nutrients into the blood.

89816.q: What does the large intestine mainly take back from the mushy food?
89816.e: In the large intestine a lot of water is taken out of the mushy food. That makes it firmer.
89816.m: The large intestine takes water from the mushy food.

89817.q: Which tiny helpers live in huge numbers in the gut?
89817.e: Countless useful bacteria live in the gut. They help with digestion and protect against illness.
89817.m: Useful bacteria help with digestion in the gut.

89818.q: Which foods with lots of fibre are good for the gut?
89818.e: Fibre is found in wholegrain foods, vegetables and fruit. It keeps the gut moving.
89818.m: Fibre from wholegrain foods and vegetables is good for the gut.

89819.q: What is left over from food and leaves the gut in the toilet?
89819.e: What the body cannot use comes out as poo. It is also called stool or faeces.
89819.m: Undigested leftovers leave the body as poo.

89820.q: What does the small intestine have inside so that it can take in lots of nutrients?
89820.e: The inner wall of the small intestine is covered in tiny finger-like villi, like a towel. That makes it very large so it can take in a lot.
89820.m: Tiny villi in the small intestine take in the nutrients.

89821.q: What is a fart made of?
89821.e: A fart is gas from the gut. It escapes through your bottom.
89821.m: A fart is gas from the gut.

89822.q: Roughly how often does a healthy person fart in a day?
89822.e: Doctors think about 20 to 25 farts a day are normal. Many of them you hardly notice.
89822.m: People fart many times every day.

89823.q: After which food do you often fart more?
89823.e: Beans contain substances that only the gut bacteria can break down. This makes a lot of gas.
89823.m: Beans often cause lots of farts.

89824.e: Farting is part of digestion. It is completely normal and healthy.

89825.q: Why do some farts smell bad?
89825.e: Some gases in a fart contain sulphur. They smell like rotten eggs.

89826.q: What do you swallow when you eat in a hurry that can later come out as a fart?
89826.e: If you eat or drink fast, you swallow a lot of air. Some of it travels all the way to the gut.
89826.m: Eating in a hurry puts air in your tummy.

89827.q: What is polite if you accidentally fart when other people are around?
a: Blame the person next to you
89827.e: A fart can happen to anyone. A quick “excuse me” is polite.
89827.m: After a fart it is polite to say excuse me.

89829.q: Where does the air come from when you burp?
89829.e: When you burp, air escapes from the stomach. It comes out of the mouth, often with a noise.
89829.m: A burp is air from the stomach.

89830.q: After which drink do you often have to burp?
89830.e: Fizzy drinks bring gas into the stomach. The gas wants to get out again, so you have to burp.

89832.q: What do you politely hold in front of your mouth when you have to burp?
89832.e: In Switzerland, burping loudly at the table is thought to be rude. You put your hand in front of your mouth and say excuse me.
89832.m: When you burp, hold your hand in front of your mouth.

89833.q: What is another word for burping?
89833.e: Burping is also called belching. Air from the stomach is pushed upwards.

89834.q: How should you drink so that you burp less?
89834.e: If you drink slowly, you swallow less air. Then less air has to come back out of the stomach.

89835.q: Which animals give off the gas methane when they burp?
89835.e: Cows have a special stomach in which bacteria digest the grass. This makes methane, which cows mainly burp out.
89835.m: Cows burp out the gas methane.

89836.q: Through which tube does the air come up when you burp?
89836.e: The air from the stomach takes the same path as food, only backwards. It rises through the food pipe into the mouth.
89836.m: The air of a burp rises through the food pipe.

89837.q: What do you always do after going to the toilet?
89837.e: After the toilet you wash your hands with soap. That removes germs.
89837.m: After the toilet, wash your hands with soap.

89838.q: What is the toilet often called for short in Switzerland?
89838.e: In Switzerland people usually say WC. It comes from the English “water closet”.
89838.m: In Switzerland people often say WC.

89839.q: What do you press after using the toilet so that the water washes everything away?
89839.e: When you flush, water flows through the toilet. It washes everything into the drain.
89839.m: After using the toilet you press the flush.

89840.q: What can you put down the toilet?
89840.e: Toilet paper dissolves in water. Wet wipes and other rubbish block the pipes and belong in the bin.
89840.m: Only toilet paper goes down the toilet.

89841.q: Where does the waste water from the toilet go in Switzerland?
89841.e: The waste water flows through pipes to the sewage treatment plant, called ARA in Switzerland. There it is cleaned before it goes back into rivers and lakes.
89841.m: Waste water is cleaned at the sewage treatment plant.

89842.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap?
89842.e: For clean hands, you rub them with soap for about 20 to 30 seconds. That is about as long as singing a short song twice.
89842.m: Wash your hands with soap for about 20 to 30 seconds.

89843.q: What is best to do with the toilet lid before flushing?
89843.e: With the lid closed, less water splashes around when you flush. That is cleaner.

89844.q: Should you wait if you urgently need the toilet?
a: Yes, until you can't feel it any more
89844.e: If you often wait too long, it confuses the body and you can get tummy ache. That is why you go to the toilet soon when you need to.
89844.m: When you need to go, go to the toilet soon.

89845.q: What do you dry your hands with after washing them?
89845.e: A clean towel or paper towel dries the hands. Dry hands spread fewer germs.
89845.m: Dry your hands well after washing them.

89846.q: What colour is urine usually if you drink enough?
89846.e: If you drink enough, your urine is usually light, pale yellow. If it is dark yellow, you should drink more.
89846.m: Pale urine shows you have drunk enough.

89847.q: Can you drink tap water in Switzerland?
89847.e: Tap water in Switzerland is clean drinking water. It is checked regularly.
89847.m: You can drink Swiss tap water.

89848.q: When does the body need especially plenty to drink?
a: On hot days and during sport
89848.e: When it is hot or you do sport, you sweat. You have to drink to replace the lost water.
89848.m: In hot weather and during sport you need to drink more.

89849.q: Roughly how long can a person survive without water?
89849.e: Without drinking, a person survives only a few days. Without food they can last much longer.
89849.m: Without water you only survive a few days.

89850.q: Is more or less than half of the human body made of water?
89850.e: More than half of the human body is water. In children the share is a little higher than in older people.
89850.m: More than half of our body is water.

89851.q: How does the body lose water?
89851.e: The body loses water when we sweat, breathe and go to the toilet. That is why you have to drink every day.
89851.m: We lose water by sweating, breathing and going to the toilet.

89852.q: Why are sweet drinks not good for quenching thirst?
a: They contain a lot of sugar
89852.e: Sweet drinks contain a lot of sugar. It harms the teeth, and water quenches thirst better.
89852.m: Sweet drinks contain lots of sugar and harm the teeth.

89853.q: What can happen if you drink too little?
89853.e: If you drink too little, you get tired and can get a headache. Thinking also becomes harder.
89853.m: Drinking too little makes you tired and gives you headaches.

89854.q: What does the body need food for?
89854.e: Food gives the body energy to play, learn and grow. When energy runs low, we get hungry.

89855.q: What is the small mid-morning snack called in Switzerland?
89855.e: The Znüni is eaten in the morning, at about nine o'clock. An apple or some bread makes a good Znüni.
89855.m: The Znüni is eaten in the morning.

89856.q: What is the afternoon snack called in Switzerland?
89856.e: The Zvieri is eaten in the afternoon, at about four o'clock. The name means “at four o'clock”.
89856.m: The Zvieri is the afternoon snack.

89857.q: What is the first meal of the morning called?
89857.e: Breakfast is the first meal of the day. In Switzerland it is also called Zmorge.
89857.m: The first meal of the day is breakfast.

89858.q: How do you feel when you have eaten enough?
89858.e: When the stomach is full enough, the body says: full. That is the best time to stop eating.
89858.m: When you have eaten enough, you are full.

89859.q: What is often harder when you are very hungry?
89859.e: With an empty tummy the brain is short of energy. That is why you find it harder to concentrate and often get grumpy more quickly.
89859.m: When you are hungry it is harder to concentrate.

89860.q: Which part of the body tells us that we are hungry?
89860.e: The stomach and the blood send signals to the brain. The brain then makes us feel hungry.
89860.m: The brain makes us feel hungry.

89861.q: Which snack keeps you full for longer?
89861.e: Wholemeal bread and cheese give energy for a long time. Sweets only fill you up briefly, then hunger soon comes back.
89861.m: Wholemeal bread keeps you full longer than sweets.

89862.q: What do you often hear when you are hungry?
89862.e: When you are hungry, your tummy often rumbles so others can hear it. People say: “My stomach is rumbling.”
89862.m: When you are hungry, your stomach often rumbles.

89863.q: What makes the noise when your stomach rumbles?
a: Air and juices being pushed along
A little animal in your tummy
89863.e: The stomach and gut move using muscles. This pushes air and liquid around, which bubbles and rumbles.
89863.m: Air and liquid moving around make your stomach rumble.

89864.q: What are the noises from the tummy also called?
89864.e: The bubbling sounds don't only come from the stomach but mainly from the gut too. That is why they are also called bowel sounds.
89864.m: Tummy noises are also called bowel sounds.

a: Yes, you must go to hospital
89865.e: A rumbling stomach is a normal sound of digestion. It happens to everyone.
89865.m: A rumbling stomach is completely normal.

89866.q: What usually helps when your stomach rumbles with hunger?
89866.e: When your stomach rumbles with hunger, a meal or a mid-morning snack helps. Then it usually goes quieter.
89866.m: Eating something calms a rumbling stomach.

89867.q: Can your tummy rumble after eating too?
89867.e: The stomach and gut also move while digesting. That is why it can bubble after eating too.
89867.m: Your tummy can rumble while digesting too.

89868.q: What does a rumbling stomach often sound like?
89868.e: A rumbling stomach sounds like a deep grumbling or gurgling. Sometimes it is so loud that others can hear it too.
89868.m: A rumbling stomach sounds like a grumble.

89869.q: What can a doctor use to hear the noises in the tummy well?
89869.e: With a stethoscope the doctor listens to the tummy. That way they can tell whether the stomach and gut are working well.
89869.m: A stethoscope lets you hear tummy noises.

90065.q: Roughly what is the average air pressure at sea level?
90065.e: Standard pressure at sea level is 1013.25 hectopascals. The actual value varies with the weather.
90065.m: At sea level, the average air pressure is about 1013 hectopascals.

90066.q: In which unit do weather services such as MeteoSwiss usually give air pressure?
90066.e: One hectopascal equals 100 pascals. People used to say millibars instead; the number is the same.
90066.m: Air pressure is given in hectopascals.

90067.q: Near the ground, by roughly how much does air pressure fall for every 8 metres of height?
90067.e: At low altitudes, air pressure falls by about 1 hectopascal for roughly every 8 metres you climb. Higher up, the decrease becomes slower.
90067.m: The higher you climb, the lower the air pressure.

90068.q: At what height is air pressure about half as great as at sea level?
90068.e: At about 5.5 kilometres up, only half of the air’s mass is above you. That is why the pressure there is about half as great.
90068.m: At 5500 metres, the air pressure is only half as great.

a: The weight of the air above us
90069.e: Air has weight. The whole column of air above a surface presses down on it and so creates air pressure.
90069.m: The weight of the column of air creates air pressure.

90070.q: When there are pressure differences, in which direction does air basically flow?
90070.e: Air evens out pressure differences, so it flows from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure. This creates wind.
90070.m: Wind is caused by differences in air pressure.

90071.q: Why does water boil below 100 °C on a high mountain?
a: Because the air pressure there is lower
Because the water there is cleaner
Because the sun shines more strongly there
Because the air there is damper
90071.e: At lower air pressure, water molecules can turn into gas more easily. On the Jungfraujoch, water boils below 90 °C.
90071.m: At low air pressure, water boils sooner.

90072.e: Hecto means 100. So you work out 1013 times 100 and get 101,300 pascals.
90072.m: One hectopascal equals a hundred pascals.

90073.q: How does the air pressure change in a train travelling from Interlaken up to the Jungfraujoch?
90073.e: With every metre of height, there is less air above the train. So the air pressure falls, and you often feel pressure in your ears.
90073.m: Air pressure falls as height increases.

90074.q: How does the air move in the centre of a high-pressure area?
90074.e: In a high, air sinks from high up to the ground and flows outwards there.
90074.m: In a high, the air sinks.

90075.q: Why do clouds usually disappear in a high-pressure area?
a: Sinking air warms up and dries out.
The wind blows all the clouds away.
The sun evaporates the clouds from above.
The clouds fall down as rain.
90075.e: Sinking air is compressed and so gets warmer. Warm air can hold more water vapour, so the cloud droplets evaporate.

90076.q: In the northern hemisphere, in which direction does air flow around a high?
90076.e: Because the Earth rotates, the air flowing out is deflected. In the northern hemisphere this makes it turn clockwise around the high.
90076.m: Here, air circles a high clockwise.

90077.q: Which high over the Atlantic often brings Switzerland fine weather in summer?
90077.e: The Azores High usually lies west of Portugal. When it stretches as far as central Europe in summer, it becomes sunny in Switzerland too.
90077.m: The Azores High often brings summer weather.

90078.q: What weather does a high often bring to the Swiss Central Plateau in winter?
90078.e: In calm high-pressure weather, cold, damp air collects in the Central Plateau. A grey blanket of fog lies over it, while it is sunny in the mountains.
90078.m: A winter high often brings a blanket of low cloud to the Central Plateau.

90079.q: What is the weather situation called in which warmer air lies above colder air in a high?
90079.e: Normally it gets colder as you go up. In an inversion it is the other way round, and the cold air stays trapped near the ground.
90079.m: In an inversion, warm air lies above cold air.

90080.q: Which cold north-easterly wind often blows in the Central Plateau when a high lies north of Switzerland?
90080.e: When a high lies over northern Europe, cold air flows from the north-east between the Jura and the Alps. On Lake Geneva the bise is often especially strong.
90080.m: The bise is a cold wind from the north-east.

90081.q: What is a high-pressure area called in technical language?
90081.e: “Anti” means “against”. An anticyclone is the opposite of a cyclone, which is a low.
90081.m: In technical language, a high is called an anticyclone.

90082.q: How does the air move in the centre of a low-pressure area?
90082.e: In a low, air flows together at the ground and then rises.
90082.m: In a low, the air rises.

90083.q: In the northern hemisphere, in which direction does air flow around a low?
90083.e: The Earth’s rotation deflects the air flowing in. In the northern hemisphere it therefore turns anticlockwise around the low.
90083.m: Here, air circles a low anticlockwise.

90084.q: In summer, what does very cold air high up over warm ground often bring?
90084.e: Warm air from the ground rises into the cold air high up. Tall heaped clouds grow, which produce showers and thunderstorms.
90084.m: Cold air high up over warm ground often brings thunderstorms.

90085.q: From which direction do low-pressure areas usually move towards Switzerland?
a: From the west, from the Atlantic
From the north, from the North Pole
90085.e: In our latitudes, westerly winds mainly blow high up. They drive the lows from the Atlantic across Europe.
90085.m: Lows usually come to us from the Atlantic.

90086.q: What is the common low-pressure area over the North Atlantic called?
90086.e: Around Iceland the air pressure is low on average. Many lows that move towards Europe form or grow stronger there.
90086.m: The Icelandic Low is an important weather maker for Europe.

90087.q: From a weather science point of view, what is a hurricane?
a: A cold front in the Alps
A wind without any pressure difference
90087.e: Hurricanes form over warm tropical seas. In the centre the air pressure is very low.
90087.m: A hurricane is a tropical low-pressure area.

90088.q: Why do many clouds form in a low?
90088.e: When air rises, it expands and cools. The water vapour condenses into cloud droplets.

90089.q: Where in Switzerland does a Genoa low often bring especially a lot of rain or snow?
a: On the south side of the Alps, for example in Ticino
90089.e: A low over the Gulf of Genoa carries damp air from the Mediterranean towards the Alps. On the south side of the Alps it then often rains or snows heavily.
90089.m: A Genoa low often brings Ticino a lot of rain or snow.

a: The boundary between two different air masses
A line of equal wind strength
The edge of a single cloud
The boundary between day and night
90090.e: At a front, air masses with different temperatures and humidity meet. The weather often changes clearly there.
90090.m: A front separates warm and cold air masses.

90091.q: What is it called when a cold front catches up with the warm front ahead of it?
90091.e: The cold front is faster and catches up with the warm front. The warm air is lifted up off the ground.
90091.m: In an occlusion, the cold front catches up with the warm front.

90092.q: Which front often brings short, heavy showers and thunderstorms?
90092.e: The cold air pushes quickly under the warm air and lifts it steeply. This creates tall thunderclouds with heavy showers.
90092.m: Cold fronts often bring showers and thunderstorms.

90093.q: Where does the term “front” in weather science come from?
a: From the battle lines of the First World War
From the front of a house
From the bow of a ship
90093.e: Norwegian researchers compared the meeting of air masses with the front lines of the First World War.
90093.m: Weather fronts are named after military front lines.

90094.q: What is the area between a warm front and the cold front that follows it called?
90094.e: Behind the warm front lies the warm air of the low. This area reaches as far as the next cold front.
90094.m: The warm sector lies between the warm front and the cold front.

90095.q: What do you call a front that hardly moves?
90095.e: At a stationary front, neither air mass pushes the other away. Then it can rain in the same place for a long time.
90095.m: A stationary front stays almost in the same place.

90096.q: In central Europe, which pressure system are warm and cold fronts usually attached to?
90096.e: Fronts form in the swirl of a low. They move across the land together with the low.
90096.m: Weather fronts usually belong to a low-pressure area.

90097.q: What almost always changes when a front passes?
90097.e: Behind a front there is a different air mass. So after it passes, it gets warmer or colder.
90097.m: With a front, the air mass changes and so does the temperature.

90098.q: What happens at a cold front?
a: Cold air pushes under warm air.
Warm air glides over cold air.
Cold air rises over warm air.
90098.e: Cold air is heavier. It pushes like a wedge under the warm air and lifts it quickly.
90098.m: At a cold front, cold air pushes under the warm air.

90099.q: What weather does a cold front often bring in summer?
90099.e: The warm air is lifted quickly and steeply. Tall heaped clouds form, with showers, gusts and thunderstorms.

90100.q: What happens to the air temperature after a cold front has passed?
90100.e: Cooler air follows behind the cold front. In summer, the temperature can drop by ten degrees or more within a short time.
90100.m: After a cold front it gets cooler.

90101.q: What symbol shows a cold front on a weather map?
90101.e: The triangles point in the direction the front is moving. The blue colour stands for the cold air.
90101.m: A cold front is drawn in blue with triangles.

90102.e: The heavy cold air pushes forward strongly. That is why the cold front often catches up with the warm front.
90102.m: Cold fronts are usually faster than warm fronts.

90103.q: Which type of cloud is typical of an active cold front?
90103.e: Cumulonimbus is a huge thundercloud that can grow up to the top of the lower atmosphere.
90103.m: A cold front often brings tall thunderclouds.

90104.q: How does the wind often behave when a cold front passes?
a: It picks up in gusts and changes direction.
90104.e: Strong gusts come with the cold front. The wind also usually turns from south-west to west or north-west.
90104.m: At a cold front, the wind becomes gusty.

90105.q: How does the air pressure change after a cold front has passed?
90105.e: Behind the cold front lies heavier, cold air. So the air pressure rises again.
90105.m: After a cold front, air pressure rises.

90106.q: What happens at a warm front?
a: Warm air glides over cold air.
Cold air pushes under warm air.
Warm air sinks to the ground.
90106.e: The lighter warm air slowly rises over the cold air that is still lying near the ground.
90106.m: At a warm front, warm air glides up over cold air.

90107.q: What weather does a warm front often bring?
90107.e: Because the warm air rises slowly, a wide layer of cloud forms. Steady rain often falls from it for hours.
90107.m: Warm fronts often bring long periods of rain.

90108.q: Which clouds often announce a warm front a day in advance?
90108.e: The surface the warm air glides up is very gentle. So the first high cirrus clouds appear far ahead of the actual front.
90108.m: Feathery clouds are often signs of a coming warm front.

90109.q: From which cloud does the long-lasting rain fall at a warm front?
90109.e: Nimbostratus is a thick, grey layer of cloud without a clear shape. Long-lasting rain or snow falls from it.
90109.m: Nimbostratus is the typical rain cloud of a warm front.

90110.q: What symbol shows a warm front on a weather map?
90110.e: The semicircles point in the direction the front is moving. Red stands for the warm air moving in.
90110.m: A warm front is drawn in red with semicircles.

90111.q: Which light effect around the sun can announce an approaching warm front?
90111.e: Thin veil clouds made of ice crystals bend the sunlight. This creates a bright ring around the sun.
90111.m: A ring around the sun can point to a warm front.

90112.q: How does the air pressure change when a warm front is approaching?
90112.e: Ahead of the warm front, the low is approaching. So the air pressure falls slowly and steadily.
90112.m: Air pressure falls ahead of a warm front.

90113.q: How steep is the boundary between warm and cold air at a warm front?
90113.e: The boundary rises only very slowly, often only about one kilometre over 100 kilometres. That is why the clouds reach far ahead.
90113.m: The boundary at a warm front is very gentle.

90114.q: What does relative humidity tell you?
a: What percentage of the possible amount of water vapour the air contains
How many raindrops fall per hour
How heavy a cubic metre of air is
How much water there is in the ground
90114.e: Relative humidity compares the actual amount of water vapour with the greatest possible amount at that temperature.
90114.m: Relative humidity is given as a percentage.

90115.q: Which air can hold more water vapour?
90115.e: The warmer the air, the more water vapour it can hold. At 30 °C it is a good six times as much as at 0 °C.
90115.m: Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.

90116.q: Air could hold 20 g of water vapour per cubic metre but contains only 10 g. What is the relative humidity?
90116.e: You work out 10 divided by 20, which gives 0.5, or 50 per cent.
90116.m: Relative humidity is the share of the greatest possible amount.

90117.q: In which unit is absolute humidity often given?
90117.e: Absolute humidity tells you how many grams of water vapour there are in one cubic metre of air.
90117.m: Absolute humidity is measured in grams per cubic metre.

90118.q: What happens when the relative humidity reaches 100 per cent?
90118.e: At 100 per cent the air is saturated. Any more water vapour turns into tiny water droplets, for example as fog or cloud.
90118.m: At 100 per cent humidity, the air is saturated.

90119.q: Which relative humidity is considered comfortable in living rooms?
90119.e: Most people feel comfortable in this range. If it stays damper for a long time, mould can form.
90119.m: Living rooms should be neither too dry nor too damp.

90120.q: Why is the air in heated rooms often dry in winter?
a: Cold outside air holds little water vapour and is warmed up indoors.
The heating sucks water out of the air.
There is no water vapour in winter.
90120.e: Cold air contains only a little water vapour. When it is warmed in the house, it could hold much more, so the relative humidity falls sharply.
90120.m: Warmed winter air is relatively dry.

90121.q: What is the typical relative humidity in fog?
90121.e: Fog is made of tiny water droplets that only form in saturated air.
90121.m: In fog, the air is saturated with water vapour.

90122.q: How does relative humidity change when air cools down without any water being added?
