90775.e: In Switzerland sugar is made from sugar beet, for example in the factories in Aarberg and Frauenfeld.
90775.m: Swiss sugar comes from sugar beet.

90776.q: How many sweet things per day does the Swiss food pyramid recommend at most?
90776.e: Sweet things are in the narrow top. You can enjoy them, but at most one small portion a day.
90776.m: Sweet things are allowed, but only a little.

90777.q: Which sweet food do bees make?
90777.e: Bees collect nectar from flowers and turn it into honey. Honey contains a lot of sugar.

90778.q: What are the white, airy bakes made of egg white and sugar, which people in Switzerland like to eat with cream?
90778.e: Meringues are baked from whipped egg white and sugar. They are especially well known in the Bernese Oberland.
90778.m: Meringues are made of egg white and sugar.

90779.q: Which biscuit is a famous sweet treat from Basel?
90779.e: Basler Läckerli are small, hard gingerbread biscuits with honey and spices. They are a speciality of Basel.

90781.q: Which meal do you eat before the Znüni?
90781.e: First, in the morning, comes breakfast, called Zmorge in Swiss German. Later in the morning comes the Znüni.
90781.m: The Zmorge comes before the Znüni.

90783.q: Which fruit is especially easy to peel by hand for a mid-morning snack?
90783.e: You can peel a mandarin without a knife and split it into segments. That is why it is good for break time.
90783.m: A mandarin is a handy mid-morning snack.

90784.q: Why are crisps not a good mid-morning snack?
a: They have lots of fat and salt
90784.e: Crisps contain a lot of fat and salt but few vitamins. They don't keep you full for long.
90784.m: Crisps are not a good mid-morning snack.

90785.q: When do you usually eat your Znüni at school?
90785.e: Many schools have a long break in the morning. That is when the children eat their Znüni.
90785.m: The Znüni is eaten at morning break.

90786.q: Why is a mid-morning snack a good idea?
a: It gives energy for the morning
90786.e: It is a long time until lunch. A small snack helps you concentrate well.
90786.m: A mid-morning snack gives new energy for the morning.

90787.q: What is the best thing to bring your mid-morning snack to school in?
90787.e: In a snack box the food stays clean and does not get squashed. You can use the box again and again.
90787.m: A snack box protects your snack.

90788.q: Which vegetable is good to nibble raw as a mid-morning snack?
90788.e: Carrots can be eaten raw and are good to nibble. Raw potatoes are not eaten.
90788.m: Carrots make a tasty snack to nibble.

90789.q: What is a classic Swiss Zvieri?
a: Bread and a piece of chocolate
90789.e: A piece of bread with a little chocolate is a typical Zvieri in Switzerland. Rösti, fondue and raclette are main meals.
90789.m: Bread and chocolate are a typical Zvieri.

90791.q: What makes a good healthy afternoon snack?
90791.e: Yoghurt with fruit gives energy and vitamins. Jelly sweets and lemonade have a lot of sugar.
90791.m: Yoghurt with fruit is a good afternoon snack.

90792.q: Why should the afternoon snack be fairly small?
a: So you are still hungry in the evening
90792.e: A small afternoon snack takes away the hunger in the afternoon. Then you still have an appetite for dinner.
90792.m: A small afternoon snack leaves room for dinner.

90793.q: Which meal comes after the Zvieri?
90793.e: After the Zvieri in the afternoon comes dinner in the evening, called Znacht in Swiss German.

90794.q: Which afternoon snack provides a lot of protein?
90794.e: Cheese is made from milk and contains a lot of protein. Squash, sweets and cucumbers have hardly any protein.

90795.q: Which afternoon snack is healthy and crunchy?
a: Vegetable sticks with a quark dip
90795.e: Vegetable sticks such as cucumber or pepper give you vitamins. With a quark dip they taste even better.
90795.m: Vegetable sticks make a crunchy afternoon snack.

90796.q: Lunch is at 12 o'clock and the Zvieri at 4 pm (16:00). How many hours are there in between?
90796.e: From 12:00 to 16:00 is 16 minus 12, which is 4 hours.
90796.m: There are a few hours between lunch and the Zvieri.

90797.q: Where does most drinking water in Switzerland come from?
90797.e: About four fifths of Swiss drinking water comes from springs and groundwater. The rest comes mainly from lakes.
90797.m: Most Swiss drinking water comes from the ground.

90798.q: How can you always have water with you when you are out?
90798.e: You can fill a water bottle with tap water at home and take it with you. That way you can always have a drink.
90798.m: Always take a water bottle with you.

90799.q: How much unsweetened drink does the Swiss pyramid recommend for adults per day?
90799.e: 1 to 2 litres of unsweetened drinks a day are recommended, ideally water. Children need a little less.
90799.m: Adults should drink 1 to 2 litres a day.

90800.q: What is water from a protected spring that is sold in bottles called?
90800.e: Mineral water comes from protected underground springs and contains minerals. It is filled into bottles.

90801.q: What is a sign that the body needs water?
90801.e: Thirst is a signal from the body. It shows that you should drink.
90801.m: Thirst shows that you should drink.

90802.q: Which is much cheaper in Switzerland: tap water or bottled water?
90802.e: A litre of tap water in Switzerland costs only a fraction of a centime. Bottled water is much more expensive.

90803.q: From which lake does the city of Zurich get a large part of its drinking water?
90803.e: Zurich's water supply takes most of its water from Lake Zurich and treats it.
90803.m: Zurich drinks water from Lake Zurich.

90804.q: Who brings drinking water to people's homes?
90804.e: The water supply, usually run by the municipality, collects the water, checks it and sends it through pipes to the houses.
90804.m: The water supply delivers our drinking water.

90805.q: Can you drink from public fountains in Swiss towns?
a: Yes, if there is no warning sign
90805.e: Most town fountains have drinking water. Where the water is not safe to drink, there is a sign saying “Not drinking water”.
90805.m: You can drink from fountains without a warning sign.

90806.q: Roughly how much sugar is in half a litre of cola?
90806.e: Half a litre of normal cola contains over 50 grams of sugar. That is more than 10 sugar cubes.
90806.m: Sweet drinks hide a lot of sugar.

90807.q: Which drink is a sweet drink?
90807.e: Lemonade contains a lot of added sugar. Water and unsweetened tea have no sugar.

90808.q: What is the tooth disease called that can be caused by lots of sugar?
90808.e: Tooth decay makes holes in the teeth. People who often have sweet drinks are more likely to get tooth decay.
90808.m: Too much sugar can cause tooth decay.

90809.q: What is a good alternative to sweet drinks?
a: Water with a slice of lemon
90809.e: A slice of lemon gives water flavour without much sugar. That keeps the drink healthy.
90809.m: Water with lemon is a tasty thirst-quencher.

90810.e: Squash is very sweet. Well diluted with water, a glass contains less sugar.

90811.e: Herbal tea without sugar or honey contains no sugar. Iced tea, lemonade and cola are sweetened.
90811.m: Unsweetened tea is a good thirst-quencher.

90812.q: Why are energy drinks not suitable for children?
a: They have lots of caffeine and sugar
90812.e: Energy drinks contain a lot of caffeine and sugar. This is not healthy for children; it can cause a racing heart and sleep problems, for example.
90812.m: Energy drinks are not for children.

90813.q: What makes the bubbles in many sweet drinks?
90813.e: Many sweet drinks contain carbon dioxide. It makes the fizzy bubbles.
90813.m: Carbon dioxide makes the bubbles in drinks.

90814.q: Do frozen vegetables count towards your “5 a day”?
90814.e: Frozen vegetables count too. They are frozen soon after harvest and keep many good nutrients.

90815.q: How many of the five daily portions should be vegetables?
90815.e: 3 portions of vegetables plus fruit are recommended. So vegetables should make up the bigger part.
90815.m: More vegetables than fruit is ideal.

90816.q: Roughly how big is one portion for “5 a day”?
90816.e: One portion is about a handful. Children have smaller hands, so their portions are smaller.
90816.m: One portion roughly fits in your own hand.

90817.q: Which is healthier: a whole apple or a glass of apple juice?
90817.e: The 2024 Swiss dietary guidelines focus on whole fruit. It has more fibre and keeps you full longer than juice.
90817.m: Whole fruit is better than juice.

90818.q: Why should you eat vegetables and fruit in lots of colours?
a: Each colour has different good substances
90818.e: Different colours show different plant substances and vitamins. If you eat lots of colours, you get lots of them.

90819.q: What is the best way to manage your “5 a day”?
a: Some vegetables or fruit with every meal
All at once in the evening
90819.e: If you eat some vegetables or fruit with every meal and with your mid-morning and afternoon snacks, five portions soon add up.
90819.m: Every meal should include some vegetables or fruit.

90820.q: Which mid-morning snack helps with your “5 a day”?
90820.e: Apple slices are a portion of fruit. Crisps, biscuits and jelly sweets don't count.
90820.m: Fruit as a mid-morning snack helps with your “5 a day”.

90821.q: Do potatoes count towards the five portions of vegetables and fruit?
90821.e: In the pyramid, potatoes belong to the group with bread, rice and pasta. That is why they don't count towards “5 a day”.
90821.m: Potatoes don't count towards “5 a day”.

90822.e: Lentils grow in small pods. That is why they are pulses.

90823.q: What do peas grow in on the plant?
90823.e: Peas grow in green pods. Inside, the peas lie in a row.

90824.q: Which pulse is the main ingredient of hummus?
90824.e: Hummus is a paste made from cooked chickpeas. It comes from the Middle East.

90825.q: What do pulses contain especially a lot of?
90825.e: Pulses have a lot of protein and fibre. That is why they can replace meat.
90825.m: Pulses provide a lot of protein.

90826.e: Lentils are pulses. They make lentil soup hearty and keep you full for a long time.

90827.q: Do dried beans have to be cooked before you eat them?
90827.e: Raw beans contain substances that can give you tummy ache. Cooking destroys them.

90828.q: Which pulse is tofu made from?
90828.e: Tofu is made from soya milk, and soya milk from soya beans. Tofu originally comes from China.
90828.m: Tofu is made from soya beans.

90829.q: Which pulse goes into chilli con carne?
90829.e: Chilli con carne has red kidney beans in it. It also has minced meat, tomatoes and chilli.

90830.q: Which pulse is small, round and green?
90830.e: Peas are small, round, green balls. They are often eaten together with carrots.
90830.m: Peas are small, round and green.

91015.q: What is the moraine that is deposited along the side edge of a glacier called?
91015.e: Debris falls from the valley slopes onto the edge of the glacier and is carried along. A long ridge forms at the edge: the lateral moraine.
91015.m: Lateral moraines lie along the edge of a glacier.

91016.q: How does a medial moraine form on a glacier?
a: The glacier breaks in the middle
A river brings sand onto the ice
91016.e: When two glaciers flow together, their inner lateral moraines join. They then form a dark stripe in the middle of the stream of ice.
91016.m: A medial moraine forms where two glaciers flow together.

91017.q: What does a terminal moraine show in the landscape?
a: How far the glacier once reached
91017.e: The terminal moraine is a ridge of debris that the glacier pushes up in front of its snout. It marks the greatest extent of the glacier.
91017.m: The terminal moraine shows how far a glacier once reached.

91018.q: What is the moraine called that forms under the glacier and covers the valley floor?
91018.e: Under the ice, rock is ground into fine and coarse material. This layer is left behind as ground moraine when the ice melts.
91018.m: Ground moraine lies under the glacier.

91019.q: How can you tell moraine material apart from river deposits?
a: It is mixed up without any order
It is made only of sand
91019.e: A glacier leaves large blocks, gravel, sand and clay all jumbled together. A river, on the other hand, sorts its material by grain size.
91019.m: Moraine material is a jumbled mix of big and small stones.

91020.q: What often forms behind a terminal moraine when the glacier melts away?
91020.e: The moraine ridge acts like a natural dam. Meltwater collects behind it, and a lake forms.
91020.m: A lake often builds up behind a terminal moraine.

91021.q: In front of many Alpine glaciers, what shows how big they were around 1850?
a: Fresh moraine ridges with few plants
91021.e: Around 1850, the Little Ice Age ended, when many glaciers were especially large. Their moraine ridges are still barely overgrown and easy to see.
91021.m: Bare moraine ridges show the size of glaciers in 1850.

91022.q: What are long hills made of ground moraine material, found for example in the Zurich Oberland, called?
91022.e: Drumlins are streamlined hills that the glacier shaped underneath it. Their long direction shows where the ice flowed.
91022.m: Drumlins are long hills shaped by a glacier.

91023.q: Why are the steep lateral moraines often dangerous after a glacier has retreated?
a: They are loose and can slide down
91023.e: In the past, the ice supported the moraine slopes. After melting, the loose material is unprotected and can come down as rockfall or a debris flow.
91023.m: Loose moraine slopes can slide after a glacier retreats.

a: The lowest part of a glacier
The highest peak above the glacier
A crack in the glacier ice
91024.e: The glacier tongue is the long, narrow end of the glacier that reaches down into the valley. It often looks like a tongue sticking out.
91024.m: The glacier tongue is the lower end of a glacier.

91025.q: In which area of a glacier is the glacier tongue?
91025.e: At the tongue, more ice melts each year than new snow is added. This part is called the ablation zone.
91025.m: The glacier tongue lies in the ablation zone, where more ice melts than is added.

91026.q: Why does a glacier tongue retreat even though the ice flows down the valley?
a: More ice melts at the bottom than flows down
The glacier is eaten by animals
91026.e: The ice does keep moving down the valley. But if more melts away at the tongue than comes down from above, the glacier gets shorter.
91026.m: A tongue shrinks when more ice melts than flows down.

91027.q: What effect does a thick layer of debris on a glacier tongue have?
a: It makes the ice melt faster
91027.e: A thick layer of stones protects the ice from sun and warm air like a blanket. Only a thin, dark layer of dust speeds up melting.
91027.m: Thick debris protects a glacier tongue from melting.

91028.q: What is the hollow called that a glacier tongue scoops out, which often later holds a lake?
91028.e: The glacier tongue scoops out a deep trough at the end of the valley. After the Ice Age, many such tongue basins filled with water.
91028.m: Many lakes lie in the tongue basins of former glaciers.

91029.q: Where do especially many transverse crevasses form on a glacier tongue?
a: Where the ice flows over a steep step
Where the ice lies completely flat
Where snow falls on the ice
Where the glacier lies in shadow
91029.e: At a steep step, the ice is stretched and tears open. Crevasses form across the direction of flow.
91029.m: Over steep steps, glacier ice tears open in transverse crevasses.

91030.q: How quickly does a glacier tongue react to a change in climate?
a: With a delay of years to decades
91030.e: It takes a while for more or less snow up high to affect the tongue. Large glaciers react especially slowly.
91030.m: Glacier tongues react to the climate with a delay.

91031.q: Why does dense ice at the glacier tongue often glow bluish?
a: It absorbs red light and lets blue through
The sky is reflected in it
91031.e: Dense ice with little air absorbs mainly red light. What is left is the blue part, which we see.
91031.m: Dense glacier ice looks blue because it absorbs red light.

91032.q: How dense is firn compared with snow and ice?
a: Denser than snow, less dense than ice
91032.e: Firn is an in-between stage. The grains are packed together, but there is still a lot of air between them.
91032.m: Firn is denser than snow but less dense than ice.

91033.q: What does the firn line on a glacier separate?
a: The accumulation zone from the ablation zone
91033.e: At the end of summer, the firn line shows how far down the winter snow is still lying. Above it the glacier grows, below it the glacier melts.
91033.m: The firn line separates the accumulation zone and the ablation zone.

91034.q: What is the bergschrund on a glacier?
a: A deep crevasse at the upper edge of the glacier
The lower end of the glacier
A stream under the glacier ice
91034.e: The glacier flows down the valley, while the rock and the ice frozen to it stay put up high. A deep crevasse opens between them: the bergschrund.
91034.m: At the top of a glacier, the bergschrund separates the moving ice from the rock.

91036.q: When does firn become glacier ice?
a: When the air pores are sealed off
As soon as it rains once
As soon as it is a week old
91036.e: Under the weight of new layers, firn gets denser and denser. When the air channels are sealed into bubbles, it is called ice.
91036.m: Firn becomes ice when the air is trapped in bubbles.

91037.q: What happens at Konkordiaplatz on the Great Aletsch Glacier?
a: Several streams of firn flow together
The glacier ends in the valley
91037.e: At Konkordiaplatz, several large firn fields meet. From there, the Great Aletsch Glacier flows down the valley as one stream.
91037.m: The firn streams of the Aletsch Glacier join at Konkordiaplatz.

91038.q: Why does a glacier melt faster when the pale layer of firn disappears?
a: Dark ice absorbs more heat from the sun
91038.e: Pale snow and firn reflect a lot of sunlight. The darker ice underneath absorbs more radiation and melts faster.
91038.m: Without a pale covering of firn, glacier ice melts faster.

91039.q: Why do ice cores contain air from earlier times?
a: The firn traps air in bubbles
The ice soaks up today’s air
91039.e: When firn turns into ice, air stays trapped in tiny bubbles. This lets researchers study the air of times long past.
91039.m: Bubbles in the ice keep air from times long past.

91040.q: Roughly how long has the present ice age been going on?
91040.e: The present ice age began with the Quaternary about 2.6 million years ago. Since then, cold periods and warm periods have taken turns.
91040.m: The present ice age began about 2.6 million years ago.

91041.q: Which phase of the ice age are we living in today?
a: After the end of all ice ages
91041.e: We live in the Holocene, a warm period within the ice age. Because there are large ice sheets at the poles, the ice age is still going on.
91041.m: Today we live in a warm period of the ice age.

91042.q: What is a warm period in the ice age?
a: A warmer time between two cold periods
The coldest time with the biggest glaciers
A hot summer in the middle of a cold period
The time before the first ice age
91042.e: In the ice age, cold periods and warm periods take turns several times. In a warm period, the glaciers melt back a lot.
91042.m: A warm period lies between two cold periods.

91043.q: What did naturalists such as Louis Agassiz make known in the 19th century?
a: That there used to be a great ice age
That there are volcanoes in Switzerland
That the Alps get smaller every year
91043.e: In 1837, Louis Agassiz gave a famous speech in Neuchâtel about an earlier great glaciation. This spread the ice age theory around the world.
91043.m: In the 19th century, people realised there had been a great ice age.

91044.q: How did people realise that glaciers once reached as far as the Central Plateau?
a: From moraines and boulders of foreign rock
From layers of salt in the ground
91044.e: Moraines and large boulders of rock from elsewhere lie far from today’s glaciers. Only huge masses of ice could have brought them there.
91044.m: Moraines and erratic boulders show how far the glaciers used to reach.

91045.q: At the height of the last cold period, by how much was sea level lower than today?
91045.e: A great deal of water was locked up in the huge ice sheets. So sea level fell by about 120 metres.
91045.m: In the cold period, sea level was about 120 metres lower.

91046.q: Which large animals lived in the Swiss Central Plateau during the cold periods?
91046.e: Mammoths and woolly rhinoceroses lived on the grassland in front of the glaciers. Several mammoth skeletons were found at Niederweningen in the canton of Zurich.
91046.m: Mammoths lived in the Central Plateau during the ice age.

91047.q: What are large boulders called that the glaciers of the cold periods carried far from where they came from into the Central Plateau?
91047.e: Erratic boulders are often made of rock that does not exist in their surroundings at all. The ice brought them from the Alps and left them behind as it melted.
91047.m: Erratic boulders are rocks that glaciers carried a long way.

91048.q: What is the cooler period from about 1350 to 1850, when the Alpine glaciers grew a lot, called?
91048.e: During the Little Ice Age it was a bit cooler than before and after. Many Alpine glaciers reached their greatest length of recent centuries around 1850.
91048.m: The Little Ice Age lasted from about 1350 to 1850.

91049.q: What is the Würm glaciation named after?
91049.e: The Würm is a river in Bavaria. The Alpine cold periods were named after rivers in the land in front of the Alps.
91049.m: The Würm glaciation bears the name of a Bavarian river.

91050.q: What position does the Würm glaciation hold among the cold periods of the Alps?
91050.e: The Würm glaciation is the most recent great glaciation of the land in front of the Alps. After it, today’s warm period began.
91050.m: The Würm glaciation is the last cold period of the Alps.

91051.q: Roughly how many years ago did the Würm glaciation end?
91051.e: The Würm glaciation ended with the start of the Holocene about 10,000 years ago. It had begun about 115,000 years ago.
91051.m: The Würm glaciation ended about 10,000 years ago.

91052.q: Roughly how many years ago did the glaciers of the Würm glaciation reach their greatest extent in Switzerland?
91052.e: The map of Switzerland at the last glacial maximum shows the ice about 24,000 years ago. After that, the glaciers gradually melted back.
91052.m: About 24,000 years ago, Switzerland was most heavily covered by glaciers.

91053.q: Where did the Rhône glacier come from that reached far into the western Central Plateau in the Würm glaciation?
91053.e: The Rhône glacier flowed from Valais over Lake Geneva into the Central Plateau. It covered large parts of western Switzerland.
91053.m: The Rhône glacier came from Valais and covered the western Central Plateau.

91054.q: How far did the Rhine glacier advance in the Würm glaciation?
91054.e: The Rhine glacier filled the basin of today’s Lake Constance. It reached as far as the area around Schaffhausen.
91054.m: The Rhine glacier reached the area around Schaffhausen.

91055.q: What did the glaciers of the Würm glaciation leave behind in the Swiss Central Plateau?
91055.e: The glaciers pushed rubble up into moraines and carried large boulders, the erratics. Many of them can still be seen in the Central Plateau today.
91055.m: Moraines and erratic boulders are traces of the ice age glaciers.

91056.q: In the Würm glaciation, roughly how much colder was the yearly average in the land in front of the Alps than today?
91056.e: Today the yearly average in front of the Alps is about plus 7 degrees. In the Würm glaciation it was below minus 3 degrees.
91056.m: In the Würm glaciation, it was about 10 degrees colder in front of the Alps.

91057.q: Which animals lived in the Swiss Central Plateau during the Würm glaciation?
91057.e: Mammoths and woolly rhinos had thick fur and were adapted to the cold. They lived on the grassland with few trees in front of the glaciers.
91057.m: In the Würm glaciation, mammoths and woolly rhinos lived in Switzerland.

91058.q: Roughly how long is the Rhône Glacier (as of the 2020s)?
91058.e: The Rhône Glacier is almost 8 kilometres long. It lies on the western slope of the Dammastock.
91058.m: The Rhône Glacier is almost 8 kilometres long.

91059.q: In which canton is the Rhône Glacier?
91059.e: The Rhône Glacier lies at the very top of Valais, near the Furka Pass. It borders the cantons of Bern and Uri.
91059.m: The Rhône Glacier is in the canton of Valais.

91060.q: Roughly how big is the area of the Rhône Glacier (as of 2018)?
91060.e: In 2018, the Rhône Glacier covered 14.64 square kilometres. Around 1850 it was still about 20 square kilometres.
91060.m: The Rhône Glacier covers about 15 square kilometres.

91061.q: To which place in the valley did the Rhône Glacier reach at its peak in 1856?
91061.e: In the 19th century, the tongue reached down to about 1800 metres, to the valley floor at Gletsch. Today it ends more than 2200 metres up.
91061.m: In 1856, the Rhône Glacier reached Gletsch.

91062.q: Between which two passes does the hamlet of Gletsch lie below the Rhône Glacier?
91062.e: At Gletsch, the roads over the Furka Pass and the Grimsel Pass meet. From there you can look up to the Rhône Glacier.
91062.m: Gletsch lies between the Furka Pass and the Grimsel Pass.

91063.q: What is cut into the Rhône Glacier again every year so that visitors can go inside?
91063.e: Because the ice flows, the grotto moves and changes shape. So it is cut into the ice anew every year.
91063.m: A new ice grotto is cut into the Rhône Glacier every year.

91064.q: What has formed in front of the tongue of the Rhône Glacier since about 2007?
91064.e: The glacier retreated over a rock step. In the hollow in front of it, meltwater collected into a new lake.
91064.m: A new glacial lake formed in front of the Rhône Glacier.

91065.q: Why are the measurements of the Rhône Glacier so valuable for research?
a: They show how the glacier has changed over more than 150 years
They show when earthquakes will happen
They count the number of tourists
91065.e: From 1874, the Rhône Glacier was measured precisely. This produced one of the longest series of measurements in the world, showing the glacier’s retreat.
91065.m: The Rhône Glacier has been measured for more than 150 years.

91066.q: During the cold periods, how thick was the ice in the Rhône valley in Valais in some places?
91066.e: In the cold periods, the Rhône glacier filled the whole Rhône valley in Valais. The ice there was up to 2000 metres thick.
91066.m: In the cold periods, there was up to 2000 metres of ice in the Rhône valley.

91067.q: What is a valley that a river has cut, with steep sides meeting at the bottom, called?
91067.e: A river cuts downwards and forms steep slopes that meet at the bottom, like a V. A glacier, on the other hand, carves out a wide U.
91067.m: A river forms a V-shaped valley, a glacier a U-shaped valley.

91068.q: Which valley in the Bernese Oberland is a well-known example of a U-shaped valley?
91068.e: The Lauterbrunnen valley has a flat floor and almost vertical rock walls. A glacier ground out this shape.
91068.m: The Lauterbrunnen valley is a typical U-shaped valley.

91069.q: What do you call a side valley that ends high above the floor of a U-shaped valley?
91069.e: The main glacier carved its valley much deeper than the small side glaciers. So the side valleys end high up in the rock wall.
91069.m: A hanging valley ends high above a U-shaped valley.

91070.q: What often plunges down from a hanging valley in the Lauterbrunnen valley?
91070.e: Streams from hanging valleys fall over the steep valley wall into the main valley. A well-known example is the Staubbach Falls.
91070.m: Waterfalls often plunge from hanging valleys.

91071.q: Why could villages such as Mürren and Wengen grow up high above the Lauterbrunnen valley?
a: They lie on flat terraces above the steep valley walls
They stand on stilts above the abyss
They lie on an old volcano
They were built on glacier ice
91071.e: Above the steep rock walls of a U-shaped valley there is often a flatter step. There is room there for alpine pastures and villages such as Mürren and Wengen.
91071.m: Mürren and Wengen lie on flat steps above the U-shaped valley.

91072.q: What do you call a U-shaped valley that has been flooded by the sea?
91072.e: After the Ice Age, sea level rose and the sea flowed into deep glacial valleys. This created fjords like those in Norway.
91072.m: A fjord is a U-shaped valley flooded by the sea.

91073.q: Why is the floor of many U-shaped valleys so flat today?
a: It was filled up with gravel and sand
It is made of glacier ice
91073.e: After the glacier retreated, streams and lakes deposited a lot of material in the trough. This created a level valley floor.
91073.m: Gravel and sand filling it make the floor of a U-shaped valley flat.

91074.q: What shape is the cross-section of a glacial trough valley?
91074.e: A glacier carves the valley out wide. So a trough valley has a flat floor and steep walls, like a U.
91074.m: A trough valley is shaped like a U.

a: A hump of rock ground smooth by a glacier
A hill of sand and gravel
A round piece of ice in the glacier
91075.e: Roches moutonnées are humps of rock shaped by a glacier flowing over them. They are often a few metres to dozens of metres in size.
91075.m: A roche moutonnée is a hump of rock ground smooth by the ice.

91076.q: What does the side of a roche moutonnée that the glacier came from look like?
91076.e: On the upstream side, the ice pressed stones against the rock and ground it smooth. This side is gentler and polished.
91076.m: The upstream side of a roche moutonnée is ground smooth.

91077.q: What does the lee side of a roche moutonnée, facing away from the glacier, look like?
91077.e: On the lee side, the ice tore out pieces of rock. That is why this side is steeper and rough.
91077.m: The lee side of a roche moutonnée is steep and rough.

91078.q: What do glacial scratches on a roche moutonnée tell you?
a: In which direction the ice flowed
Where there is water in the ground
91078.e: Stones in the glacier ice scratched lines into the rock. These scratches run in the direction the glacier flowed.
91078.m: Glacial scratches show the direction the ice flowed.

91079.q: How do the broken rock faces on the lee side of a roche moutonnée form?
a: Ice frozen to the rock tears out blocks
The wind wears the rock away
91079.e: On the lee side, the ice can freeze onto the rock. When the glacier flows on, it tears out blocks along cracks.
91079.m: Ice freezing onto the rock tears out blocks on the lee side.

91080.q: The French name “roches moutonnées” is also used in English. What does the shape of these rocks remind people of?
91080.e: The French word “mouton” means sheep. The round humps of rock look like sheep lying in a field.
91080.m: Roches moutonnées look like sheep lying down.

91081.q: Where in the Alps are there especially many roches moutonnées?
a: In cirques and on mountain passes
91081.e: In cirques and on passes that glacier ice once flowed over, the ice ground down the rock. There are often whole landscapes of roches moutonnées there.
91081.m: Roches moutonnées are common in cirques and on passes.

91082.q: What are small rocky islands smoothed by ice off the coasts of Scandinavia called?
91082.e: On the coasts of Sweden and Finland, many ice-smoothed humps of rock rise out of the sea. They are called skerries.
91082.m: Skerries are ice-smoothed rocks rising out of the sea.

a: Ice that has broken away from the glacier and lies still
Ice that freezes on lakes in winter
Ice that floats in the sea
91083.e: When a glacier retreats, blocks of ice are often left behind that are no longer connected to it. This ice that no longer moves is called dead ice.
91083.m: Dead ice is glacier ice that no longer moves.

91084.q: Why can a block of dead ice survive for a long time?
91084.e: Meltwater deposits sand and gravel over the block of ice. This layer insulates it, so it melts only slowly.
91084.m: A blanket of sand and gravel protects dead ice from melting.

91085.q: How does a kettle hole form?
a: The ground sinks above melting ice
91085.e: When the buried block of ice melts, the ice under the layer of soil is gone. The ground above sinks, and a hollow forms.
91085.m: A kettle hole forms when the ground sinks above melting ice.

91086.q: What do you call a kettle hole that is filled with groundwater?
91086.e: If the bottom of the hole lies below the water table, it fills with water. This makes a small kettle lake.
91086.m: A kettle hole filled with water is called a kettle lake.

91087.q: When were most kettle holes in the Swiss Plateau formed?
a: At the end of the last ice age
In the time of the dinosaurs
91087.e: When the glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age, blocks of ice were left behind in the gravel. When they melted, kettle holes formed.
91087.m: Kettle holes on the Swiss Plateau date from the end of the last ice age.

91088.q: What shape and size are most kettle holes?
a: Roundish and smaller than one hectare
Long and many kilometres in size
Square and as big as a canton
Pointed like a cone and a hundred metres high
91088.e: Most kettle holes are small and roundish. But they can be more than ten metres deep.
91088.m: Kettle holes are usually small and roundish.

91089.q: Where do you find kettle holes?
91089.e: Kettle holes form when glaciers break up. That is why you find them in the foothills of the Alps and in northern Germany.
91089.m: Kettle holes lie in areas from which glaciers have retreated.

91090.q: What often forms when a small kettle lake slowly fills in?
91090.e: Plant remains collect at the bottom of the lake over many centuries. Gradually the lake fills up and a bog forms.
91090.m: Kettle lakes that have filled in often turn into bogs.

a: A lake held back by glacier ice
A lake that freezes in winter
A lake in a volcanic crater
91091.e: A glacier can block a side valley like a dam. Behind it, water collects to form an ice-dammed lake.
91091.m: An ice-dammed lake is held back by glacier ice.

91092.q: Which well-known ice-dammed lake lies at the edge of the Great Aletsch Glacier?
91092.e: The Märjelensee lies in a hollow on the eastern edge of the Aletsch Glacier. In the 19th century it was up to 1.6 kilometres long.
91092.m: The Märjelensee is dammed by the Aletsch Glacier.

91093.q: What holds back the Märjelensee at the edge of the Aletsch Glacier?
91093.e: The Märjelensee lies in a hollow on the eastern edge of the Aletsch Glacier. The glacier ice blocks the outflow like a dam.
91093.m: The Märjelensee is dammed by the Aletsch Glacier.

91094.q: Through which valley did the water drain when the Märjelensee burst in the 19th century?
91094.e: The water drained through crevasses in the glacier and caused floods in the Massa. The Massa flows from the Aletsch Glacier to the Rhône.
91094.m: Outbursts of the Märjelensee caused floods in the Massa valley.

91095.q: Which big river does the meltwater of the Aletsch Glacier flow into?
91095.e: The meltwater flows through the Massa into the Rhône valley. Outbursts of the Märjelensee also caused floods there.
91095.m: The water of the Aletsch Glacier flows into the Rhône.

91096.q: Why is the Märjelensee much smaller today than in the 19th century?
91096.e: The glacier is much thinner today and holds back less water. The natural lake is hardly 100 metres long any more and drains almost every year.
91096.m: Because the glacier is shrinking, the Märjelensee has become small.

91097.q: What is a sudden outburst of a glacier lake called, using a word from Icelandic?
91097.e: In Iceland, dammed glacier lakes often burst. The Icelandic word “jökulhlaup” means roughly “glacier run”.
91097.m: A jökulhlaup is the sudden outburst of a glacier lake.

91098.q: Which huge ice-dammed lake in North America was named after a Swiss scientist?
91098.e: After the last cold period, a huge lake was dammed up at the edge of the North American ice sheet. It was named after Louis Agassiz.
91098.m: The huge Lake Agassiz in North America was an ice-dammed lake.

91099.q: What is a rock glacier made of?
a: Rock debris with ice in between
91099.e: A rock glacier is a mixture of stones and ice. It creeps slowly down the slope like a thick paste.
91099.m: A rock glacier consists of debris and ice.

91100.q: What ground condition does an active rock glacier need?
91100.e: The ice in a rock glacier only remains if the ground is permanently frozen. That is why rock glaciers are typical of permafrost.
91100.m: Rock glaciers exist where there is permafrost.

91101.q: How fast does an active rock glacier typically move?
a: About 10 centimetres to 1 metre per year
91101.e: Active rock glaciers typically creep 0.1 to 1 metre per year. That is much slower than most ice glaciers.
91101.m: Rock glaciers creep only a few decimetres per year.

91102.q: What happens to rock glaciers when the climate gets warmer?
a: The ice inside thaws and the slope can become unstable
91102.e: If the permafrost thaws, the ice between the stones melts. The debris can then creep faster or slide away.
91102.m: Warmth makes the ice in rock glaciers thaw.

91103.q: Why do non-experts often not recognise a rock glacier?
a: The ice is hidden under blocks of rock
It is only visible at night
91103.e: The surface is made of coarse blocks of rock. You cannot see the ice underneath, so it looks like an ordinary scree slope.
91103.m: In rock glaciers, the ice hides under stones.

91104.q: What does a fossil rock glacier that no longer contains ice tell us?
a: That it used to be colder there
That there was a sea there
That there was a desert there
91104.e: Fossil rock glaciers lie outside today's permafrost. They show that there used to be permafrost there, and therefore a colder climate.
91104.m: Fossil rock glaciers are evidence of a colder climate in the past.

91105.q: Where in Switzerland do you find rock glaciers?
a: On the shores of Lake Geneva
91105.e: Rock glaciers need permanently frozen ground. In Switzerland this only exists high up in the Alps, for example in the Engadine.
91105.m: Rock glaciers are found high in the mountains.

a: A cable car up the Titlis
91106.e: GLAMOS stands for “Glacier Monitoring Switzerland”. The network observes and records the changes in Swiss glaciers.
91106.m: GLAMOS measures the changes in Swiss glaciers.

91107.q: Why are Swiss glaciers measured every year?
a: To see how the climate affects them
To turn their ice into drinking water
91107.e: Glaciers react to temperature and amounts of snow. The GLAMOS measurements therefore show how the climate is changing.
91107.m: Glacier measurements show the effects of climate change.

91108.q: How long have the lengths of Swiss glaciers been observed?
91108.e: Systematic observation of glacier lengths began in 1880. The Swiss records are among the oldest in the world.
91108.m: Swiss glacier lengths have been observed for more than 140 years.

91109.q: What happened to the Swiss glaciers in the glacier year 2026?
a: They lost a great deal of ice
They stayed exactly the same size
They moved onto the Swiss Plateau
91109.e: In 2026, more than 5 per cent of the remaining ice melted away. The causes were a winter with little snow and a hot, dry summer.
91109.m: In 2026, the Swiss glaciers lost a great deal of ice.

91110.q: About how many glaciers did the Swiss glacier inventory of 2016 count?
91110.e: The 2016 inventory counted about 1400 glaciers. Many of them are very small, and since 1970 more than 1000 glaciers in Switzerland have disappeared completely.
91110.m: The 2016 glacier inventory counted about 1400 Swiss glaciers.

91111.q: What do glaciologists use to measure how much ice melts in summer?
91111.e: Poles are drilled into the ice, and later scientists measure how far they stick out. This shows how many centimetres of ice have melted.
91111.m: Poles drilled into the ice show how much ice has melted.

91112.q: Why does the glacier year end at the end of September?
a: The summer melt is over by then
It is the coldest day of the year
91112.e: The glacier year runs from 1 October to 30 September. It begins in autumn with new snow and ends when the summer melt is over.
91112.m: The glacier year ends after the summer melt at the end of September.

91113.q: By how much did the ice volume of Swiss glaciers decrease in the five years up to 2026?
91113.e: According to GLAMOS, the ice volume shrank by almost a fifth in these five years. The years 2022, 2023 and 2026 brought especially large losses.
91113.m: In five years, Swiss glaciers lost almost 20 per cent of their ice.

91114.q: What do you call the clear liquid that runs through the filter paper during filtration?
91114.e: Whatever passes through the filter is called the filtrate. It only contains particles small enough for the pores.
91114.m: The liquid that has run through is called the filtrate.

91115.q: What is the solid that stays behind in the filter paper during filtration called?
91115.e: Particles too large for the pores of the filter stay behind in the filter as residue.
91115.m: What gets caught in the filter is called the residue.

91116.q: Which mixture can you separate by filtering?
91116.e: Sand does not dissolve in water; its grains are much larger than the pores in the filter paper and so they get caught.
91116.m: Undissolved solids can be filtered out.

91117.q: Why can’t you filter table salt out of salt water?
a: The salt is dissolved and fits through the pores
The salt is heavier than water
The salt blocks the filter at once
The salt evaporates in the filter
91117.e: When salt dissolves, it breaks up into tiny particles much smaller than the pores of the filter paper. So they run through with the water.
91117.m: Dissolved substances pass through any ordinary filter.

91118.q: Which property of substances is used in filtration?
91118.e: The filter works like a very fine sieve: large particles are held back, small ones get through.
91118.m: A filter separates substances by the size of their particles.

91119.q: What do you call a mixture of a liquid with undissolved solid grains spread through it?
91119.e: In a suspension, solid particles float in a liquid, for example clay in water. Such mixtures can be filtered easily.
91119.m: A suspension contains undissolved solid particles in a liquid.

91120.q: What is a filter paper with many folds, through which liquid runs faster, called?
91120.e: The many folds make the area the liquid can flow through larger. So a fluted filter filters faster than a simply folded paper.
91120.m: A fluted filter has more area and so filters faster.

91121.q: Which piece of lab equipment do you put the folded filter paper into when filtering?
91121.e: The filter paper is placed in a funnel that stands on a container. The liquid runs down through the paper and funnel.
91121.m: When filtering, the filter paper sits in a funnel.

91122.q: In many waterworks, what material is water passed through to filter out suspended particles?
91122.e: Sand filters hold back suspended particles and cloudiness. They are often used in treating drinking water, for example lake water.
91122.m: Sand filters clean water in waterworks.

91123.q: What is the liquid collected after the condenser during distillation called?
91123.e: The vapour turns back into liquid in the condenser and drips into the receiver. This collected liquid is called the distillate.
91123.m: The collected product of a distillation is called the distillate.

91124.q: What is the glass tube surrounded by cold water, in which the vapour turns back into liquid during distillation, called?
91124.e: The Liebig condenser is a double-walled glass tube. Cold water flows on the outside, and on the inside the hot vapour cools and turns back into liquid.
91124.m: In the Liebig condenser, the vapour turns back into liquid.

91125.q: At roughly what temperature does pure alcohol (ethanol) boil?
91125.e: Ethanol boils at around 78 °C, water only at 100 °C. So when a mixture is heated, mostly the alcohol evaporates first.

91126.q: Which substance is distilled off from fermented cherries when making schnapps?
91126.e: Alcohol boils before water. When heated, it evaporates first and is collected in the condenser.
91126.m: When making schnapps, the alcohol is separated off.

91127.q: What do you get as the distillate when you distil salt water?
91127.e: Only the water evaporates and turns back into liquid in the condenser. The salt stays behind in the flask.
91127.m: When salt water is distilled, the salt stays in the flask.

91128.q: Which process is used in a refinery to split crude oil into petrol, diesel and other parts?
91128.e: In the distillation tower, the vapours rise. Parts with different boiling ranges are drawn off at different heights as fractions.
91128.m: Crude oil is split into fractions with different boiling ranges.

91129.q: What is it called when a gas turns into a liquid?
91129.e: In condensation, a substance changes from a gas to a liquid. In distillation, this happens in the condenser.
91129.m: Condensing means vapour turns back into liquid.

91130.q: In a distillation, at what height is the thermometer bulb placed?
a: Level with the side arm leading to the condenser
Right at the bottom in the boiling liquid
91130.e: The thermometer should measure the temperature of the vapour flowing into the condenser. This shows which substance is passing over.
91130.m: In distillation, the thermometer measures the vapour at the side arm to the condenser.

91131.q: What do you do when you decant?
a: Carefully pour off the liquid above the sediment
91131.e: When decanting, you let the solid sink and then carefully pour off the liquid above it.

91132.q: What is the sinking of solid particles in a liquid, which you wait for before decanting, called?
91132.e: Heavier particles slowly sink to the bottom because of gravity. This settling is called sedimentation.
91132.m: In sedimentation, solids settle at the bottom.

91133.q: Which property of substances is used when letting a mixture settle and decanting?
91133.e: Particles with a greater density than the liquid sink to the bottom. This separates the sediment from the liquid.
91133.m: Decanting relies on the difference in density.

91134.q: What do you have to wait for before decanting?
a: Until the solid has settled at the bottom
91134.e: Only when the solid lies at the bottom can you pour off the clear liquid above it.
91134.m: Before decanting, you let the solid settle.

91135.q: What is the glass carafe that wine is poured into when it is decanted called?
91135.e: The decanter gets its name from decanting. The wine is poured in slowly and the sediment stays in the bottle.
91135.m: A decanter is a carafe for pouring wine into.

91136.q: In the lab, what do you let the liquid run down when decanting, so that nothing splashes?
91136.e: A glass rod held at an angle guides the liquid calmly into the new container. That way the sediment is hardly stirred up.
91136.m: A glass rod helps you pour off cleanly.

91137.q: Why is decanting a less clean way of separating than filtering?
a: Fine particles are easily carried along
91137.e: When pouring off, some liquid always stays with the sediment, and very fine, light particles float along. So people often filter afterwards as well.
91137.m: Decanting is quick, but not completely exact.

91138.q: In which part of a sewage works do the undissolved bits of dirt in waste water settle at the bottom?
91138.e: In the primary settling tank, the waste water flows slowly. Undissolved substances sink as sludge, and the water at the top flows on.
91138.m: Sludge settles in the primary settling tank.

a: A substance is dissolved out with a solvent
A substance is evaporated by heat
91139.e: In an extraction, a suitable solvent dissolves certain substances out of a mixture. Other substances stay behind.
91139.m: Extracting means dissolving a substance out with a solvent.

91140.q: Which everyday activity is an extraction?
91140.e: Hot water dissolves colour, scent and flavour substances out of the tea leaves. The leaves themselves stay behind.
91140.m: When making tea, hot water extracts flavour substances.

91141.q: In the school lab, what do you use to dissolve the green leaf pigment out of crushed leaves?
91141.e: Green chlorophyll hardly dissolves in water but dissolves well in alcohol. So the leaves are ground up with methylated spirits or ethanol.
91141.m: Chlorophyll can easily be dissolved out with alcohol.

91142.q: Which piece of lab equipment is used to separate two liquids that do not mix, for example after an extraction?
91142.e: In the separating funnel, the two liquids form two layers. You let the lower layer run out through the tap at the bottom.
91142.m: A separating funnel separates liquids that do not mix.

91143.q: How is sugar obtained from cut-up sugar beet in the sugar factories at Aarberg and Frauenfeld?
a: By soaking it out with hot water
91143.e: The beet slices are soaked in hot water. The sugar dissolves; this raw juice is then cleaned and thickened.
91143.m: Sugar is extracted from the beet slices with hot water.

91144.q: Which property of substances is used in extraction?
91144.e: A solvent dissolves only certain substances well. Because substances dissolve in it to different degrees, they can be separated.
91144.m: In extraction, solubility is what counts.

91145.q: How is caffeine removed from coffee beans to make decaffeinated coffee?
a: By roasting for a long time
91145.e: The beans are treated, for example, with water or with carbon dioxide under pressure. This solvent takes up the caffeine.
91145.m: Decaffeinated coffee is made by extraction.

91146.q: Why do you make tea with hot water rather than cold?
a: Hot water dissolves the substances out faster
Cold water dissolves nothing at all
Hot water makes the leaves bigger
Cold water turns bitter at once
91146.e: In hot water the particles move faster. Colour and flavour substances are therefore dissolved out of the leaves more quickly.

91147.q: In chromatography, what is the solvent that moves through the paper called?
91147.e: The solvent moves and carries the substances with it, so it is called the mobile phase.
91147.m: The mobile phase is the moving solvent.

91148.q: In paper chromatography, what is the paper, which stays in place, called?
91148.e: The paper does not move; it is the stationary, or fixed, phase. The substances stick to it with different strengths.
91148.m: The stationary phase stays in its place.

91149.q: What can you use at home to separate the dyes in a felt-tip pen?
91149.e: You draw a dot on a coffee filter and stand it in a little water. The water rises and separates the dyes.
91149.m: You can separate dyes with filter paper and water.

91150.q: Why do the dyes in an ink separate during chromatography?
a: They stick with different strengths and dissolve to different degrees
They have different weights and sink
They are bleached by light to different degrees
91150.e: A dye that dissolves well in the solvent and sticks only weakly to the paper travels far. Another stops sooner.
91150.m: Substances travel different distances depending on how they stick and dissolve.

91151.q: What often appears when you do chromatography on a black felt-tip pen?
a: It is made of several dyes
It is made of black only
91151.e: Different colours such as blue, yellow and red separate on the paper. Together they look black.
91151.m: Black ink is often a mixture of several dyes.

91152.q: Why do you draw the start line in paper chromatography with a pencil?
a: Graphite does not dissolve in the solvent
Pencil is easier to rub out
Pencil makes the paper more absorbent
91152.e: Ink from a biro or felt-tip pen would travel along too and spoil the result. Graphite stays where it is.
91152.m: The start line is drawn in pencil because graphite does not travel.

91153.q: Why must the start line be above the level of the solvent?
a: Otherwise the samples dissolve straight into the solvent
Otherwise the solvent does not move
Otherwise the solvent evaporates too quickly
91153.e: If the starting spot dips into the solvent, the sample is washed into the container instead of being carried upwards.
91153.m: The samples must not dip into the solvent.

91154.q: What is the result of a chromatography, with its separated spots or bands, called?
91154.e: The finished, dried paper with the separated spots of substances is called a chromatogram.
91154.m: A chromatogram shows the separated substances.

91155.q: What is chromatography used for in laboratories, for example?
91155.e: Chromatography separates mixtures into their parts. This makes it possible to find even tiny amounts of doping substances or poisons.
91155.m: Chromatography helps to detect substances in mixtures.

91156.q: By which property does a centrifuge separate a mixture?
91156.e: Because of the fast spinning, particles with greater density are pushed outwards more strongly. This separates them from lighter parts.
91156.m: A centrifuge separates substances by their density.

91157.q: Which force pushes the heavy particles outwards in a centrifuge?
91157.e: When spinning fast, a centrifugal force acts. It is much stronger than gravity, so separation is quicker than letting things settle.
91157.m: Centrifugal force speeds up separation in the centrifuge.

91158.q: Which part collects at the top of the tube when blood is spun in a centrifuge?
91158.e: The heavier blood cells sink to the bottom. The yellowish, liquid blood plasma stays at the top.
91158.m: When blood is centrifuged, the plasma is at the top.

91159.q: Which kitchen gadget works on the principle of a centrifuge?
91159.e: In a salad spinner, a basket spins quickly. The water drops fly outwards through the holes and the salad stays inside.
91159.m: A salad spinner separates water from salad by spinning.

91160.q: In a dairy, what is separated from milk with a centrifuge?
91160.e: Milk fat has a lower density than the rest of the milk. In the milk centrifuge it collects on the inside as cream and is separated off.
91160.m: A centrifuge is used to separate cream from milk.

91161.q: What must you check before starting a lab centrifuge?
a: Opposite tubes must weigh the same
The tubes must be completely empty
All tubes must have different weights
91161.e: If the centrifuge is loaded unevenly, it starts to wobble and can be damaged. So tubes of equal weight are placed opposite each other.
91161.m: A centrifuge must always be loaded in balance.

91162.q: In which unit do you give how fast a centrifuge spins?
91162.e: The speed is usually given in revolutions per minute. Lab centrifuges often reach several thousand revolutions per minute.
91162.m: Spinning speed is measured in revolutions per minute.

91163.q: Which washing machine programme step uses the principle of a centrifuge?
91163.e: During the spin, the drum turns very fast. The water is pushed outwards through the holes in the drum.
91163.m: During the spin, water is pushed out of the washing.

91164.q: What must you do with long hair before working with a Bunsen burner?
91164.e: Loose hair can get into the flame and catch fire. That is why you always tie it back in the lab.
91164.m: Tie long hair back when using a Bunsen burner.

91165.q: What colour is the Bunsen burner flame when the air hole is closed?
91165.e: Without extra air there is too little oxygen and the gas burns incompletely. The flame is then calm, bright yellow and less hot.
91165.m: With the air hole closed, a yellow, luminous flame burns.

91166.q: What is the hot blue flame with the air hole open called?
91166.e: With plenty of air, the gas burns completely and very hot. The flame is blue and makes a roaring sound.
91166.m: The roaring flame is blue and very hot.

91167.q: Where is the roaring flame of a Bunsen burner hottest?
a: Just above the tip of the inner cone
At the very outer edge of the flame
91167.e: In the inner cone, the gas has not yet burnt completely. Just above it, burning is strongest and the temperature highest.
91167.m: The hottest point is just above the inner cone.

91168.q: How do you set the air hole when you light a Bunsen burner?
91168.e: With the air hole closed, lighting gives a clearly visible, calm flame, and the flame does not strike back. Afterwards you open the air hole as needed.
91168.m: Light a Bunsen burner with the air hole closed.

91169.q: Why is the flame luminous when the air hole is closed?
a: Because of metal in the burner tube
91169.e: When there is too little air, tiny carbon particles form. They glow yellow in the flame and make it luminous.
91169.m: Glowing soot makes the flame yellow.

91171.q: Which gas usually burns in the Bunsen burner in a school lab?
91171.e: Most labs have a natural gas supply. Natural gas is mainly methane; there are also burners for propane or butane from cartridges.
91171.m: A Bunsen burner usually burns natural gas.

91172.q: What do you wear to protect your eyes when working with a Bunsen burner?
91172.e: When heating, liquid can spray or glass can crack. Safety goggles protect your eyes from this.
91172.m: In the lab you wear safety goggles.

91173.q: What do you hold a test tube with when heating it over a flame?
91173.e: The glass gets very hot. A wooden or metal holder grips it safely and protects your fingers.
91173.m: Hold hot test tubes with a holder.

91174.q: Up to what level do you fill a test tube at most for heating?
91174.e: If there is too much liquid in the tube, it can easily shoot out when it boils. A third is a usual upper limit.
91174.m: Fill a test tube only a little for heating.

91175.q: What is the sudden, violent boiling of an overheated liquid, which can make it spray out, called?
91175.e: A liquid can be heated above its boiling point without forming bubbles. Then a lot of vapour suddenly forms and the liquid sprays out.
91175.m: Bumping can throw hot liquid out.

91176.q: How do you hold a test tube when heating it over a flame?
a: At an angle, shaking it gently
91176.e: Tilting and gently shaking spreads the heat evenly. This prevents liquid suddenly spraying out.
91176.m: When heating, hold the test tube at an angle and move it gently.

91177.q: Why does lab glass hardly ever crack when heated?
a: It expands only a little when warm
91177.e: Lab glass is a special glass that hardly expands when warm. So it rarely shatters, even with sudden temperature changes.
91177.m: Lab glass can cope with sudden temperature changes.

91178.q: What do you stand several test tubes in on the lab bench?
91178.e: Test tubes have round bottoms and cannot stand on their own. A rack holds them upright.
91178.m: Test tubes stand in a rack.

91179.q: What do you clean the inside of a test tube with?
91179.e: The long, narrow brush reaches the bottom of the narrow tube. This removes leftovers thoroughly.
91179.m: Test tubes are cleaned with a long brush.

91180.q: What is a conical flask usually made of?
91180.e: Conical flasks are usually made of a special glass that can withstand heat. You can also see clearly what is happening inside.
91180.m: Conical flasks are made of heat-resistant glass.

91181.q: What shape is a conical flask?
91181.e: The flask is wide and flat at the bottom and narrows towards the top into a narrow neck.
91181.m: A conical flask is cone-shaped with a flat bottom.

91182.q: What is the advantage of the narrow neck of a conical flask?
a: You can swirl the contents without spilling
It is easier to pour out
91182.e: Thanks to the sloping sides and narrow neck, hardly anything slops out when swirling. Less also evaporates.
91182.m: A conical flask is good for swirling.

91183.q: Which piece of equipment drips the solution into the conical flask during a titration?
91183.e: The burette is a long tube with a fine scale and a tap. With it you can read exactly how much solution has been added.
91183.m: In a titration, the solution drips from a burette.

91184.q: Why can a conical flask stand on the bench without a stand, but a round-bottomed flask cannot?
91184.e: The round-bottomed flask has a ball-shaped bottom and needs a cork ring or a stand. The conical flask stands safely thanks to its flat bottom.
91184.m: The flat bottom makes the conical flask stable.

91185.q: Which piece of equipment do you use instead of a conical flask to measure an amount of liquid accurately?
91185.e: The scale on a conical flask only gives rough amounts. A measuring cylinder is much more accurate.
91185.m: For accurate volumes you use a measuring cylinder.

91186.q: Why must you never close a conical flask tightly when heating it?
a: The pressure inside could burst it
The liquid would lose its colour
91186.e: When heated, air and vapour expand. In a tightly closed container the pressure rises until the glass can burst.
91186.m: Never heat containers that are tightly closed.

91187.q: What do you do with long hair in the lab?
91187.e: Loose hair can get into a flame or into chemicals. Tied back, it is safe.
91187.m: Long hair is tied back in the lab.

91188.q: What is forbidden while working in the chemistry lab?
91188.e: Chemicals could get onto food or into your mouth. That is why you never eat or drink in the lab.
91188.m: No eating and no drinking in the lab.

91189.q: When diluting a concentrated acid, what do you put into the container first?
91189.e: Mixing releases a lot of heat. If you pour the acid slowly into the water, the heat spreads out and nothing splashes. A rhyme to remember: “Do what you oughta, add acid to water.”

91190.q: How do you check the smell of a substance in the lab?
a: You waft the smell towards you with your hand
You hold your nose right over it
You breathe in deeply over the opening
You taste a little of it
91190.e: Some vapours irritate or damage the airways. By wafting, only a little of it reaches your nose.

91191.q: Where do you work with substances that give off poisonous or sharp-smelling fumes?
91191.e: The fume cupboard sucks the fumes away and carries them outside. That way they do not get into the air in the room.
91191.m: Poisonous fumes belong in the fume cupboard.

91192.q: What do you do first if a chemical splashes into your eye?
a: Rinse the eye with lots of water for a long time
Wait to see if it gets better
91192.e: Rinsing immediately for several minutes with lots of water, for example at the eyewash station, dilutes and removes the chemical. Then you go to the doctor.
91192.m: If a chemical gets into your eye, rinse at once with lots of water.

91193.q: Which emergency number do you call in Switzerland in case of poisoning to reach Tox Info Suisse?
91193.e: Tox Info Suisse gives advice on poisoning around the clock on 145. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 1414 Rega.
91193.m: In Switzerland, number 145 helps with poisoning.

91194.q: Why do you never suck liquids into a pipette with your mouth?
a: The liquid would get too warm
91194.e: When sucking with your mouth, some liquid easily gets into it. So you always use a pipette filler, for example a pipette bulb.
91194.m: Fill pipettes only with a pipette filler.

91195.q: In the lab, what do you use to smother a small fire on someone’s clothing?
91195.e: The fire blanket is wrapped around the person or laid over the fire. It takes the oxygen away from the fire.

91196.q: What are the hazard pictograms on chemicals for?
a: They warn about the dangers of the substance
They show where the substance was made
91196.e: The pictograms show at a glance whether a substance is, for example, toxic, corrosive or flammable. They are the same all over the world.
91196.m: Hazard pictograms warn about the dangers of a substance.

91197.q: What do today’s hazard pictograms on chemicals look like?
a: A black symbol in a diamond with a red border
A white symbol on a green circle
A yellow triangle with a blue border
A black symbol on an orange square
91197.e: Today’s pictograms are squares standing on their corner, with a red border, white background and black symbol. The orange squares are the old symbols.
91197.m: Hazard pictograms are diamonds with a red border.

91198.q: What does the GHS pictogram showing a person’s upper body with a star on the chest warn about?
a: Serious health damage, such as cancer
91198.e: This pictogram stands, for example, for substances that cause cancer, change genetic material or seriously damage the airways.
91198.m: The silhouette with a star warns of serious long-term health damage.

91199.q: What does the GHS pictogram with an exclamation mark mean?
91199.e: The exclamation mark warns of less serious dangers, such as irritation of the skin, eyes or airways.
91199.m: The exclamation mark stands for irritant or harmful substances.

91200.q: Which GHS pictogram do you often find on a drain cleaner?
91200.e: Drain cleaners often contain strong alkalis. The pictogram shows liquid attacking a hand and a surface.
91200.m: Corrosive cleaners carry the corrosive pictogram.

91201.q: What should you do before using a cleaning product with a hazard pictogram?
a: Read the instructions on the label
91201.e: The label says what the dangers are and how to protect yourself, for example with gloves or safety goggles.
91201.m: Always read the label before use.

91202.q: What does the GHS pictogram with a gas cylinder stand for?
91202.e: It marks containers with compressed or liquefied gases. These can burst when heated.
91202.m: The gas cylinder warns of gases under pressure.

91203.q: Which two signal words appear next to the pictograms on GHS labels?
91203.e: “Danger” is used for serious hazards, “Warning” for less serious ones.

91204.q: What did the older hazard symbols look like that were used in Switzerland before the GHS pictograms?
91204.e: As in the EU, orange squares with a black symbol used to be the rule. After a transition period they were replaced by the GHS pictograms.
91204.m: The old hazard symbols were orange squares.

91205.q: When do you wear safety goggles in chemistry lessons?
a: Only when the teacher is looking
91205.e: Splashes and splinters come unexpectedly. So you wear the goggles from the beginning to the end of an experiment.
91205.m: Safety goggles stay on throughout the experiment.

91206.q: What do people who wear glasses put on in the lab for protection?
a: Over-goggles on top of their own glasses
91206.e: Normal glasses have no side protection and are not shatterproof enough. Over-goggles fit over your own glasses.
91206.m: If you wear glasses, put over-goggles on top in the lab.

91207.q: Why do lab safety goggles have side shields?
a: So they do not steam up
91207.e: Chemicals or glass splinters can also get into the eye from the side. The side shields prevent this.
91207.m: Side shields protect the eyes from the side.

91208.q: Why are the lenses of many safety goggles made of plastic instead of glass?
a: Plastic does not shatter on impact
91208.e: Glass can break when hit and throw splinters into the eye. Impact-resistant plastic stays whole.
91208.m: Safety goggles have shatterproof plastic lenses.

91209.q: Which safety goggles protect best against liquid splashes?
a: Ones that fit tightly against the face all round
91209.e: Safety goggles that seal all the way round let no splashes through from above, below or the side.
91209.m: Tight-fitting safety goggles keep splashes out.

91210.q: Why do welding goggles have dark lenses?
a: To protect against glaring light and UV radiation
So you can see better in the dark
So they do not get scratched
91210.e: Welding produces extremely bright light with a lot of UV radiation. Without dark filters, the eyes could be injured.
91210.m: Dark welding lenses protect against glaring light.

91211.q: What does the mandatory sign “Wear eye protection” look like?
a: A blue circle with a white goggles symbol
A yellow triangle with black goggles
A red circle with crossed-out goggles
A green square with white goggles
91211.e: Mandatory signs are round blue signs with a white symbol. They show what you must do.
91211.m: Round blue signs show something you must do.

91212.q: Why is it better to wear glasses rather than contact lenses under your safety goggles in the lab?
a: Chemicals can get under the lens
91212.e: If a chemical gets into the eye, it can be trapped under the contact lens. This makes rinsing it out harder.
91212.m: Contact lenses make it harder to rinse out the eyes.

91313.q: What is a social network on the internet?
a: A platform where you have a profile and connect with others
A cable network that supplies houses with electricity
A search engine that only finds books
91313.e: In social networks, users create profiles, share posts and follow others. Well-known examples are Instagram and TikTok.
91313.m: Social networks connect people through profiles and posts on the internet.

91314.q: From what age do many large social networks allow your own account according to their terms of use?
91314.e: Platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Facebook set a minimum age of 13 in their terms of use.
91314.m: Many social networks are only allowed from the age of 13.

91315.q: Which social network did Mark Zuckerberg found in 2004 with fellow students?
91315.e: Facebook started in 2004 at Harvard University and then spread around the world.
91315.m: Facebook was founded by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004.

91316.q: What does it mean when a profile on a social network is set to “private”?
a: Only approved contacts see the posts
Everyone can see all the posts
The profile has been deleted for ever
The profile costs money every month
91316.e: With a private profile you have to approve requests before others can see the posts. This protects your privacy.
91316.m: A private profile shows posts only to approved contacts.

a: A keyword with a # sign in front of it
A secret password for the account
91317.e: Hashtags such as #Switzerland tag posts with a topic and make them easier to find.
91317.m: A hashtag links posts to a topic with the # sign.

91318.q: How do free social networks mainly make money?
91318.e: The platforms show advertising that is often tailored to the users' interests. To do this, they analyse data about their behaviour.
91318.m: With free networks you often pay with your data.

91319.q: Which detail should not go in a public profile for safety reasons?
91319.e: Your home address tells strangers where you live. You should not show personal details like this publicly.
91319.m: Personal details such as your address stay private.

91320.q: What is the “feed” on a social network?
a: The constantly updated list of new posts
The storage space for your own photos
91320.e: The feed shows posts from accounts you follow and often recommended content too. You scroll through it from top to bottom.
91320.m: In the feed you keep seeing new posts.

91321.q: What does a recommendation system on a video platform do?
a: It suggests content you might like
It only counts the number of subscribers
91321.e: A recommendation system works out which videos, songs or products suit a person and shows them.

91322.q: Which data does a recommendation system typically use?
a: What you have watched or clicked on so far
Your shoe size from your passport
91322.e: Your past behaviour, for example videos watched, clicks and ratings, shows what interests you.
91322.m: Recommendations are based on what you clicked on before.

91323.q: An online shop shows: “Customers who bought this also bought ...”. What is this suggestion based on?
a: On the purchases of other customers with similar taste
On the weather where you live
On the colour of the packaging
91323.e: This method is called collaborative filtering. If you like similar things to others, you get suggestions from their preferences.
91323.m: Recommendations are often based on the behaviour of similar users.

91324.q: An app recommends more crime novels to you because you have already read crime novels. What is this recommendation based on?
a: On features of the content you like
On the colour of the book cover
91324.e: This is called content-based filtering: the system looks for content with similar features such as genre or topic.
91324.m: Content-based recommendations look for things similar to what you already like.

91325.q: Why do platforms want their recommendations to fit as well as possible?
a: So that users stay on the platform longer
So that the computer uses less electricity
So that the internet gets faster
So that fewer videos are uploaded
91325.e: The longer people stay, the more adverts they see or the more they buy. That is why good recommendations are valuable to companies.
91325.m: Good recommendations keep users on a platform for a long time.

91326.q: Which streaming service offered a prize of 1 million US dollars in 2006 for a better recommendation algorithm?
91326.e: In the “Netflix Prize”, teams were to improve the film suggestions by 10 per cent. In 2009 a team won the prize money.
91326.m: Netflix used a competition to look for better film suggestions.

91327.q: What is the cold start problem with recommendation systems?
a: There is hardly any data yet about new users
The servers run more slowly in winter
The phone does not start in the cold
91327.e: A recommendation system needs information about preferences. With a new account this is missing, which is why apps often ask for favourite topics at the start.
91327.m: Without data a recommendation system cannot suggest anything suitable yet.

91328.q: How can you influence the suggestions of a recommendation system yourself?
a: By deleting the history or choosing “Not interested”
91328.e: Many apps let you delete the viewing history or mark content as not interesting. Then the suggestions change.
91328.m: With your history and feedback you help steer your recommendations.

91329.q: What is a filter bubble on the internet?
a: You mainly see content that matches your own opinion
A soap bubble on the screensaver
91329.e: Algorithms mainly show you what matches your previous clicks. So you see fewer and fewer other opinions. Eli Pariser made the term well known in 2011.
91329.m: In a filter bubble you mainly see your own opinion.

91330.q: What is an echo chamber on the internet?
a: A group in which like-minded people confirm each other
A room with especially good loudspeakers
91330.e: In an echo chamber you hear your own opinion again and again, like an echo. Opposing voices hardly appear.
91330.m: In an echo chamber your own opinion keeps echoing back.

91331.q: What helps most to get out of a filter bubble?
a: Deliberately reading different sources and opinions
Liking as many posts as possible
91331.e: If you use newspapers, broadcasters and websites with different points of view, you get a fuller picture.
91331.m: Different sources open your view beyond your own bubble.

91332.q: How does a filter bubble mainly come about?
a: Algorithms choose content based on your previous clicks
The internet is switched off at night
Too many people are online at the same time
The computer has too little memory
91332.e: If you often click on similar content, you are shown even more of it. So the choice becomes more and more one-sided.
91332.m: Every click helps shape what you will see in future.

91333.q: Which danger to democracy is often linked to filter bubbles?
a: Other opinions are hardly noticed any more
The right to vote becomes more expensive
Newspapers are no longer allowed to appear
91333.e: Democracy depends on people knowing and weighing up different arguments. If someone only sees their own view, this becomes harder.
91333.m: For good decisions you also need to know other opinions.

91334.q: Is the strength of the effect of filter bubbles scientifically undisputed?
a: Yes, it has been measured and proven exactly
Yes, filter bubbles only exist in Switzerland
No, because filter bubbles are banned
91334.e: Some studies find clear effects, others only weak ones. Many people still use different sources anyway.
91334.m: How strongly filter bubbles work is still being discussed in research.

91335.q: What is the tendency to believe mainly information that supports your own opinion called?
91335.e: Confirmation bias is a well-known thinking pattern: you are more likely to notice information that fits and to think it more believable.
91335.m: Our brain likes information that confirms our opinion.

91336.q: Which two terms make up the word “deepfake”?
91336.e: Deep learning is a method of machine learning, and “fake” means not genuine.
91336.m: Deepfakes are made with deep learning and are fake.

91338.q: How can you sometimes recognise a deepfake video?
a: By blurred edges around the face or unnatural blinking
By a particularly short file name
91338.e: Errors often show in hair, teeth, the edges of the face or in facial expressions that do not match the sound. But good fakes can hardly be recognised any more.
91338.m: Strange edges and unnatural facial expressions can point to a deepfake.

91339.q: What should you do before forwarding a surprising video of a famous person?
a: Check whether reliable sources are reporting it
Send it to all your contacts immediately
Convert it to black and white first
91339.e: If well-known news sources report nothing about it, be careful. That way you do not spread fakes any further.

a: With AI programs that learn from many pictures
With a magnifying glass and scissors
91340.e: AI programs are trained with many photos and videos of a person. After that they can create new, fake recordings.
91340.m: Deepfakes are made with AI that learns from many pictures.

91341.q: What do fraudsters misuse voices copied with AI for?
a: To pretend to be relatives on the telephone
91341.e: With just a few seconds of recording, AI can imitate a voice. Fraudsters then call and ask for money, supposedly as a family member.
91341.m: If someone asks for money on the telephone, always call back on a number you know.

a: Exchanging one face for another in a picture or video
91342.e: To swap means to exchange. Face swap is a common form of deepfake.
91342.m: In a face swap one face is exchanged for another.

a: A program that talks with people in writing
91343.e: A chatbot answers questions in a chat window or by voice. “Bot” is short for robot.
91343.m: A chatbot is a program for chatting.

91344.e: Joseph Weizenbaum developed ELIZA in the mid-1960s. The program played a therapist, and many people believed it understood them.
91344.m: ELIZA is considered one of the first chatbots.

91345.q: Which company released the chatbot ChatGPT in November 2022?
91345.e: ChatGPT was released by OpenAI on 30 November 2022 and had over a million users after just a few days.
91345.m: ChatGPT comes from the company OpenAI.

91346.q: How does a language model like ChatGPT produce its answer?
a: It calculates word by word what is likely to fit
It looks up every answer in an encyclopaedia
A person types the answer in the background
It always copies the first website
91346.e: GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer. The model was trained with a huge number of texts and builds the answer piece by piece from likely words.
91346.m: GPT is a pre-trained language model that creates text.

91347.q: What is a “hallucination” in an AI chatbot?
a: An invented answer that sounds convincing
A colourful picture on the screen
91347.e: Language models calculate likely words and can invent false facts or sources while doing so. That is why you must check important statements.
