92817.q: Roughly how many seismic measuring stations does the Swiss Seismological Service run?
92817.e: The stations are spread across the whole country. Some are in caves, tunnels or boreholes.
92817.m: The Seismological Service monitors Switzerland with over 200 measuring stations.

92818.q: On average, how many earthquakes a year can people feel in Switzerland?
92818.e: Most recorded quakes are too weak to feel. Only 10 to 20 a year on average are noticed by the population.
92818.m: In Switzerland, about 10 to 20 earthquakes are felt each year.

92819.q: How quickly does the Swiss Seismological Service publish the first automatic information about a quake?
92819.e: The measurement data are analysed automatically. The location, time and strength appear on the website within about 90 seconds.
92819.m: The first information about a quake appears after about 90 seconds.

92820.q: Why can earthquake instruments also detect banned nuclear bomb tests?
a: Underground explosions shake the ground like earthquakes
Nuclear bombs send out radio waves
92820.e: Underground nuclear tests cause vibrations like earthquakes. A station near Davos is part of a worldwide network that monitors the ban on such tests.
92820.m: Seismometers also help to detect banned nuclear tests.

92821.q: In which app does the Swiss Seismological Service publish earthquake reports from magnitude 2.5?
92821.e: Quakes from magnitude 2.5 are also shown in the MeteoSwiss app. The service also provides information on its website and on naturgefahren.ch.
92821.m: Earthquake reports from magnitude 2.5 appear in the MeteoSwiss app.

92822.q: Who else does the Swiss Seismological Service inform about large damaging quakes abroad?
92822.e: After big disaster quakes anywhere in the world, help from Switzerland may be needed. That is why the Humanitarian Aid Unit is informed quickly.
92822.m: After big quakes abroad, the Seismological Service informs humanitarian aid.

92823.q: Who monitors earthquakes in Switzerland on behalf of the federal government?
a: The Seismological Service at ETH Zurich
The fire brigade of each municipality
92823.e: Since 1914, monitoring earthquakes has been a federal task. Today the Swiss Seismological Service is a unit of ETH Zurich.
92823.m: The Swiss Seismological Service is part of ETH Zurich.

92824.q: Roughly how often can an earthquake of magnitude 6 or more be expected in Switzerland?
92824.e: According to the Swiss Seismological Service, such strong quakes only happen every 50 to 150 years. But they could cause great damage.
92824.m: A magnitude 6 quake can be expected in Switzerland every 50 to 150 years.

92825.q: On average, how often can an earthquake that causes damage be expected in Switzerland?
92825.e: Damaging quakes are rarer in Switzerland than ones you can feel. According to the Swiss earthquake risk model, such a quake can be expected about every 8 to 15 years.
92825.m: A damaging quake happens in Switzerland about every 8 to 15 years.

92826.q: Besides Valais, which two regions are among those most at risk from earthquakes in Switzerland?
92826.e: Valais, the Grisons and the Basel region are most at risk. On the Swiss Plateau and in Ticino the risk is lower.
92826.m: Besides Valais, Basel and the Grisons are especially at risk from earthquakes.

92827.q: Which geological structure does Basel lie on, which explains the earthquake risk there?
92827.e: The Upper Rhine Graben is a zone where the Earth's crust is being pulled apart. The quakes there are only indirectly linked to the formation of the Alps.
92827.m: Basel lies on the earthquake-active Upper Rhine Graben.

92828.q: What do Swiss building standards require of new buildings today?
a: They must be built to withstand earthquakes
They may only be made of wood
They may have at most two storeys
They may not have a cellar
92828.e: Since 2003, modern rules for earthquake-resistant building have applied in Switzerland. New buildings must be designed so that they survive a quake well.
92828.m: New buildings in Switzerland must be built to withstand earthquakes.

92829.q: How much can soft ground such as lake deposits strengthen the shaking compared to rock?
a: Up to about a thousand times
92829.e: In soft ground, the waves build up. That is why areas on lake shores or in river valleys are more strongly affected in a quake.
92829.m: Soft ground can make shaking up to ten times stronger.

92830.q: Which way of building helps a building to survive an earthquake better?
a: A symmetrical floor plan and walls that run down to the foundations
As many large windows on the ground floor as possible
A heavy roof on thin supports
A different floor plan on every storey
92830.e: Load-bearing walls should run from the roof down to the foundations. A regular floor plan stops the building from twisting when it is shaken.
92830.m: Earthquake-proof houses have a regular floor plan and continuous walls.

92831.q: What does the Swiss earthquake risk model show?
a: What damage a quake could cause
Exactly when the next quake will come
Where there are volcanoes in Switzerland
What the weather will be like after a quake
92831.e: The risk model combines hazard, ground, building methods and population. It estimates what damage a quake could cause to people and buildings.
92831.m: The earthquake risk model estimates possible damage.

92832.q: Why is the earthquake risk higher in densely populated cities than in rural areas with the same hazard?
a: There are more people and buildings that can be harmed
The ground shakes more in cities
There are no earthquakes in the countryside
92832.e: The hazard only describes how often and how strongly the ground shakes. The risk also depends on how many people and assets would be affected.
92832.m: The more people and buildings are affected, the greater the earthquake risk.

92833.q: In which canton did the severe Visp earthquake of 1855 take place?
92833.e: The quake shook Upper Valais in 1855. It is probably the strongest earthquake in the history of Valais.
92833.m: The Visp earthquake of 1855 hit Valais.

92834.q: In which valley was the epicentre of the 1855 earthquake?
92834.e: The epicentre was in the Vispertal south of Visp. Many buildings there, including churches, were badly damaged.
92834.m: The epicentre of the 1855 quake was in the Vispertal.

92835.q: Roughly what magnitude did the Visp earthquake of 1855 have, according to modern estimates?
92835.e: Estimates are about 6.2 to 6.4. That makes it one of the strongest quakes in Switzerland in recent centuries.
92835.m: The Visp earthquake of 1855 had a magnitude of a little over 6.

92836.q: What did the 1855 earthquake trigger near St. Niklaus?
92836.e: The shaking loosened masses of rock near St. Niklaus. The only known victim of the quake was killed by falling rocks.
92836.m: The Visp quake triggered a rockfall near St. Niklaus.

92837.q: What followed the main Visp quake of 1855?
92837.e: After the main quake, the ground in the Vispertal shook many more times. This made the population even more anxious.
92837.m: The Visp earthquake was followed by many aftershocks.

92838.q: How far away could the Visp earthquake of 1855 be felt?
a: Throughout Switzerland and in neighbouring countries
Only in the village of Visp
Only in the canton of Valais
92838.e: The quake was felt throughout Switzerland. There are also reports from Savoy, northern Italy, the Tyrol and southern Germany.
92838.m: The Visp earthquake was felt far beyond Switzerland.

92839.q: What can an earthquake change about springs?
a: How much water flows out of them
The height of the mountains above them
92839.e: Earthquakes can change the paths of groundwater in the rock. After the Visp quake of 1855, some springs had a different amount of water.
92839.m: Earthquakes can make springs dry up or flow more strongly.

92840.q: What does the intensity of an earthquake describe?
a: How strong the effects are at a place
How deep the source of the earthquake is
92840.e: The intensity describes what people feel and what damage is done to buildings. In the Visp quake of 1855 there was severe damage to buildings.
92840.m: The intensity describes the effects of a quake at a place.

a: A mudflow of volcanic ash, rock and water
92841.e: A lahar forms when loose volcanic material mixes with water. It flows down the valleys like wet concrete.
92841.m: A lahar is a volcanic mudflow.

92842.q: Why is a lahar so destructive?
a: It is as heavy as wet concrete and sweeps houses away
It consists only of poisonous gas
It moves only a few metres per year
92842.e: A lahar is a thick mass of water, ash and rock. With great force it sweeps away bridges, houses and trees.
92842.m: Lahars are heavy and sweep everything away.

92843.q: Where do lahars usually flow down a volcano?
92843.e: Like water, lahars follow the land. They flow down stream beds and valleys, where there are often villages.

92844.q: Roughly how many people died from the lahars in Armero in 1985?
92844.e: Most of the inhabitants were taken by surprise in their sleep. It was one of the worst volcanic disasters of the 20th century.
92844.m: The lahar disaster of Armero claimed over 20,000 lives.

92845.q: What can cause a lahar even long after a volcanic eruption?
92845.e: Fresh ash lies loosely on the slopes. Heavy rain can turn it into a mudflow even years later.
92845.m: Heavy rain can trigger lahars even years after an eruption.

92846.q: Why are volcanoes covered by glaciers especially dangerous for lahars?
a: During an eruption, ice melts and provides lots of water
92846.e: Hot material melts snow and ice in a short time. The meltwater sweeps ash and rock along with it.
92846.m: Melting glaciers on volcanoes can feed huge lahars.

92847.q: What should you do if a lahar is coming?
a: Wait in the car in the valley
92847.e: Lahars flow in valleys and river beds. Anyone who quickly escapes to higher ground is safest.
92847.m: If a lahar comes, escape to higher ground.

92848.q: How can people in valleys below a volcano be warned about lahars in time?
92848.e: Measuring instruments in the valleys notice a mudflow early. Then sirens sound, and people have time to escape.
92848.m: Measuring instruments and sirens warn of lahars.

92849.q: How does a pyroclastic flow often form?
a: A column of ash or a lava dome collapses
Lava slowly cools in the sea
Rain washes ash into the valley
A glacier slides off the volcano
92849.e: If a column of ash becomes too heavy, it collapses. A breaking lava dome can also set off a glowing avalanche of gas, ash and rock.
92849.m: Pyroclastic flows often form when a column of ash or a lava dome collapses.

92850.q: How fast can a pyroclastic flow travel?
a: Over 100 km/h, sometimes several hundred km/h
About as fast as someone walking
92850.e: The hot mixture flows down the slope like a heavy gas. You cannot escape it on foot or by car.
92850.m: Pyroclastic flows are faster than any escape vehicle.

92851.q: How hot are pyroclastic flows typically?
92851.e: Temperatures are usually between about 200 and 700 degrees, sometimes even higher. That is enough to kill every living thing in their path.
92851.m: Pyroclastic flows are several hundred degrees hot.

92852.q: What destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre on the Caribbean island of Martinique in 1902?
a: A glowing cloud from the volcano Mont Pelée
92852.e: On 8 May 1902, a pyroclastic flow from Mont Pelée hit the town of Saint-Pierre. About 28,000 people died.
92852.m: In 1902, a glowing cloud from Mont Pelée destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre.

92853.q: Why is it deadly for volcanologists to film pyroclastic flows from close up?
a: The flows are extremely fast and hot
The flows are loud and damage hearing
92853.e: Pyroclastic flows race down the slope at over 100 km/h and several hundred degrees. In 1991, the scientists Katia and Maurice Krafft died this way on the Japanese volcano Unzen.

92854.q: What is another name for a pyroclastic flow?
92854.e: A pyroclastic flow is a red-hot cloud of gas, ash and rock. That is why it is also called a glowing cloud, in French “nuée ardente”.
92854.m: A pyroclastic flow is also called a glowing cloud.

92855.q: Which volcano destroyed the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum in the year 79?
92855.e: When Vesuvius erupted, pyroclastic flows hit the towns on the Bay of Naples. Hundreds of skeletons were later found on the beach at Herculaneum.
92855.m: Vesuvius destroyed Pompeii and Herculaneum in the year 79.

92856.q: Which volcano near Naples is monitored especially closely because so many people live near it?
92856.e: Millions of people live around Vesuvius. That is why it has had its own observatory watching it since 1841.
92856.m: Vesuvius is closely monitored because of the many people living nearby.

92857.q: What can it mean if the ground on a volcano slowly rises?
a: Magma is rising and collecting underground
The volcano is extinct for good
The volcano is sinking into the sea
92857.e: Rising magma pushes the rock above it upwards. With GPS devices and tilt meters, such uplift is measured to the millimetre.
92857.m: If the ground on a volcano rises, magma may be rising.

92858.q: Which gas do volcanologists measure especially often to detect changes in a volcano?
92858.e: When fresh magma rises, it gives off more sulphur dioxide. An increase can therefore signal an eruption.
92858.m: More sulphur dioxide can be a sign of rising magma.

92859.q: What do many small earthquakes under a volcano, so-called earthquake swarms, often indicate?
a: That the volcano is cooling down
That the volcano is growing without ever erupting
92859.e: When magma forces its way up, it breaks rock open. This causes many weak quakes, which seismometers on the volcano register.
92859.m: Earthquake swarms under a volcano can point to moving magma.

92860.q: What mainly decides how big a volcanic eruption is rated?
a: The amount of material thrown out
The time of day of the eruption
92860.e: Experts estimate how much ash and rock a volcano has thrown out. The more material, the higher the eruption is rated.
92860.m: The size of an eruption is measured by the amount of material thrown out.

92861.q: How do satellites measure ground changes on volcanoes from space?
92861.e: Radar satellites compare images of the same area taken at different times. This lets them detect uplift of a few centimetres over large areas.
92861.m: Radar satellites detect ground uplift on volcanoes from space.

92862.q: What do volcanologists use thermal imaging cameras for?
a: To spot hot places and fresh lava
To identify the colour of the ash
To count animals on the volcano
92862.e: Thermal cameras show differences in temperature even through smoke and at night. New hot spots can be a sign of an eruption.
92862.m: Thermal cameras show hot spots on volcanoes.

92863.q: In which group of islands is the very active volcano Kilauea?
92863.e: Kilauea is on the biggest island of Hawaii in the Pacific. It is one of the most active volcanoes in the world and has been monitored since 1912.
92863.m: Kilauea in Hawaii is one of the most active volcanoes.

92865.q: Which separation method is first used in a refinery to split crude oil into different fractions?
92865.e: The crude oil is heated strongly and evaporates. The parts condense at different heights in the column depending on their boiling point.
92865.m: Crude oil is separated into its fractions by fractional distillation.

92866.q: Where in the distillation column are the low-boiling fractions such as gases and petrol drawn off?
a: In the storage tank before it
92866.e: The column is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. Substances with a low boiling point rise highest before they condense.
92866.m: The lower the boiling point, the higher up a fraction is drawn off.

92867.q: Which thick residue is left at the bottom in oil distillation and is used for road surfaces?
92867.e: Bitumen has a very high boiling point and so does not evaporate. Mixed with stones and sand it makes asphalt.
92867.m: Bitumen is the heavy residue of crude oil and is found in asphalt.

92868.q: What is the process called in which long hydrocarbon molecules are split into shorter ones to get more petrol?
92868.e: Crude oil contains fewer short molecules than are needed for petrol. In cracking, long chains are broken into shorter ones using heat and catalysts.
92868.m: In cracking, long molecules are broken into shorter ones.

92869.q: From which crude oil fraction is the fuel for jet aircraft mainly obtained?
92869.e: Kerosene is a medium fraction that boils between petrol and diesel. It is used as aviation fuel for jet engines.

92870.q: Which two elements make up the hydrocarbons that form most of crude oil?
92870.e: The name gives it away: hydrocarbons are compounds of hydrogen and carbon. Crude oil is a mixture of a great many such compounds.
92870.m: Hydrocarbons consist of carbon and hydrogen.

92871.q: Why is sulfur removed from oil products in the refinery?
a: So that less sulfur dioxide forms when they burn
So that they flow faster through pipes
So that they get a lighter colour
So that they contain less energy
92871.e: Sulfur burns to form sulfur dioxide, which pollutes the air and contributes to acid rain. That is why it is removed beforehand.
92871.m: Fuels with the sulfur removed pollute the air less.

92872.q: What is the tall tower in a refinery in which crude oil is separated called?
92872.e: A distillation column has many trays stacked above one another. On each tray, a fraction with a similar boiling point collects.
92872.m: Crude oil is separated in a distillation column.

92873.q: For which type of engine is petrol the usual fuel?
92873.e: In a spark-ignition engine, a mixture of petrol and air is lit by a spark plug. Diesel engines, by contrast, ignite their fuel by compression.

92874.q: What does the octane rating of petrol tell you?
a: How much it costs per litre
92874.e: Knocking is uncontrolled self-ignition in the engine. The higher the octane rating, the better the petrol resists it.
92874.m: A high octane rating means petrol that resists knocking.

92875.q: What octane rating does the usual unleaded petrol at Swiss filling stations have?
92875.e: In Switzerland, standard petrol is called “Bleifrei 95” (unleaded 95). There is usually also a 98 octane type.
92875.m: Standard petrol in Switzerland has 95 octane.

92876.q: Why is lead no longer added to petrol today?
a: Lead is poisonous and ruins catalytic converters
92876.e: A lead compound used to make petrol resist knocking better. But lead is a poisonous heavy metal and makes catalytic converters useless.
92876.m: Petrol is unleaded today because lead is poisonous.

92877.q: Which two elements are the molecules in petrol mainly made of?
92877.e: Petrol is a mixture of hydrocarbons. These molecules are made of carbon and hydrogen atoms.

92878.q: Which substances mainly form when petrol burns completely?
92878.e: The carbon combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide, and the hydrogen forms water. A lot of energy is released.
92878.m: When petrol burns completely, carbon dioxide and water form.

92879.q: Roughly what is the density of petrol?
92879.e: Petrol is lighter than water, which weighs 1 kilogram per litre. That is why spilt petrol floats on water.

92880.q: Why is petrol very dangerous even at room temperature?
a: Its vapours form an explosive mixture with air
It freezes into ice at once
92880.e: Petrol evaporates easily. Even a small spark can set the vapours in the air alight.
92880.m: Petrol vapours can be lit by just a spark.

92881.q: From which raw material is petrol mainly obtained?
92881.e: Petrol is a fraction obtained from crude oil in the refinery. More petrol is also made by splitting longer molecules.
92881.m: Petrol is a crude oil product.

92882.q: What happens to a thermoplastic when you heat it?
a: It becomes soft and can be shaped
92882.e: Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be reshaped. When they cool, they become solid again.

92883.q: How are the molecules arranged in a thermoplastic?
a: As long chains that are not cross-linked
As ions in a crystal lattice
92883.e: The chains are only loosely connected to each other. When warm, they can slide past one another, which is why the material softens.
92883.m: Thermoplastics are made of chains that are not cross-linked.

92884.q: Which of these objects is usually made of a thermoplastic?
92884.e: PET is a plastic that softens when heated. So PET bottles can be melted down and made into new bottles.
92884.m: PET bottles are made of a plastic that can be melted.

92885.q: Why are thermoplastics easy to recycle?
a: They can be melted down and reshaped
They break down into crude oil by themselves
92885.e: Since thermoplastics melt when heated, they can be made into pellets. New products are then made from these.
92885.m: Thermoplastics can be melted down and reused.

92886.q: Which method is used to make many small thermoplastic parts in large numbers?
92886.e: In injection moulding, melted plastic is pressed into a mould under pressure. After cooling, the finished part drops out.
92886.m: Thermoplastics are often shaped by injection moulding.

92887.q: Which thermoplastic contains chlorine and is used for drainpipes and window frames?
92887.e: Polyvinyl chloride, PVC for short, has chlorine atoms in its chains. It is tough and weatherproof.
92887.m: PVC is a plastic that contains chlorine.

92888.q: Which thermoplastic is the white packaging foam made of that people in Switzerland often call “Sagex”?
92888.e: The foam is made of expanded polystyrene and contains a great deal of air. That is why it is light and insulates well.
92888.m: Packaging foam is usually made of expanded polystyrene.

92889.q: What is nylon, which ropes are made of, for example?
92889.e: Nylon was the first fully synthetic fibre and is a plastic. It is tear-resistant and elastic.

92890.q: What does the word part “thermo” in thermoplastic mean?
92890.e: “Thermos” is Greek and means warm. So a thermoplastic becomes plastic, that is mouldable, through heat.
92890.m: A thermoplastic can be shaped using heat.

92891.q: What happens to a thermoset when it is heated very strongly?
a: It becomes soft and can be shaped
It becomes as runny as water
92891.e: Thermosets cannot melt. If it gets too hot, the chemical bonds break and the material chars.
92891.m: Thermosets do not melt; they break down.

92892.q: How are the molecules in a thermoset connected to each other?
a: Loosely linked like a rubber band
Not at all, they are single atoms
92892.e: The chains are joined by many strong bonds into a dense network. That is why a thermoset is hard and keeps its shape.

92893.q: Which thermoset is considered the world’s first fully synthetic plastic?
92893.e: Bakelite was invented at the start of the 20th century. It was used, for example, for old telephones and radio cases.
92893.m: Bakelite was the first fully synthetic plastic.

92894.q: What was the plastic Bakelite used for in the past, for example?
92894.e: Bakelite is hard, heat-resistant and insulates against electricity. So it was used for the cases of telephones, radios and plugs.
92894.m: Many telephones used to be made of Bakelite.

92895.q: Why are pan handles and sockets often made of thermoset plastic?
a: Because it resists heat and does not melt
92895.e: Thermosets keep their shape even when warm. They also insulate electrically, which makes them suitable for sockets.
92895.m: Thermosets are suitable for hot handles and electrical parts.

92896.q: Which material, with synthetic resin as its binder, is used for boat hulls and wind turbine blades?
92896.e: In glass-fibre reinforced plastic, hardened resins hold the glass fibres together. The material is light and very strong.
92896.m: Glass-fibre reinforced plastic is light and strong.

92897.q: Which glue hardens into a thermoset after two components are mixed?
92897.e: In epoxy resin glue, the resin and hardener react with each other. A firmly cross-linked plastic forms that no longer melts.
92897.m: Epoxy resin glue hardens into a thermoset.

92898.q: Which group of plastics is only loosely cross-linked and therefore stretchy like rubber?
92898.e: Elastomers such as rubber can be stretched and spring back. Their chains are linked at only a few points.
92898.m: Elastomers are loosely cross-linked and stretchy.

92899.q: Which small molecule is polyethylene made from?
92899.e: Ethene, also called ethylene, has a double bond. Many ethene molecules join together to form long chains.
92899.m: Polyethylene is made from many ethene molecules.

92900.q: What is the reaction called in which many small molecules join to form a long chain?
92900.e: In polymerisation, monomers are linked to form a polymer. “Poly” means many.
92900.m: In polymerisation, small molecules form long chains.

92901.q: Which plastic is produced in the largest amount worldwide?
92901.e: Polyethylene is cheap, light and versatile. It is found in films, bags, bottles and pipes.
92901.m: Polyethylene is the most produced plastic in the world.

92902.q: Why is polyethylene good for shampoo and detergent bottles?
a: It falls apart in a few days
92902.e: Polyethylene is tough, does not break and lets no water through. So many bottles for the bathroom and household are made of it.

92903.q: Which kind of polyethylene are soft films and plastic bags usually made of?
92903.e: In low-density polyethylene (LDPE) the chains are highly branched. So they lie more loosely and the material is soft.
92903.m: Soft films are usually made of LDPE.

92904.q: Which elements is polyethylene made of?
92904.e: The chain of polyethylene consists of carbon atoms with hydrogen atoms attached. No other elements are present.

92905.q: Why does a piece of polyethylene float on water?
a: Its density is lower than that of water
92905.e: Polyethylene has a density of about 0.91 to 0.97 grams per cubic centimetre. Water has 1 gram per cubic centimetre.
92905.m: Polyethylene floats because it is less dense than water.

92906.q: What is polyethylene often used for in everyday life?
92906.e: Polyethylene is cheap, light and flexible. It is used to make bags, films, bottles and pipes.
92906.m: Plastic bags and films are often made of polyethylene.

92907.q: How is a PET bottle formed from a small, thick-walled blank?
a: By stretch blow moulding with compressed air
By casting in a sand mould
92907.e: The blank is warmed, placed in a mould and blown up with compressed air. The material is stretched and the bottle gets its shape.
92907.m: PET bottles are blown up from warmed blanks.

92908.q: Why should you squash PET bottles flat before collecting them?
a: So they take up less space during transport
So they become lighter in colour
92908.e: Squashed bottles take up much less volume. So more bottles fit into collection bags and lorries.
92908.m: Flattened PET bottles save space during transport.

92909.q: Roughly what was the recycling rate for PET drinks bottles in Switzerland in 2024?
92909.e: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, over 84 per cent of PET drinks bottles were recycled in 2024. The law requires at least 75 per cent.
92909.m: In Switzerland, over 80 per cent of PET bottles are recycled.

92910.q: Under which name is PET used as a textile fibre for fleece jackets?
92910.e: PET is one of the polyesters. As a fibre it is tear-resistant, light and dries quickly.

92911.q: From which raw material is PET mainly made?
92911.e: The starting materials for PET come from the petrochemical industry. Today, a small part can also come from plants.
92911.m: PET is mostly made from crude oil.

92912.q: Which properties make PET especially suitable for drinks bottles?
92912.e: PET bottles weigh much less than glass bottles and do not break. They are also clear and hold in the fizz well.
92912.m: PET is light, unbreakable and clear.

92913.q: Which group of plastics does PET belong to?
92913.e: PET softens when heated and can be reshaped. When it cools, it becomes solid again.

92914.q: Where do you take empty PET drinks bottles in Switzerland?
92914.e: Almost every shop that sells drinks in PET has a collection point. The collected bottles are made into new bottles or fibres.
92914.m: PET bottles belong in the PET collection.

92915.q: Which number in the recycling triangle stands for PET?
92915.e: Plastics are marked with numbers in the recycling triangle. PET has the number 1.
92915.m: PET has the number 1 in the recycling triangle.

92917.q: By which everyday name is glucose known?
92917.e: Glucose is found in large amounts in grapes. That is where the name grape sugar comes from.
92917.m: Glucose is also known as grape sugar.

92918.q: How sweet does glucose taste compared with ordinary table sugar?
92918.e: Glucose has only about two thirds to three quarters of the sweetness of table sugar. Fructose, on the other hand, tastes sweeter than table sugar.
92918.m: Glucose is a little less sweet than table sugar.

92920.q: Which group of nutrients does glucose belong to?
92920.e: Glucose is a simple sugar and therefore the simplest carbohydrate. It is the most important energy supplier for cells.

92921.q: What forms when yeast ferments glucose without oxygen?
92921.e: In alcoholic fermentation, yeast turns sugar into alcohol and gas. The gas also makes bread dough rise.
92921.m: Yeast ferments sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide.

92922.q: Which hormone lowers the amount of glucose in the blood?
92922.e: Insulin is made in the pancreas. It makes the cells take up glucose from the blood.

92924.q: What colour does iodine solution turn when you drip it onto starch?
92924.e: Iodine fits inside the spiral-shaped starch molecules. This produces a deep blue to black colour.

92925.q: What building blocks is starch made of?
92925.e: Starch consists of hundreds to thousands of linked glucose units. During digestion it is broken back down into these building blocks.
92925.m: Starch is built from glucose units.

92926.q: In which part of the potato plant is starch stored as a reserve?
92926.e: The potato tuber grows underground and is a storage organ. It contains a lot of starch as an energy store for new shoots.

92927.q: What is starch in our food mainly for?
92927.e: During digestion, starch is broken down into glucose. The body uses this sugar as energy for the muscles and brain.

92928.q: What happens when you heat starch in water, for example to thicken a sauce?
a: It swells and thickens the liquid
92928.e: When heated, the starch grains take up water and burst. The starch turns gel-like and the liquid becomes thick.
92928.m: Heated starch binds water and thickens sauces.

92929.q: Which of these foods contains a lot of starch?
92929.e: Rice, pasta, bread and potatoes are rich in starch. Cucumbers are mostly water, butter is mostly fat.
92929.m: Rice, bread and pasta contain a lot of starch.

92930.q: Which substance is built from glucose like starch, but cannot be digested by humans?
92930.e: Cellulose forms the cell walls of plants and is found in wood and paper. Our body cannot split its bonds; it serves as dietary fibre.
92930.m: For humans, cellulose is indigestible fibre.

92931.q: Which type of carbohydrate is starch?
92931.e: Starch consists of a great many linked sugar units. Such carbohydrates are called polysaccharides.

92933.q: Which simple test can show fat in foods?
92933.e: If you rub the food on paper, fat leaves a see-through spot. A water spot disappears again as it dries.
92933.m: Fat leaves a see-through spot on paper.

92934.q: What makes oils different from solid fats such as butter?
a: Oils are liquid at room temperature
Oils are made of amino acids
92934.e: Chemically, oils and fats are built the same way. Oils contain more unsaturated fatty acids and therefore have a lower melting point.

92935.q: What is the reaction of fat with sodium hydroxide solution, which produces soap, called?
92935.e: The alkali splits the fat into glycerol and salts of fatty acids. These salts are the soap.
92935.m: In saponification, fat and alkali make soap.

92936.q: Apart from storing energy, what job does fatty tissue do in the body?
a: It protects organs and insulates against cold
It carries oxygen in the blood
It carries nerve signals to the brain
92936.e: Fat pads surround the kidneys, for example, and cushion knocks. Under the skin, a layer of fat keeps body heat in.
92936.m: Fatty tissue protects organs and keeps you warm.

92937.q: Roughly how much energy does 1 gram of fat provide?
92937.e: Fat provides around 9 kilocalories or 37 kilojoules per gram. That is about twice as much as carbohydrates or proteins.
92937.m: Fat is the most energy-rich nutrient.

92938.q: Why do butter and cooking oil go rancid over time?
a: Fats are broken down by oxygen, light and heat
Fats take up salt from the air
92938.e: Unsaturated fatty acids in particular react with oxygen. This produces substances that smell and taste unpleasant.
92938.m: Store fats cool, dark and sealed so they do not go rancid.

92939.q: Which fatty acids contain double bonds and are found especially in plant oils?
92939.e: Double bonds put kinks in the fatty acid chains. So the molecules pack together less tightly.
92939.m: Unsaturated fatty acids have double bonds.

92940.q: What building blocks are proteins made of?
92940.e: Proteins are long chains of amino acids. The order of the amino acids decides the shape and job of the protein.
92940.m: Proteins are built from amino acids.

92941.q: Roughly how many different amino acids does the human body use to build proteins?
92941.e: Humans build their proteins from around 20 different amino acids. Some of these must be taken in with food.
92941.m: Proteins are built from around 20 amino acids.

92942.q: Why does runny egg white turn solid and white when you cook an egg?
a: The proteins are denatured by the heat
92942.e: Heat destroys the three-dimensional shape of the proteins. The chains clump together and the egg white becomes solid and opaque.

92943.q: Which element is found in all proteins but not in fats and sugars?
92943.e: Every amino acid has an amino group containing nitrogen. Fats and carbohydrates consist only of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

92944.q: Which of these foods contains the most protein?
92944.e: Dairy products such as quark, as well as meat, eggs and pulses, contain a lot of protein. Fruit, vegetables and sugar provide hardly any protein.

92945.q: What does our body mainly need proteins for?
92945.e: Proteins are the body’s most important building materials. Muscles, skin and many parts of cells are made of them.
92945.m: Proteins are building materials for muscles and cells.

92946.q: Which protein makes up hair and fingernails?
92946.e: Keratin is a tough fibrous protein. It is also found in feathers, hooves and horns.
92946.m: Hair and nails are made of keratin.

92947.q: Which milk protein curdles when rennet is added in cheese-making?
92947.e: Rennet makes the casein in milk clump together. It forms the solid cheese curd; the liquid separated off is the whey.
92947.m: Cheese is made from the milk protein casein.

92948.q: How is a surfactant molecule built?
a: A water-loving head and a fat-loving tail
A metal core with a shell
92948.e: The head is hydrophilic and is drawn into the water. The long tail is hydrophobic and attaches to fat.
92948.m: Surfactants have a water-loving part and a fat-loving part.

92949.q: What do surfactants do at the surface of water?
92949.e: Surfactants gather at the surface and weaken the hold between water molecules. This lets water wet things better.
92949.m: Surfactants reduce the surface tension of water.

92950.q: What do surfactants do with droplets of fat when washing up?
a: They surround the fat so it is rinsed away
They make the fat go hard
They turn the fat into water
They stick the fat to the plate
92950.e: The fat-loving ends of the surfactants attach to the fat, and the water-loving ends point outwards. So the fat floats in the water and is rinsed away.
92950.m: Surfactants surround fat so water can rinse it away.

92951.q: In which products are surfactants the most important active ingredient?
92951.e: Surfactants loosen fat and dirt from surfaces and fabrics. That is why they are the main ingredient of cleaning products.
92951.m: Detergents and washing-up liquids clean with surfactants.

92952.q: What is the oldest surfactant made by humans?
92952.e: Soap has been made for thousands of years. Modern synthetic surfactants have only existed since the 20th century.

92953.q: How does a solution of classic hard soap in water react?
92953.e: Soaps are salts of weak fatty acids. In water they form a slightly alkaline solution with a pH above 7.

92954.q: Which property must surfactants in detergents have today so that they do not harm rivers and lakes?
a: They must be insoluble in water
92954.e: In the past, surfactants that broke down poorly formed mountains of foam on rivers. Today, surfactants must break down in sewage works and in water.

92955.q: What do you call a finely spread mixture of oil in water, which surfactants can stabilise?
92955.e: In an emulsion, small droplets of one liquid are spread through another. Milk and mayonnaise are examples.
92955.m: An emulsion is a mixture of two liquids that do not mix.

92956.q: Which substance is the main ingredient of methylated spirits?
92956.e: Methylated spirits consist mostly of ethanol, the same alcohol as in alcoholic drinks. But it has been made undrinkable.
92956.m: Methylated spirits consist mainly of ethanol.

a: So that nobody uses it as drinking alcohol
So that it burns more brightly
So that it evaporates less quickly
92957.e: Denatured alcohol tastes and smells so bad that it cannot be drunk. In return, it is not taxed like drinking alcohol.
92957.m: Denatured alcohol has been made undrinkable.

92958.q: What does denatured methylated spirits taste like?
92958.e: When denaturing, bitter substances are added. Even tiny amounts make the spirits undrinkable.
92958.m: Bitter substances make methylated spirits undrinkable.

92959.q: Why does methylated spirits feel cold on your skin?
a: It evaporates quickly and takes heat from the skin
It is kept in the fridge
It conducts electricity away from the skin
92959.e: A liquid needs energy to evaporate. The spirits take this heat from the skin, which cools down as a result.

92960.q: What is the formula of ethanol?
92960.e: An ethanol molecule contains two carbon atoms, six hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. The formula is written so that you can see the structure.

92961.q: What is methylated spirits often used for in Swiss households?
a: As fuel for the fondue burner
As heating oil for central heating
92961.e: In the fondue burner, methylated spirits burns and keeps the fondue warm. It is also used to clean glass.
92961.m: Methylated spirits heats the fondue burner.

92962.q: Why is the flame of burning spirits especially treacherous?
a: It is almost invisible in daylight
92962.e: Ethanol burns with a faint blue flame that hardly makes soot. It is easy to miss that something is still burning.
92962.m: Flames from spirits are hard to see in daylight.

92963.q: Why must you never pour methylated spirits into a fondue burner that is still burning or hot?
a: The vapours catch fire and there is a sudden flash of flame
92963.e: The spirits evaporate at once on the hot spot. The flame can flash back through the vapours into the bottle and cause serious burns.
92963.m: Only refill a fondue burner when it is cold and out.

93356.q: What is the part of the ear you can see on the outside of your head called?
93356.e: The outer ear is the part of the ear you can see. All the other parts are hidden inside the head.
93356.m: You can see the outer ear on the outside of your head.

93357.q: What is the outer ear for?
93357.e: The outer ear is shaped like a funnel. It collects sounds and guides them into the ear.
93357.m: The outer ear collects sounds like a funnel.

93358.q: What do people often do with their hand to hear better?
a: Hold it in front of the eyes
93358.e: A cupped hand behind the ear makes the outer ear bigger. That way it catches more sound.
93358.m: A hand behind the ear helps you hear.

93359.q: What is the soft lower part of the outer ear called?
93359.e: The earlobe has no cartilage, so it is soft. Many people wear earrings there.

93360.q: What makes the outer ear firm but bendy?
93360.e: There is cartilage in the outer ear. It is firmer than skin, but you can bend it.
93360.m: Cartilage makes the outer ear bendy.

93361.q: Which animal can turn its ears in different directions?
93361.e: Cats have lots of muscles in their ears. They turn their ears towards a sound.
93361.m: A cat can turn its ears.

93362.q: How many ears does a person have?
93362.e: People have one ear on each side of the head. With two ears you can tell better where a sound comes from.
93362.m: With two ears you can hear where a sound comes from.

93363.q: Which animal has especially big ears that it also uses to cool down?
93363.e: African elephants have huge ears. By flapping their ears they cool their blood.
93363.m: Elephants cool down with their ears.

93364.q: Which animals have no outer ears, only hidden ear openings on the head?
93364.e: Birds have no outer ears. Their ear openings are on the sides of the head under the feathers.

93365.q: Can a small hole in the eardrum heal again?
a: Yes, it often heals by itself
Only with a plaster on the outside
Only if you drink lots of milk
93365.e: The eardrum can often close small tears by itself within a few weeks. Even so, a doctor should look at the ear.
93365.m: A small hole in the eardrum often heals by itself.

93366.q: Why is the eardrum called that?
a: It vibrates like the skin of a drum
It is made of animal skin
It is round like a ball
93366.e: A drum has a tight skin stretched over the top. The eardrum is stretched in a similar way and vibrates.
93366.m: The eardrum is stretched like the skin of a drum.

93367.q: What can a very loud bang do to the eardrum?
93367.e: A very strong bang can injure the eardrum. It can get a small hole.
93367.m: A strong bang can injure the eardrum.

93368.q: What are the three tiny bones behind the eardrum called?
93368.e: The three ear bones are named after tools. They pass the vibrations of the eardrum further inside.
93368.m: Behind the eardrum are the hammer, anvil and stirrup.

93369.q: What should you never do right next to another child's ear?
93369.e: A loud shout right next to the ear is very strong. It can hurt and damage the ear.
93369.m: Never shout right into someone's ear.

a: At the end of the ear canal
On the outside of the outer ear
93370.e: The eardrum separates the ear canal from the middle ear. You cannot see it from the outside.
93370.m: The eardrum separates the ear canal from the middle ear.

93371.q: What do you often feel in your ears when a plane is landing?
93371.e: When landing, the air pressure changes. This presses on the eardrum until the pressure evens out again.
93371.m: On a plane your ears often feel pressure.

93372.q: What helps against the pressure in your ears on a plane?
93372.e: When you swallow and chew, a little air flows into the middle ear. That evens out the pressure.
93372.m: Swallowing evens out the pressure in your ears.

93373.q: What is an ear doctor more exactly called?
93373.e: The ears, nose and throat are connected inside. That is why an ear, nose and throat doctor looks after all three.
93373.m: For your ears you go to an ear, nose and throat doctor.

93374.q: What is the yellowish, sticky stuff in the ear canal called?
93374.e: A waxy substance forms in the ear canal. It is called earwax.
93374.m: Earwax forms in the ear canal.

a: It protects the ear from dirt
93375.e: Earwax traps dust and tiny particles. It also keeps the skin in the ear canal soft.

93376.q: Why should you not push cotton buds deep into your ear?
a: They push the earwax further in
93376.e: A cotton bud pushes earwax inwards. It can form a plug or injure the ear.
93376.m: Cotton buds do not belong deep in the ear.

93377.q: How does earwax normally get out of the ear?
a: You have to scrape it out every day
93377.e: The ear cleans itself. The earwax slowly moves to the opening of the ear canal.

93378.q: What is the right way to clean your ears?
a: Poke a pencil into the ear
93378.e: It is enough to clean the outer ear and the entrance of the ear with a flannel. Deep inside the ear needs no cleaning.
93378.m: You only wash the outside part of the ear.

93379.q: What can happen if too much earwax blocks the ear?
93379.e: A plug of earwax can block the ear canal. Then sounds reach the eardrum less well.
93379.m: Too much earwax can muffle your hearing.

93380.q: Who is best at removing a hard plug of earwax?
93380.e: A doctor can remove the plug safely with water or small instruments. That way the ear is not injured.
93380.m: A doctor removes a plug of earwax.

93381.q: What can the doctor put into the ear to make hard earwax soft?
93381.e: Ear drops soften hard earwax. Afterwards it can come out more easily or be rinsed out.
93381.m: Ear drops make hard earwax soft.

93382.e: A jet plane taking off is extremely loud close up. That can damage your ears.
93382.m: A plane taking off is very loud.

93383.e: Rustling leaves are a very quiet sound. The other sounds are much louder.
93383.m: Rustling leaves are a quiet sound.

93384.q: What can music that is too loud in headphones do over time?
93384.e: Very loud sounds can destroy the tiny hearing cells in the inner ear. They do not grow back.
93384.m: Music that is too loud harms your ears.

93385.q: What can you sometimes hear in your ear after a very loud concert?
93385.e: After a lot of noise, your ear sometimes rings or hisses. That is a warning sign that it was too loud.
93385.m: Ringing in the ear warns of too much noise.

93386.q: What is the part of the inner ear that looks like a snail shell called?
93386.e: The cochlea is coiled like a snail shell. Inside it are the hearing cells that report sounds to the brain.
93386.m: The hearing cells sit in the cochlea.

93387.q: Where does a person notice what they hear?
93387.e: The ears pick up the sounds. Only the brain understands what you hear, for example a word or a song.
93387.m: The brain understands what the ears hear.

93388.q: Which symbol is often used for the volume on a mobile phone?
93388.e: A small loudspeaker symbol shows the volume. With the buttons you make it louder or quieter.
93388.m: The loudspeaker symbol stands for the volume.

93389.q: Who often wears ear protection at work?
93389.e: A pneumatic drill is very loud. Ear protection keeps the ears from being damaged.
93389.m: For loud work you wear ear protection.

93390.q: When should children wear ear protection?
93390.e: Fireworks bang very loudly, for example on 1 August. Children's ears are especially sensitive.
93390.m: At fireworks you protect children's ears.

93391.e: Ear protection muffles sound before it reaches the ear. So less noise gets in.

93392.q: During which hobby do many people in Switzerland wear ear protection?
93392.e: A shot is a very loud bang. That is why shooters at the shooting range wear ear protection.
93392.m: When shooting, you protect your ears.

93393.q: What is good for your ears at a loud party if you have no ear protection?
a: Going to a quiet place now and then
Standing right next to the speakers
Turning the music up even louder
93393.e: Breaks in a quiet place let your ears recover. That way they are under less strain.
93393.m: Breaks from noise are good for your ears.

93394.q: Apart from ear protection, what else is good for your ears in a loud place?
93394.e: The further you are from the source of the noise, the quieter it gets. That is why you do not stand right in front of the speakers.
93394.m: Distance from the noise protects your ears.

93395.q: Which animal has no ear protection but hears fireworks especially well and is often frightened?
93395.e: Dogs hear much better than people. That is why the bangs of fireworks often scare them a lot.
93395.m: Dogs are often frightened by fireworks.

93396.q: What does a hearing aid do?
93396.e: A hearing aid picks up sounds and plays them louder into the ear. That way people who are hard of hearing hear better.
93396.m: A hearing aid makes sounds louder.

93397.q: Where do you wear a hearing aid?
93397.e: Many hearing aids sit behind the ear. Others are so small that they fit in the ear canal.
93397.m: You wear a hearing aid on or in the ear.

93398.q: What does a hearing aid need to work?
93398.e: A hearing aid is a small electrical device. It needs power from a battery or a rechargeable battery.
93398.m: A hearing aid runs on power from a battery.

93399.q: Which part of a hearing aid picks up the sounds?
93399.e: A tiny microphone catches the sounds. The device makes them louder and passes them on through a small loudspeaker.
93399.m: A microphone in the hearing aid catches the sounds.

93400.q: Who often needs a hearing aid?
a: People who do not hear well
People who do not see well
93400.e: People who are hard of hearing find it difficult to follow conversations. A hearing aid helps them.
93400.m: People who are hard of hearing often wear a hearing aid.

93401.q: What did people use before there were electric hearing aids?
93401.e: An ear trumpet is a funnel that you hold to your ear. It collects sound and guides it into the ear.
93401.m: In the past, an ear trumpet helped people hear.

93402.q: What should you not do with a hearing aid?
a: Take it out in the evening
93402.e: Most hearing aids are electrical devices and cannot take much water. That is why you take them out to shower.
93402.m: You take the hearing aid out before showering.

93403.q: Which specialist fits a hearing aid?
93403.e: Audiologists test your hearing and set up the hearing aid to suit you. That way you hear well with it.
93403.m: An audiologist sets up the hearing aid.

93404.q: Where in Switzerland do you often hear an echo?
93404.e: If you shout towards a rock face, the shout comes back. That is why there is often an echo in the Alps.
93404.m: In the mountains you often hear an echo.

93405.q: What is needed for an echo to happen?
93405.e: The sound has to bounce off something hard, for example rock. The wall must be far enough away for you to hear the shout separately.
93405.m: An echo needs a hard, distant wall.

93406.q: Which animal finds its way in the dark using echoes?
93406.e: Bats make very high sounds. From the echoes they can tell where obstacles and insects are.
93406.m: Bats find their way using echoes.

93407.q: Why do you hear the echo a little later than your own shout?
a: The sound needs time to travel
The wall only calls back later
93407.e: Sound is fast, but not endlessly fast. It needs time to reach the wall and come back.
93407.m: Sound needs time to travel to the wall.

93408.q: When does an echo come back to you faster?
a: When the rock face is closer
When the rock face is further away
When you shout in a deeper voice
93408.e: The sound has to travel to the wall and back. If the wall is close, the path is short and the echo comes back faster.
93408.m: The closer the wall, the faster the echo comes back.

93409.q: Which sea animal also uses echoes to find its way?
93409.e: Dolphins make clicking sounds. The echoes show them where fish and rocks are.
93409.m: Dolphins find their way with echoes.

93410.q: Where indoors do you often hear sound ringing out like an echo?
a: In a room full of cushions
93410.e: In an empty hall, sound bounces off the hard walls. Soft things would swallow the sound.

93411.q: What do you do when you whisper?
93411.e: When you whisper, you speak without your voice, only with your breath. That is why it is very quiet.

93412.q: Where do people often whisper so as not to disturb others?
93412.e: In a library, people want to read in peace. That is why you speak quietly there.

93413.q: What is the game called where a word is whispered from ear to ear?
93413.e: In Telephone, each child whispers the word into the next child's ear. At the end, something completely different often comes out.

93414.q: What does not vibrate when you whisper, unlike when you speak normally?
93414.e: When you speak normally, the vocal cords in your throat vibrate. When you whisper they stay still, and only the air rushes.
93414.m: When you whisper, the vocal cords do not vibrate.

93415.q: What do you often hold in front of your mouth when you whisper a secret to someone?
93415.e: With your hand next to your mouth, you direct the whisper to the ear. That way the others see and hear less of it.
93415.m: When whispering to someone, you often hold your hand in front of your mouth.

93416.q: Why do you whisper something into someone's ear?
a: So that others do not hear it
So that the ear gets warm
93416.e: A secret is meant for only one person to hear. That is why you whisper it close to the ear.
93416.m: You whisper a secret into someone's ear.

93417.q: When do people often whisper at home?
a: When calling someone from far away
93417.e: A sleeping baby should not wake up. That is why people speak quietly.
93417.m: Next to a sleeping baby, you whisper.

93418.q: What helps if you want to hear someone whispering in a noisy room?
93418.e: Quiet sounds get even quieter with distance. Very close up, you understand a whisper better.
93418.m: You can only understand a whisper from close up.

93419.q: What is a common cause of earache in children?
93419.e: In children, the middle ear often gets inflamed. That hurts and often comes after a cold.
93419.m: A middle ear infection often causes earache.

93420.q: After which illness do children often get earache?
93420.e: With a cold, germs can travel from the nose to the ear. Then the ear gets inflamed.
93420.m: After a cold, the ears often hurt.

93421.q: What should you do if your ear hurts a lot or you also have a fever?
a: Push a cotton bud deep inside
93421.e: Bad earache with a fever should be looked at by a doctor. They can find out what is wrong.
93421.m: With bad earache you go to the doctor.

93422.q: What does the doctor use to look into the ear?
a: A small light with a funnel
93422.e: The instrument is called an otoscope. It has a light and a small funnel so you can see as far as the eardrum.
93422.m: You look into the ear with an otoscope.

93423.q: What can often cause earache after swimming?
a: Water that stays in the ear canal
93423.e: If water stays in the ear canal for a long time, the skin gets soft. Then germs can cause an infection.
93423.m: Water in the ear can lead to an infection.

93424.q: What protects your ears in a cold wind?
93424.e: A cold wind can make your ears hurt. A hat or a headband keeps your ears warm.
93424.m: A hat protects your ears from the cold.

93425.q: What do you do if your ear hurts?
a: Pour cold water into your ear
93425.e: Sharp things can injure the ear canal or the eardrum. If it hurts, leave your ear alone and tell a grown-up who will take you to the doctor.
93425.m: Sharp objects never belong in the ear.

93426.q: What helps if your ears feel pressure when travelling up a mountain?
a: Holding your breath for a long time
93426.e: A thin tube connects the ear with the throat. When you swallow or yawn it opens, the air pressure evens out and the pressure stops.
93426.m: Swallowing helps when your ears feel pressure.

93427.q: What do you use to speak in sign language?
93427.e: In sign language you show words with your hands, face and body. You see the language instead of hearing it.
93427.m: Sign language is spoken with the hands and face.

93428.e: Deaf people cannot hear spoken language. With sign language they can talk with each other easily.
93428.m: Deaf people often use sign language.

93429.q: How many sign languages are there in Switzerland?
93429.e: In Switzerland there is a Swiss German, a French and an Italian sign language. They belong to the language regions.
93429.m: There are three sign languages in Switzerland.

93430.q: Is there only one sign language in the whole world?
93430.e: Just like spoken languages, there are many different sign languages. Each country usually has its own.
93430.m: There are many different sign languages.

93431.q: How do you spell out a name in sign language?
93431.e: In the finger alphabet, each letter has its own hand sign. That way you can spell out names.
93431.m: Names are spelled out with the finger alphabet.

93432.q: Why is the face important in sign language?
93432.e: With your face you show whether you are asking something or whether you are happy or angry. It is part of the grammar.
93432.m: The face is part of sign language.

93433.q: How do deaf people often applaud?
a: They wave both hands in the air
93433.e: You cannot see clapping, only hear it. That is why deaf people wave their raised hands, which everyone can see.
93433.m: Deaf people applaud with waving hands.

93434.q: Who translates between spoken language and sign language?
93434.e: Sign language interpreters translate on television, for example. You then see them in a small picture at the edge of the screen.

a: You cannot hear, or can hardly hear
93435.e: Deaf people hear nothing or almost nothing. Some are deaf from birth, others become deaf later.
93435.m: Deaf people hear nothing or almost nothing.

93436.q: How does a deaf person know that someone is ringing the doorbell?
93436.e: For many deaf people, the doorbell is connected to a lamp. Instead of a sound, a light flashes.
93436.m: Deaf people see the doorbell as a light signal.

93437.q: Which famous composer went deaf during his life?
93437.e: Ludwig van Beethoven gradually lost his hearing. Even so, he went on writing great music.
93437.m: Beethoven composed even though he went deaf.

93438.q: What helps deaf people understand a film?
93438.e: Subtitles show what is said as text at the bottom of the picture. That way you can read along.

93439.q: Which device is placed in the ear of some deaf people during an operation?
93439.e: A cochlear implant sends sounds as electrical signals straight to the hearing nerve. That way some deaf people can perceive sounds again.
93439.m: A cochlear implant can help with hearing.

93440.q: What is it called when you recognise words from someone's lips?
93440.e: Some deaf people watch the mouth closely. From the movements of the lips they recognise some of the words.
93440.m: In lip reading you recognise words from the mouth.

93441.q: What is important when you talk to a person who lip-reads?
a: Look at them and speak clearly
Cover your mouth with your hand
93441.e: The person must be able to see your mouth well. Speaking clearly while looking at them helps them understand.
93441.m: Speaking clearly and looking at the person helps with lip reading.

93442.q: What can deaf people still feel, for example at a concert?
93442.e: Deep notes make the floor and the body vibrate. Deaf people can feel music this way.
93442.m: You can also feel music as vibration.

93443.q: Why do people put earplugs in their ears?
93443.e: Earplugs block the ear canal. So less noise gets into the ear.

93444.q: What are many earplugs for sleeping made of?
93444.e: You squeeze foam earplugs and put them in your ear. There they expand and seal well.
93444.m: Many earplugs are made of foam.

93445.q: When do earplugs help you sleep?
a: When someone in the room snores
93445.e: Snoring can disturb your sleep. Earplugs make the noise quieter.
93445.m: Earplugs help against disturbing noises while you sleep.

93446.q: Why do some children wear earplugs when swimming?
a: So that no water gets into the ear
So that they can see under water
So that they do not get cold
93446.e: Special earplugs keep the water out. That is important if someone often gets ear infections.
93446.m: Swimming earplugs keep water out of the ear.

93447.q: What were many earplugs made of in the past?
93447.e: Soft wax can be shaped and seals the ear canal well. Earplugs like this still exist today.
93447.m: Wax earplugs have been around for a long time.

93448.q: What should you do with used foam earplugs?
a: Replace them with new ones soon
Leave them in your ear all day
93448.e: Foam earplugs get dirty over time. That is why you replace them regularly, so the ear stays clean.
93448.m: You soon replace used foam earplugs.

93449.q: How do you put foam earplugs in properly?
a: Roll them up and put them in the ear
Squash them flat and lay them on the ear
Wet them and push them in
Press them deep in with a pencil
93449.e: You roll the earplug thin and put it into the ear canal. There it gets thicker again and seals.
93449.m: You roll up foam earplugs before putting them in.

93450.q: In an ancient Greek legend, whose men blocked their ears so as not to hear the song of the Sirens?
93450.e: The sailors of Odysseus blocked their ears. So they did not hear the dangerous song and sailed safely past.
93450.m: Odysseus's men blocked their ears against the Sirens.

93451.q: Where does the echo get its name from?
a: From a nymph in a Greek legend
93451.e: In a Greek legend, the nymph Echo could only repeat the last words of others. The echo is named after her.
93451.m: The echo is named after a nymph.

93452.q: What can you do with your hands so that a shout can be heard further away?
a: Hold them like a funnel at your mouth
93452.e: Hands held like a funnel send the sound in one direction. That way the shout carries further.
93452.m: Cupping your hands round your mouth makes a shout carry further.

93649.q: Roughly when did the Goldau landslide happen?
93649.e: On 2 September 1806, a huge mass of rock crashed into the valley. That is about 200 years ago.

93650.q: Which mountain did the Goldau landslide break away from?
93650.e: The mass of rock broke away from the southern side of the Rossberg below the Gnipenspitze. Opposite is the Rigi, up which the masses surged.
93650.m: The Goldau landslide came from the Rossberg.

93651.q: Roughly how many people died in the Goldau landslide?
93651.e: 457 people died in the landslide. More than 300 animals were also killed.
93651.m: 457 people died in the Goldau landslide.

93652.q: In which canton is Goldau, which became known for a huge landslide?
93652.e: Goldau belongs to the municipality of Arth in the canton of Schwyz. The village lies between Lake Zug and Lake Lauerz.
93652.m: Goldau is in the canton of Schwyz.

93653.q: Which rock was the mass of the Goldau landslide mainly made of?
93653.e: The mountain consists of sloping layers of cemented gravel, called Nagelfluh. This rock is very common in the foothills of the Alps.
93653.m: At Goldau, mainly Nagelfluh crashed into the valley.

93654.q: What made the slope of the Rossberg slippery before the Goldau landslide?
a: Lots of rain softened layers of rock
93654.e: Rainwater got in through cracks and softened clay-rich marl layers. The slabs of rock slid off on them like on a slide.
93654.m: At Goldau, softened rock layers became a slide.

93655.q: Which lake was partly buried by the Goldau landslide, causing a flood wave?
93655.e: Part of the mass of rock went into Lake Lauerz, which became about a seventh smaller as a result. Eyewitnesses reported a flood wave about 20 metres high.
93655.m: The Goldau landslide made Lake Lauerz smaller.

93656.q: What is there today between the big boulders of the Goldau landslide area?
93656.e: The Goldau Nature and Animal Park lies in the middle of the debris field of the landslide. The boulders still shape the landscape today.
93656.m: Today there is an animal park in the Goldau landslide area.

93657.q: Roughly how much rock crashed into the valley in the Goldau landslide?
93657.e: Experts estimate the mass at almost 40 million cubic metres. It buried an area of about 6.5 square kilometres.
93657.m: At Goldau, almost 40 million cubic metres of rock came down.

93658.q: In which canton is Elm, which became known for a devastating landslide?
93658.e: Elm lies at the far end of the Sernf valley in the canton of Glarus. Today it belongs to the municipality of Glarus Süd.
93658.m: Elm is in the Sernf valley in Glarus.

93659.q: Roughly when did the Elm landslide happen?
93659.e: On 11 September 1881, a huge mass of rock fell from the Plattenbergkopf onto the village of Elm. That is about 150 years ago.

93660.q: Which human activity contributed greatly to the Elm landslide?
93660.e: For years slate was quarried on the slope, which hollowed out the mountain. Together with heavy rain, the slope lost its hold.
93660.m: Slate quarrying made the slope near Elm unstable.

93661.q: Roughly how many people died in the Elm landslide?
93661.e: 114 people died in the landslide. In addition, 83 buildings were destroyed.
93661.m: More than 100 people died in the Elm landslide.

93662.q: What was the rock quarried at Elm once used for, among other things?
93662.e: The rock can be split into thin slabs. Among other things, it was used to make slates and slate pencils for schoolchildren.
93662.m: The rock from Elm used to be made into writing slates.

93663.q: Which experts study landslides like the one at Elm?
93663.e: Geologists study rock and mountains. The Elm landslide was studied, for example, by the well-known geologist Albert Heim.

93664.q: Roughly how much rock came down in the Elm landslide?
93664.e: About 10 million cubic metres of rock broke away from the Plattenbergkopf. This mass buried a large part of the village.
93664.m: At Elm, about 10 million cubic metres of rock came down.

93665.q: How did the Elm landslide happen?
a: Two smaller falls were followed by the main fall
Everything came down in one second
The slope slid slowly over weeks
An earthquake blew the summit away
93665.e: First two smaller falls came down, which attracted curious onlookers. Shortly afterwards came the main fall, which hit many of these people.
93665.m: At Elm, three rockfalls came one after another.

93666.q: What is the difference between a rockfall and a rock avalanche?
a: In a rock avalanche, much more rock comes down
A rock avalanche only happens in winter
A rockfall is made only of ice
93666.e: Rockfalls are smaller. With huge masses of over a million cubic metres, as at Goldau, it is called a rock avalanche.
93666.m: A rock avalanche is much bigger than a rockfall.

93667.q: What often triggers a debris flow?
93667.e: Heavy rain or fast snowmelt soaks loose material in steep gullies. This then suddenly starts to move.
93667.m: Heavy rain can trigger debris flows.

93668.q: Where are the biggest boulders in a debris flow usually found?
a: At the front of the debris flow
Right at the end of the debris flow
Only at the bottom under the mud
93668.e: The big boulders collect at the front, in the so-called head of the flow. This front is especially destructive.
93668.m: The head at the front carries the biggest boulders.

93669.q: Why do scientists measure debris flows in the Illgraben in Valais every year?
a: To understand debris flows better and warn about them
To find gold in the debris
To use the stream for a reservoir
93669.e: The Illgraben near Leuk is one of the most active debris flow streams in the Alps. Instruments record several debris flows there every year so that they can be better understood.
93669.m: Debris flows are measured in the Illgraben in Valais.

93670.q: Which village in the Grisons was hit by debris flows in 2017 after a landslide on Piz Cengalo?
93670.e: In August 2017, about three million cubic metres of rock fell from Piz Cengalo. This led to debris flows that reached the village of Bondo in the Bregaglia.
93670.m: In 2017, debris flows reached the village of Bondo in the Bregaglia.

93671.q: Which change in the high mountains can make debris flows more frequent because of climate change?
93671.e: When permanently frozen ground thaws, a lot of loose material is set free. In heavy rain it can flow away as a debris flow.
93671.m: Thawing permafrost provides material for debris flows.

93672.q: Why are debris flows much more dangerous than an ordinary flood?
a: They carry heavy stones and mud
They consist only of clear water
93672.e: A debris flow is much denser and heavier than water alone. It can destroy houses, bridges and roads and bury everything under debris.
93672.m: Debris flows destroy things because of their heavy load.

93673.q: What is the fan-shaped pile of debris called that debris flows leave at the mouth of a mountain stream?
93673.e: Where the mountain stream comes out into the flatter valley, the material is left behind. Over a long time this forms an alluvial fan, on which villages often stand.
93673.m: Debris flows leave debris on alluvial fans.

93676.q: What is a debris basin on a debris flow stream for?
93676.e: A debris basin is a big basin with a grid or dam. It holds back the rock carried along before it reaches villages.
93676.m: Debris basins hold back debris from debris flows.

93677.q: Which river's catchment area do all of Liechtenstein's debris flow streams belong to?
93677.e: Liechtenstein lies on the Alpine Rhine. Sooner or later all the streams in the country flow into the Rhine.
93677.m: Liechtenstein's debris flow streams drain into the Rhine.

93678.q: What are the barriers across a stream bed called that reduce the slope and slow down debris flows?
93678.e: Check dams are step-like walls made of concrete, wood or stone. They stop the stream from cutting deeper and carrying away more material.
93678.m: Check dams slow down water and rubble in the stream bed.

93679.q: Which plants help most on steep slopes to prevent debris flows?
a: The trees of a dense forest
93679.e: Tree roots hold the soil together, and the forest soaks up a lot of rainwater. As a result, less material is washed away.
93679.m: A dense forest protects slopes from debris flows.

93680.q: In which season do debris flows happen especially often in the Alps?
93680.e: In summer the ground has thawed and is free of snow, and short, heavy downpours are common. In the depths of winter the ground is frozen and covered with snow.
93680.m: Most debris flows in the Alps come down in summer.

93681.q: Why are debris flow streams often led through a village in concrete channels?
a: So that debris flows away quickly and in a controlled way
So that people can swim in them
So that fish can migrate better
So that the water gets warmer
93681.e: A smooth, wide channel leads the material along a fixed path through the village. This makes it less likely that the debris flow bursts its banks.
93681.m: Channels lead debris flows safely through villages.

93682.q: What does it mean when people are evacuated during a flood?
a: They are taken out of danger to safety
They have to pump out the water
They have to stay at home
93682.e: During the flood in August 2005, many people in Switzerland had to leave their homes. Rescue teams took them to safe places.
93682.m: To evacuate means to bring people to safety.

93683.q: What is a map called that shows where, for example, floods or avalanches threaten?
93683.e: After events like the 2005 flood, hazard maps became even more important. They show where you have to build carefully or take protective measures.
93683.m: Hazard maps show where natural hazards threaten.

93684.q: In which city did the Aare flood a whole old town district in August 2005?
93684.e: The Matte district in Bern lies right on the Aare below the old town. In August 2005 it was under water.
93684.m: In 2005, the Aare flooded a district of Bern.

93685.q: What is a debris flow, like the one that destroyed houses in Brienz in August 2005?
a: A stream of water, mud and stones
A strong wind in the valley
93685.e: In a debris flow, a stream carries along lots of mud, stones and wood. This mass is heavy and can destroy houses.
93685.m: A debris flow is a stream of water, mud and stones.

93686.q: Which river burst its banks near Bern and Thun in August 2005?
93686.e: After days of rain, the Aare rose sharply. It flooded parts of Bern and also Bern-Belp airport.
93686.m: In the 2005 flood, the Aare burst its banks.

93687.q: Which monastery and holiday village in Obwalden was cut off for days in August 2005?
93687.e: The Engelberger Aa destroyed the road and railway line into the valley. Engelberg could therefore only be reached by air.
93687.m: Engelberg was cut off after the 2005 flood.

93688.q: What was built in Thun after the 2005 flood to drain Lake Thun more quickly during floods?
93688.e: A flood relief tunnel carries extra water from Lake Thun into the Aare. This lets the lake level be lowered more quickly.
93688.m: A tunnel in Thun lowers the lake level during floods.

93689.q: What was the main cause of the August 2005 flood in Switzerland?
a: Several days of heavy rain on the northern side of the Alps
A dam bursting at the Grimsel lake
93689.e: A low-pressure area brought very large amounts of rain over several days. Streams and rivers burst their banks, and lakes rose sharply.
93689.m: Days of heavy rain caused the 2005 flood.

93690.q: What are the lattice-like steel frames on steep slopes called that stop snow from sliding?
93690.e: Snow bridges are put up in rows on steep slopes. They support the snow cover so that no avalanche breaks loose at all.
93690.m: Snow bridges support the snow cover on steep slopes.

93691.q: In which part of a slope are supporting structures against avalanches put up?
93691.e: Supporting structures are meant to stop an avalanche from starting at all. That is why they stand where avalanches typically break loose.
93691.m: Supporting structures stand where avalanches start.

a: A roof over a road that avalanches slide over
A viewing tower in a ski resort
93692.e: An avalanche gallery is a structure open at the side with a strong roof. The avalanche slides over it, while the traffic underneath stays protected.
93692.m: An avalanche slides over an avalanche gallery.

93693.q: What are snow fences on mountain ridges for?
a: They hold back snow blown by the wind
93693.e: The wind blows snow and piles it up behind ridges in dangerous cornices. Fences slow the wind so that the snow settles in a harmless place.
93693.m: Snow fences prevent dangerous build-ups of snow.

93694.q: What does a deflecting dam do with an avalanche?
a: It steers the avalanche past a village
It sets off the avalanche artificially
It measures the depth of the snow
93694.e: A deflecting dam is a bank built at an angle to the avalanche path. It guides the masses of snow in a harmless direction.
93694.m: Deflecting dams steer avalanches away from villages.

93695.q: Why are young trees often planted above avalanche barriers?
a: So that later a forest takes over the job
So that wood grows for stoves
So that the snow melts faster
93695.e: A healthy mountain forest also holds the snow cover in place. The barriers protect the young trees until the forest is big enough.
93695.m: Planting trees is meant to protect against avalanches in future.

93696.q: How do safety services set off avalanches in a controlled way before they come down uncontrolled?
93696.e: When avalanche danger is high, dangerous slopes are blasted on purpose. Pistes and roads are closed while this happens.
93696.m: Controlled blasting sets off avalanches safely.

93697.q: What is a catching dam in avalanche protection?
a: A bank that stops an avalanche
93697.e: A catching dam stands across the avalanche path. It slows the avalanche down and holds back the masses of snow before they reach the village.
93697.m: Catching dams stop avalanches before they reach villages.

93699.q: In which canton is the SLF (Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research)?
93699.e: The SLF is based in Davos in the canton of the Grisons. Davos lies at more than 1500 metres above sea level.
93699.m: The SLF is in the canton of the Grisons.

93700.q: WSL is the research institute that the SLF belongs to. Its letters come from German. What does the W stand for?
93700.e: WSL is the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research. The SLF in Davos is one of its sites.
93700.m: The WSL researches forest, snow and landscape.

93701.q: What does the SLF publish every day in winter for the Swiss mountains?
93701.e: The avalanche bulletin shows how great the avalanche danger is in different areas. Anyone going off-piste should read it first.
93701.m: In winter, the SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.

93702.q: How many danger levels does the avalanche warning in Switzerland have?
93702.e: The scale goes from level 1, low, to level 5, very high. It is the same throughout Europe.

93703.q: Which topic does the SLF also study besides snow and avalanches?
93703.e: The SLF also studies permanently frozen ground in the Alps. Thawing permafrost can lead to rockfalls.

93704.q: What does the SLF measure with its stations in the mountains to assess the avalanche danger?
a: The water level of the lakes
93704.e: Automatic stations constantly measure how much snow is lying, how strongly the wind is blowing and how warm it is. These values help with avalanche warnings.
93704.m: Snow depth, wind and temperature show the avalanche danger.

93705.q: What do SLF experts investigate after serious avalanche accidents?
a: How and why the avalanche came down
Who has to pay for the accident
What the weather will be like in summer
93705.e: The SLF writes expert reports on avalanche accidents. From these we learn how to prevent accidents better in future.
93705.m: The SLF looks into the causes of avalanche accidents.

93706.q: Which level of the avalanche danger scale is called “considerable”?
93706.e: The European scale has five levels, and “considerable” is right in the middle. At this level, avalanches can be triggered on many steep slopes even by a single person.

93707.q: What is the highest level of the avalanche danger scale called?
93707.e: Level 5 is called “very high”. Then many large avalanches can be expected, even on moderately steep ground.
93707.m: The highest avalanche danger level is called very high.

93708.q: When should you read the avalanche bulletin?
a: Before every trip away from the pistes
Only when the sun is shining
93708.e: The avalanche bulletin shows the current danger. Anyone going away from the secured pistes uses it to plan their trip in advance.
93708.m: Read the avalanche bulletin before every trip in the snow.

93709.q: Which colour is used for avalanche danger level 1, “low”?
93709.e: The levels are shown in colours from green through yellow and orange to red. Green stands for low danger.

93710.q: At which danger levels do most fatal avalanche accidents involving winter sports enthusiasts happen?
93710.e: At these middle levels, many people are out in the mountains, and the danger is often underestimated. When the danger is very high, most people stay at home.
93710.m: Never underestimate moderate and considerable avalanche danger.

93711.q: Which avalanche problem does the bulletin mention when the snow cover is soaked and weakened by warmth or rain?
93711.e: Water weakens the bonds between snow grains. That is why the danger of wet snow avalanches often rises during the day and in spring.
93711.m: Soaked snow leads to the avalanche problem wet snow.

93712.q: Besides the danger level, what information about the danger spots does the avalanche bulletin contain?
93712.e: The bulletin shows at which altitudes and on which slope directions the danger is especially high. This lets you avoid dangerous slopes.
93712.m: The bulletin gives the altitude and slope direction of the danger spots.

93713.q: From what steepness does a slope count as a steep slope in the avalanche bulletin?
93713.e: A slope steeper than about 30 degrees counts as a steep slope. From this steepness, slab avalanches can break loose.
