93713.m: Steep slopes are steeper than about 30 degrees.

93714.q: What is a rockfall net on a rock face for?
a: It keeps birds away from the rock
93714.e: Rockfall nets are stretched between posts and the rock. They catch stones and boulders before they hit roads or houses.

93715.q: What material are modern rockfall nets usually made of?
93715.e: The nets are woven from very strong steel wire. They have to withstand enormous forces from falling boulders.
93715.m: Rockfall nets are made of high-strength steel wire.

93716.q: What else absorbs the force of a stone hitting a rockfall barrier?
93716.e: Braking elements are built into the supporting cables and change shape on impact. This slowly takes away the energy of the movement.
93716.m: Braking elements absorb the energy of the impact.

93717.q: In which unit is the impact energy a rockfall net can absorb given?
93717.e: The energy of a falling stone depends on its mass and speed. It is given in joules or kilojoules.
93717.m: The protective power of a net is measured in kilojoules.

93718.q: What has to happen to a protective net after a rockfall?
a: It has to be emptied and checked
It has to be painted again
It has to be taken down
93718.e: The stones it has caught put further strain on the net. Experts empty it and replace damaged parts.
93718.m: Full rockfall nets have to be emptied.

93719.q: What are the posts and cables of a rockfall net fixed to the slope with?
a: Anchors in the rock or ground
93719.e: Long anchors are drilled into the ground. They carry the forces into the ground when a stone hits.
93719.m: Anchors hold rockfall nets on the slope.

93720.q: What especially often loosens stones in the mountains, which then fall as rockfall?
a: Water freezing and thawing in cracks in the rock
93720.e: Water expands when it freezes and forces cracks in the rock open. When it thaws, stones can then fall out.
93720.m: Frost shattering loosens stones in the rock.

93721.q: Where in Switzerland do you often see rockfall nets?
a: Above roads and railway lines in mountain valleys
Above lakes on the Swiss Plateau
93721.e: On steep rock faces along transport routes there is often a danger of rockfall. Nets protect cars and trains there.
93721.m: Rockfall nets mainly protect transport routes.

93722.q: What does the colour blue mean on a Swiss hazard map?
93722.e: Blue marks areas with medium hazard. Building is only allowed there with conditions, for example with reinforced walls.
93722.m: On the hazard map, blue stands for medium danger.

93723.q: Which colour shows a low hazard on a Swiss hazard map?
93723.e: Yellow areas show a low hazard. People inside buildings are hardly at risk there, but damage to property is possible.
93723.m: On the hazard map, yellow means low danger.

93724.q: Who draws up the hazard maps for natural hazards in Switzerland?
93724.e: The cantons are responsible for the hazard maps, often working with specialist firms. The federal government supports them with guidelines and money.
93724.m: The cantons draw up the hazard maps.

93725.q: Which colour shows a considerable hazard on a Swiss hazard map, where you may not build new houses?
93725.e: Red areas are at high risk. Even people inside buildings are in danger there, so new building is not allowed.
93725.m: On the hazard map, red means considerable danger.

93726.q: What are hazard maps mainly used for in municipalities?
a: For planning where building is allowed
93726.e: Hazard maps feed into land-use planning and zoning plans. This avoids new houses in dangerous areas.
93726.m: Hazard maps help with planning where to build.

93727.q: What does a yellow and white striped area mean on a Swiss hazard map?
a: A remaining hazard from very rare events
93727.e: Yellow and white stripes show areas with a remaining hazard. These are events with a very low probability but possibly a big impact.
93727.m: Yellow and white stripes show a remaining hazard.

93728.q: Which two things are combined on a hazard map?
93728.e: The hazard level comes from how strong and how frequent an event is. A frequent, strong event gives the highest level.
93728.m: Hazard maps combine the strength and frequency of an event.

93729.q: What is the rougher overview map called that only shows where a natural hazard is possible?
93729.e: The hazard indication map shows over large areas where hazards could occur. The more detailed hazard map then grades the hazard.
93729.m: A hazard indication map shows possible hazard areas.

93730.q: Which karst cave on the north shore of Lake Thun can you visit?
93730.e: The St. Beatus Caves lie above Sundlauenen on Lake Thun. Part of the cave system is open to visitors.
93730.m: The St. Beatus Caves are on Lake Thun.

93731.q: Which substance in rainwater makes it able to dissolve limestone?
93731.e: Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide from the air and soil and forms carbonic acid. This slowly dissolves limestone.
93731.m: Carbonic acid in water dissolves limestone.

93732.q: Which large cave system in the Muota valley is one of the longest caves in Europe?
93732.e: The Hölloch in the canton of Schwyz has been surveyed at more than 200 kilometres long. It is the second-longest cave system in Europe (as of 2022).
93732.m: The Hölloch in the Muota valley is one of the longest caves in Europe.

93733.q: What are the dripstones hanging from the ceiling of a karst cave called?
93733.e: Stalactites grow downwards from the ceiling. Stalagmites grow upwards from the floor.
93733.m: Stalactites hang from the cave ceiling.

93734.q: What can form when water dissolves limestone underground over a long time?
93734.e: Water containing carbonic acid slowly dissolves limestone. Over thousands of years this creates cracks, passages and large caves.

93735.q: What often happens to rainwater in karst areas?
a: It seeps away and flows underground
93735.e: In karst areas there are few streams on the surface. The water disappears into cracks and comes out again at karst springs.
93735.m: In karst, water mostly flows underground.

93736.q: Why is drinking water from karst springs especially easy to pollute?
a: It flows fast and is hardly filtered
It contains a lot of salt
93736.e: In cracks and caves, water flows quickly without being filtered through fine layers of soil. Pollutants therefore reach the spring quickly.
93736.m: Karst water is hardly filtered and is sensitive.

93737.q: Which Swiss mountain range consists largely of limestone and has many karst features?
93737.e: The Jura is made mostly of limestone rocks. That is why there are many caves, sinkholes and karst springs there.
93737.m: The Jura is rich in karst features.

93738.q: How does a collapse sinkhole form?
a: The roof of a hollow space caves in
93738.e: Under the surface, water dissolves a hollow space. If the roof becomes too thin, it caves in and a funnel forms.
93738.m: A collapse sinkhole forms when a cave roof caves in.

93739.q: How does a solution sinkhole form?
a: The rock is slowly dissolved from above
The wind blows the sand away
93739.e: In places where a lot of water seeps in, the rock is dissolved more strongly. There the surface gradually sinks into a hollow.
93739.m: Solution sinkholes form slowly through dissolving.

93740.q: In which Swiss region are there especially many sinkholes?
93740.e: The Jura consists mainly of limestone, which water can dissolve. That is why there are very many sinkholes there.
93740.m: There are many sinkholes in the limestone mountains of the Jura.

93741.q: Apart from limestone, in which easily dissolved rock can sinkholes also form?
93741.e: Gypsum dissolves even more easily than limestone. In gypsum areas, sinkholes can therefore form especially quickly.

93742.q: Why can sinkholes be dangerous for houses and roads?
a: The ground can suddenly cave in
93742.e: There can be hollow spaces under a sinkhole. If it caves in, buildings or roads can sink.
93742.m: Above sinkholes, the ground can suddenly cave in.

93743.q: What is a hole called where a stream in karst suddenly disappears into the ground?
93743.e: In a swallow hole, also called a ponor, surface water sinks underground. It is often at the bottom of a sinkhole.
93743.m: In a swallow hole, water disappears into the karst.

93744.q: What does a sinkhole usually look like?
a: Like a funnel in the ground
93744.e: A sinkhole is a round hollow or funnel in the ground. It forms when water dissolves limestone or gypsum.
93744.m: A sinkhole is a funnel in the ground.

93745.q: Roughly how far did the mass of rock from Elm flow across the flat valley floor?
93745.e: After falling freely for several hundred metres, the rock spread out like a stream. It flowed about two kilometres down the valley.
93745.m: The mass of rock from Elm flowed about two kilometres.

93746.q: What is avalanche danger level 4 called?
93746.e: Level 4 is the second-highest level on the scale. Then large avalanches that start on their own are likely.
93746.m: Avalanche danger level 4 is called high.

a: A rock from which metal can be obtained profitably
A pure metal from the ground
93747.e: Ores contain metal compounds in such large amounts that mining them is worthwhile. The metal then has to be extracted chemically.

93748.q: Which ore is the most important raw material for producing aluminium?
93748.e: Bauxite contains a lot of aluminium oxide. First pure aluminium oxide is made from it, and this is then turned into aluminium.

93749.q: Which metal is obtained from haematite and magnetite?
93749.e: Haematite and magnetite are iron oxides. They are among the most important iron ores in the world.
93749.m: Haematite and magnetite are iron ores.

93750.q: What used to be mined at the Gonzen mine near Sargans?
93750.e: The Gonzen was one of the most important iron mines in Switzerland. Today you can visit it as a show mine.
93750.m: Iron ore was mined at the Gonzen near Sargans.

93751.q: Why does mined ore have to be processed first?
a: Because it contains a lot of worthless rock
93751.e: Ore is mixed in with worthless rock. During processing, it is separated from this as far as possible.
93751.m: Ore contains a lot of worthless rock.

93752.q: In what form are metals found in most ores?
a: As chemical compounds, such as oxides
As pure, shiny lumps of metal
93752.e: In nature, most metals are combined with oxygen or sulfur. Only a few, such as gold, are often found native, that is pure.
93752.m: Metals in ores are mostly found as compounds.

93753.q: Which metal is obtained from the ore chalcopyrite?
93753.e: Chalcopyrite is a compound of copper, iron and sulfur. It is the most important copper ore.

93754.q: What is mining ore in a huge open pit at the surface called?
93754.e: If the ore lies close to the surface, it is dug out in large pits. If it lies deep, tunnels are built underground.
93754.m: In open-cast mining, ore is dug out at the surface.

93755.q: How does the liquid iron get out of the blast furnace?
a: It flows out through a hole opened at the bottom
It is scooped out at the top
It is blown out as a powder
93755.e: A hole is opened at the bottom of the blast furnace. The glowing pig iron then flows out along channels. This is called tapping.
93755.m: The liquid iron flows out of the bottom of the blast furnace.

93756.q: Which substance serves as fuel and reducing agent in the blast furnace?
93756.e: Coke is almost pure carbon made from coal. It provides the heat and removes the oxygen from the iron ore.
93756.m: Coke heats the blast furnace and reduces the ore.

93758.q: Why is limestone added to the blast furnace?
a: It binds the waste rock into slag
93758.e: Limestone combines with the waste rock to form slag. This can easily be separated from the iron.
93758.m: Limestone helps remove the waste rock as slag.

93759.q: Why does the liquid slag float on top of the pig iron in the blast furnace?
a: It is hotter than the iron
93759.e: Slag is lighter than liquid iron. So it collects on top and can be drained off separately.
93759.m: Slag is lighter and floats on the iron.

93760.q: Roughly how much carbon does pig iron from the blast furnace contain?
93760.e: Pig iron takes up a lot of carbon in the blast furnace, around 4 per cent. That is why it is brittle and can hardly be forged.
93760.m: Pig iron contains around 4 per cent carbon.

93761.q: What is blown into the bottom of the blast furnace to make the fuel burn fiercely?
93761.e: Hot blast stoves heat air to over 1000 degrees. This hot air is blown into the bottom of the furnace as the “blast”.
93761.m: Hot air fans the fire in the blast furnace.

93762.q: Once it has been started, how long does a blast furnace usually run without a break?
93762.e: Ore, fuel and limestone are constantly filled in at the top, and liquid iron is taken out at the bottom. A blast furnace usually runs for many years until it has to be relined.
93762.m: A blast furnace runs for years without a break.

93763.q: At most, how much carbon does steel contain?
93763.e: Iron with at most about 2 per cent carbon counts as steel. More carbon makes the material brittle, like cast iron.
93763.m: Steel contains at most around 2 per cent carbon.

93764.q: What do you get if you remove a large part of the carbon from pig iron?
93764.e: Pig iron contains a lot of carbon and is brittle. If oxygen is blown onto it, carbon burns away and tough steel forms.
93764.m: Removing carbon turns pig iron into steel.

93765.q: Which metal mainly makes stainless steel rust-free?
93765.e: Stainless steel contains at least about 10.5 per cent chromium. The chromium forms a thin, protective oxide layer.

93766.q: What is steel in Switzerland mainly made from?
93766.e: Iron ore is no longer mined in Switzerland. Steelworks such as the one in Gerlafingen melt down scrap metal and make new steel from it.
93766.m: Swiss steel is made from scrap.

93767.q: How is scrap steel melted in an electric steelworks?
93767.e: Electric arcs with a very high temperature form between graphite electrodes and the scrap. These melt the scrap.
93767.m: Electric arc furnaces melt scrap with electricity.

93768.q: What happens to steel if you heat it strongly and then cool it quickly in water?
a: It becomes as soft as lead
93768.e: Rapid cooling, called quenching, changes the inner structure of the steel. It becomes harder. This process is called hardening.

93769.q: Why is steel an especially good material for recycling?
a: It can be melted down again without losing quality
It turns back into ore when it rusts
93769.e: Scrap steel can be melted down again and again and made into new steel. This saves ore and a lot of energy.
93769.m: Steel can be recycled again and again.

93770.q: What is the steel called that is placed inside concrete structures to make them strong under tension?
93770.e: Concrete copes well with pressure but cracks under tension. Steel bars placed inside, the reinforcement, take up the pulling forces.
93770.m: Reinforcing steel makes concrete strong under tension.

93771.q: Which metal is today obtained almost only by molten salt electrolysis?
93771.e: Aluminium is so reactive that it cannot be reduced with carbon. It is obtained with electricity from molten aluminium oxide.
93771.m: Aluminium is obtained by molten salt electrolysis.

93772.q: From which ore is aluminium obtained?
93772.e: Bauxite is a reddish rock with a lot of aluminium oxide. Pure aluminium oxide is obtained from it first, and then the metal is made using electricity.

93774.q: At which pole does the aluminium collect in molten salt electrolysis?
93774.e: Aluminium ions are positively charged. They move to the negative pole, the cathode, and become metal there.
93774.m: Aluminium forms at the negative pole.

93775.q: What are the anodes made of in aluminium electrolysis, which are slowly used up in the process?
93775.e: The carbon anodes react with the oxygen produced to form carbon dioxide. So they have to be replaced regularly.
93775.m: The carbon anodes burn away during electrolysis.

93776.q: Why does making new aluminium use so much energy?
a: The electrolysis needs a huge amount of electricity
Aluminium must be made in a vacuum
You need a lot of gold for it
93776.e: For one kilogram of aluminium, electrolysis needs over ten kilowatt hours of electricity. Recycling needs only a small part of that.
93776.m: New aluminium uses a huge amount of electricity.

93777.q: What does “molten salt” mean in the term molten salt electrolysis?
a: The substance is melted instead of dissolved in water
The metal is cooled with water
93777.e: In this electrolysis, the starting compound is melted. In a water solution, hydrogen would form instead of aluminium.
93777.m: In molten salt electrolysis, a melt is split up.

93778.q: Which metal is obtained by electrolysis of molten table salt?
93778.e: Table salt is sodium chloride. In the electrolysis of the melt, sodium forms at the negative pole and chlorine at the positive pole.
93778.m: Sodium is obtained from molten table salt.

93779.q: In which canton is Chippis, with its well-known aluminium works?
93779.e: Chippis lies near Sierre in the Rhône valley. The aluminium works have shaped the village for over a hundred years.
93779.m: The Chippis aluminium works are in Valais.

93780.q: From which raw material is aluminium obtained?
93780.e: Bauxite is a reddish rock with a lot of aluminium oxide. Aluminium is made from it in several steps.

93781.q: Why was an aluminium works built in a mountain valley in Valais, as at Chippis?
a: Because of water power for lots of electricity
Because of the many bauxite mines there
93781.e: Aluminium electrolysis needs an enormous amount of electricity. The mountain streams of Valais supplied it cheaply from water power.
93781.m: Water power made Valais attractive for aluminium works.

93782.q: Why is aluminium popular for vehicles and aircraft?
a: It is light and hardly corrodes
93782.e: Aluminium has a much lower density than steel. It also protects itself from corrosion with a thin oxide layer.
93782.m: Aluminium is light and hardly corrodes.

93783.q: Which process uses electric current to obtain aluminium?
93783.e: In electrolysis, electric current separates the aluminium from its compound. This needs a lot of electricity.

93784.q: Which things made of aluminium does almost every child know?
93784.e: Aluminium can easily be rolled into thin sheets and foils. Drinks cans and kitchen foil, for example, are made from it.
93784.m: Cans and kitchen foil are made of aluminium.

93785.q: Why is it especially worthwhile to recycle aluminium?
a: It needs much less energy than making it new
New aluminium can no longer be made
93785.e: Making it from bauxite needs an enormous amount of electricity. Melting down old aluminium saves most of this energy.
93785.m: Recycling aluminium saves a lot of energy.

93786.q: On which large river does Chippis lie?
93786.e: Chippis lies on the left bank of the Rhône. The Navisence from the Val d’Anniviers also flows into it there.

93787.q: What do you do when electroplating?
a: Coat an object with metal using electricity
93787.e: In electroplating, metal ions move from a solution onto the workpiece. There they form a thin layer of metal.

93788.q: In electroplating, which pole is the object to be coated connected to?
93788.e: The metal ions in the solution are positively charged. They are attracted by the negative pole and settle there as metal.
93788.m: In electroplating, the workpiece hangs on the negative pole.

93789.q: What do you absolutely need for electroplating?
93789.e: Only the current makes the metal ions move to the workpiece. There they settle as a thin layer of metal.
93789.m: Electroplating only works with electric current.

93790.q: What is electroplating with chromium called, for example on shiny taps?
93790.e: A layer of chromium is hard, shiny and resists corrosion. That is why many taps and fittings are chrome-plated.

93791.q: What must be dissolved in the liquid of an electroplating bath for a layer of silver to form?
93791.e: The solution contains a silver salt. The positively charged silver ions become silver metal on the workpiece.
93791.m: For a silver layer, the bath needs silver ions.

93792.q: In electroplating, what often happens to an anode made of the coating metal?
93792.e: At the positive pole, metal atoms go into solution as ions. This supplies the metal that settles on the workpiece.
93792.m: In electroplating, the metal anode supplies new ions.

93793.q: Why is cheap jewellery often gold-plated instead of made of pure gold?
a: A thin layer of gold is much cheaper
Gold is too light for jewellery
93793.e: In gold plating, only a wafer-thin layer of gold is applied. It looks like gold but uses very little of it.

93794.q: Apart from making things look nicer, what is electroplating often used for?
93794.e: A layer of metal can protect the base material from rust. Many screws, for example, are zinc-plated.
93794.m: Electroplated layers often protect against corrosion.

93795.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a battery when it powers a device?
93795.e: Chemical reactions take place in the battery in which electrons flow. This produces electric current.
93795.m: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy.

93796.q: Which Italian scientist built the first battery around 1800?
93796.e: Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with soaked cardboard in between. This voltaic pile was the first to supply a steady current.
93796.m: Alessandro Volta built the first battery around 1800.

93797.q: What voltage does an ordinary AA alkaline battery have?
93797.e: An alkaline manganese cell supplies 1.5 volts. For 9 volts, several cells are connected together in one block.

93798.q: Which rechargeable batteries are in most mobile phones and electric cars today?
93798.e: Lithium-ion batteries store a lot of energy for little weight. That is why they are used in mobile phones, laptops and electric cars.
93798.m: Mobile phones mostly run on lithium-ion batteries.

93799.q: What rule applies in Switzerland to shops that sell batteries?
a: They must take back used batteries free of charge
They may only sell rechargeable batteries
They must not take back batteries
93799.e: In Switzerland, shops are obliged to take batteries back. Disposal is paid for by an advance fee when you buy them.
93799.m: You take used batteries back to the shop.

93800.q: Why don’t old batteries belong in the household rubbish?
a: They contain pollutants and valuable metals
They are too heavy for the rubbish bag
They dissolve in the rubbish at once
They charge up again in the rubbish
93800.e: Batteries can contain poisonous substances that harm the environment. Also, metals such as zinc, nickel or lithium can be recovered.
93800.m: Batteries belong at the collection point.

93801.q: What is the battery pole called from which electrons flow into the circuit when it discharges?
93801.e: At the negative pole, electrons are released by the chemical reaction. They flow through the device to the positive pole.
93801.m: Electrons flow from the negative to the positive pole.

93802.q: Which two metals are often pushed into a lemon to build a lemon battery?
93802.e: You need two different metals as electrodes. Copper and zinc work well because they differ in how reactive they are.
93802.m: For a lemon battery you need copper and zinc.

93803.q: What does the lemon juice do in a lemon battery?
a: It conducts the ions as an electrolyte
It supplies all the energy as sugar
It insulates the metals from each other
93803.e: The sour juice contains dissolved ions and so completes the circuit inside the battery. Without an electrolyte, no current flows.
93803.m: The lemon juice acts as the electrolyte in the battery.

93804.q: Why does a light bulb usually not light up with a single lemon battery?
a: The voltage and current are too small
Lemon juice does not conduct electricity at all
93804.e: A lemon supplies just under 1 volt and only a very small current. That is not enough for a light bulb.
93804.m: A single lemon supplies too little current for a light bulb.

93805.q: How do you increase the voltage when you use several lemon batteries?
a: You put them in the fridge
93805.e: In a series circuit, the copper of one lemon is connected to the zinc of the next. The voltages add up.
93805.m: Lemons connected in series give more voltage.

93806.q: Which metal is the negative pole in a lemon battery?
93806.e: Zinc is more reactive than copper and gives up electrons more easily. It slowly dissolves and forms the negative pole.
93806.m: In a lemon battery, zinc is the negative pole.

93807.q: How many lemons of about 0.9 volts each do you need at least in series for 2.5 volts?
93807.e: Two lemons give 2 times 0.9 volts, so 1.8 volts, which is too little. Three lemons give 3 times 0.9 volts, so 2.7 volts.
93807.m: Three lemons in series supply about 2.7 volts.

93808.q: What can you use to check whether a lemon battery is supplying voltage?
93808.e: A voltmeter measures the electrical voltage between the two metals. You connect it to the copper and the zinc.
93808.m: A voltmeter measures the voltage of the lemon battery.

93809.q: With which other fruit or vegetable does this kind of battery also work?
93809.e: Potatoes and apples also contain water with dissolved ions. So they can serve as an electrolyte too.
93809.m: You can also build a battery with a potato.

93810.q: What makes a metal a precious metal?
a: It hardly reacts with air and water
It is as light as polystyrene
93810.e: Precious metals such as gold and platinum resist corrosion very well. They do not rust and keep their shine.
93810.m: Precious metals hardly react with air and water.

93811.q: Which of these metals is a precious metal?
93811.e: Platinum, like gold and silver, is a precious metal. Iron, aluminium and zinc are base metals.

93812.q: What is the chemical symbol for silver?
93812.e: The symbol Ag comes from the Latin word “argentum” for silver. Si stands for silicon.

93813.q: How much pure gold does 18-carat gold contain?
93813.e: Pure gold is 24 carat. 18 divided by 24 gives 0.75, so 75 per cent gold.
93813.m: 18 carat means three quarters pure gold.

93814.q: What role does Switzerland play in the world gold trade?
a: A large share of the gold is refined here
It has the biggest gold mines
Gold is made from lead here
93814.e: Several large gold refineries, mainly in Ticino, purify gold from all over the world. That makes Switzerland a centre of the gold trade.
93814.m: A lot of gold is refined in Switzerland.

93815.q: In which part of a car are precious metals such as palladium and rhodium used?
93815.e: In the catalytic converter, palladium and rhodium help turn poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances. They are not used up themselves.

93816.q: Which mixture of two acids can even dissolve gold?
93816.e: Aqua regia, or “royal water”, is a mixture of hydrochloric acid and nitric acid. It dissolves gold, which otherwise can hardly be attacked.

93817.q: Why does silver cutlery go dark over time?
a: It reacts with sulfur compounds in the air
It takes on colour from food
93817.e: Silver forms a dark layer of silver sulfide with sulfur compounds. This can be polished off again.
93817.m: Silver tarnishes because of sulfur compounds.

93818.q: Which two substances does iron need in order to rust?
93818.e: Iron only rusts when moisture and oxygen are both present. In dry air it hardly rusts.
93818.m: Iron rusts with water and oxygen.

93819.q: What is the greenish layer called that forms on copper roofs over time and protects the copper?
93819.e: Copper slowly reacts with substances in the air. This produces a green patina that protects the metal beneath.
93819.m: The green patina protects copper roofs.

93820.q: What is a sacrificial anode on a ship’s hull?
a: A piece of more reactive metal that corrodes instead of the hull
93820.e: A more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium is connected to the steel hull. It dissolves first and so protects the steel.
93820.m: A sacrificial anode corrodes instead of the steel.

93821.q: What is a simple way to protect bare tools from rust?
a: With a thin film of oil
93821.e: A film of oil stops water and oxygen reaching the iron. That is why tools and bicycle chains are oiled.
93821.m: A film of oil protects iron from rust.

93822.q: Why doesn’t aluminium rust right through, even though it is a base metal?
a: A thin oxide layer protects it
Aluminium is always covered with paint
93822.e: In air, a thin, dense oxide layer forms on aluminium straight away. It protects the metal beneath from further corrosion.
93822.m: A thin oxide layer protects aluminium.

93823.q: Which simple method protects an iron garden gate from rust?
93823.e: The paint forms a layer that keeps water and oxygen away from the iron. If it is damaged, rust can form there.
93823.m: Anti-rust paint keeps water and oxygen away from iron.

93824.q: Why is rust on iron so harmful, while the layer on aluminium protects it?
a: Rust is loose and flakes off
93824.e: Rust is porous and lets water and air keep reaching the iron. So the corrosion eats deeper and deeper.
93824.m: Loose rust does not protect the iron.

a: The destruction of a metal by chemical reaction with its surroundings
The melting of a metal in a furnace
93825.e: Corrosion is a chemical reaction of the metal with substances from its surroundings, such as oxygen and water. Rusting is the corrosion of iron.
93825.m: Corrosion is chemical attack on metals.

a: Steel parts are dipped in liquid zinc
93826.e: The steel parts are dipped in a bath of molten zinc. Afterwards they are covered with a firm layer of zinc.
93826.m: In hot-dip galvanising, steel is dipped in liquid zinc.

93827.q: Roughly how hot is a zinc bath in hot-dip galvanising?
93827.e: Zinc melts at around 420 degrees. So the bath is kept at about 450 degrees.
93827.m: A zinc bath is around 450 degrees hot.

93828.q: Why does a zinc layer still protect the steel even when it is scratched?
a: Zinc is more reactive and corrodes first
93828.e: Zinc gives up electrons more easily than iron. So at a scratch the zinc corrodes first, and the steel next to it stays protected.
93828.m: Zinc protects steel even at scratches.

93829.q: Which parts along Swiss roads are typically hot-dip galvanised?
93829.e: Crash barriers stand outdoors all year and get splashed with salt water in winter. The zinc layer reliably protects them from rust.

93830.q: What is done to steel parts before hot-dip galvanising so that the zinc sticks well?
93830.e: In pickling, acid removes rust and scale from the surface. Zinc only bonds well to clean steel.
93830.m: Before galvanising, the steel is pickled.

93831.q: What forms at the boundary between steel and zinc in hot-dip galvanising?
93831.e: In the hot bath, iron and zinc combine at the surface. This makes the layer stick very firmly to the steel.
93831.m: Hot-dip galvanising forms an iron-zinc alloy.

93832.q: What does freshly hot-dip galvanised steel often look like?
a: Shiny silver with a crystal pattern
93832.e: The zinc layer shines silver and often shows a pattern of zinc crystals. Over time it turns dull grey.

93833.q: Which large pharmaceutical company has its headquarters in Basel?
93833.e: Novartis is one of the largest pharmaceutical companies in the world and is based in Basel. Nestlé is based in Vevey, Swatch in Biel and Swisscom in Bern.
93833.m: Novartis has its headquarters in Basel.

93834.q: What happened on 1 November 1986 at Schweizerhalle near Basel?
a: A chemical warehouse burnt down and poisoned the Rhine
A nuclear power station was opened
A new bridge over the Rhine collapsed
93834.e: When a Sandoz warehouse caught fire, firefighting water carrying chemicals flowed into the river. Fish and other animals died along many kilometres.
93834.m: The Schweizerhalle fire in 1986 caused a huge fish kill.

93835.q: What do the Basel companies Roche and Novartis mainly make?
93835.e: Roche and Novartis are among the largest pharmaceutical companies in the world. They develop and sell medicines.
93835.m: Basel is a centre of the pharmaceutical industry.

93836.q: Which river was important to Basel’s chemical industry as a transport route and water source?
93836.e: Raw materials could be delivered by ship along the Rhine. The factories also needed a lot of water.
93836.m: The Rhine was central to Basel’s chemical industry.

93837.q: What was DDT, discovered in Basel, used for?
93837.e: In 1939 it was discovered in Basel that DDT kills insects. Later it was banned in many countries because of the harm it does to the environment.

93838.q: What does the Basel company Syngenta mainly make?
93838.e: Syngenta is an agrochemical company. It sells products against pests and seeds for farming.

93839.q: Which building in Basel, at 205 metres, is the tallest in Switzerland (as of 2025)?
93839.e: The Roche Tower Building 2 was completed in 2022 and is 205 metres tall. It towers over the neighbouring Building 1, which is 178 metres.
93839.m: Switzerland’s tallest tower belongs to Roche in Basel.

93840.q: How long does hot-dip galvanising typically protect steel outdoors?
93840.e: The zinc layer wears away only very slowly. Depending on the surroundings, the protection often lasts from 25 to over 50 years.
93840.m: Hot-dip galvanising protects steel for decades.

93841.q: What does the figure 999.9 on a gold bar mean?
a: It is 999.9 parts per thousand gold
It was made in the year 999
93841.e: The number gives the purity in thousandths. 999.9 means almost pure gold.
93841.m: A bar marked 999.9 is almost pure gold.

93842.q: What did many Basel chemical companies start out making in the 19th century?
93842.e: Basel’s silk ribbon industry needed a lot of colours. So the first chemical companies made artificial dyes.
93842.m: Basel’s chemical industry began with dyes.

93843.q: What is slag from the blast furnace often used for afterwards?
a: As a building material, for example for cement
93843.e: Cooled blast furnace slag is a stone-like material. It is used in road building and to make cement.
93843.m: Blast furnace slag is used as a building material.

93844.q: Why must a workpiece be thoroughly cleaned and degreased before electroplating?
a: So that the metal layer sticks well
93844.e: Grease and dirt stop the metal settling directly on the surface. Otherwise the layer flakes off later.
93844.m: An electroplated layer only sticks to clean surfaces.

94238.q: Where in the nose are the cells that recognise smells?
a: Right at the top of the nose
At the tip of the nose
94238.e: The smell cells are in the lining right at the top of the nasal cavity. That is why you sniff, to pull air upwards.
94238.m: The smell cells are at the top of the nose.

94239.q: Where do the smell cells send their message?
94239.e: The smell cells send signals along nerves to the brain. Only there do we notice what we smell.
94239.m: The brain recognises what the nose smells.

94240.q: Which animal can smell much better than a person?
94240.e: Dogs have many more smell cells than people. That is why they can sniff out trails.
94240.m: Dogs have a very fine nose.

94241.q: What do avalanche dogs in Switzerland search for with their noses?
94241.e: Avalanche dogs smell people lying under the snow. That way they help with rescues in the mountains.
94241.m: Avalanche dogs find buried people with their noses.

94242.q: What does a snake do with its forked tongue?
94242.e: The snake catches scent particles from the air with its tongue. A special organ in its mouth then recognises the smell.
94242.m: Snakes smell with the help of their tongue.
